Name: categorical_warping_llm
Title: Categorical Warping: Can an Ad-Hoc Label Scheme Causally Reshape What an LLM Can Discriminate?
Short Hypothesis: A core Whorfian claim is that the categories a language provides warp perception of within-category vs. across-category differences (compression within, expansion across a boundary). We hypothesize that this warping is a dynamic, controllable property of a trained LLM: introducing a novel, ad-hoc labeling scheme in-context causally compresses the model's internal representation of items sharing a new label and expands the gap across new label boundaries, and that this induced geometric warp measurably changes the model's fine-grained discrimination and relational reasoning on the very same items — even when the labels are meaningless nonce words with no pretraining semantics.
Related Work: Cognitive science establishes categorical perception and label-feedback effects, framing them as inference under uncertainty (Cibelli/Regier, 2016/2017; Lupyan, 2012). A deep-learning account (2021) shows fine- vs coarse-grained labels distort semantic geometry, but by *training* a network on those labels. In LLMs, BICAUSE (2025) shows language internalizes causal-order biases and Sapir-Whorf-reproduction studies (2025) probe behavioral alignment; 'When Less Language is More' (2025) ablates language components to help reasoning; number-geometry work (2025/2026) characterizes fixed relational structure. All existing LLM work is observational on *pretrained* vocabularies (color, number, causal order) or removes language rather than adding new categories. No prior work asks whether an *arbitrary, in-context ad-hoc labeling scheme* can causally rewarp an already-trained model's discrimination geometry within a single forward pass, dissociates this from pretrained label semantics using nonce labels, or links the induced geometric warp to changes in downstream relational reasoning. We turn linguistic relativity into a controllable, mechanistic intervention.
Abstract: Linguistic relativity predicts that the category boundaries a language supplies warp cognition: items sharing a label are perceived as more similar (within-category compression) and items across a boundary as more different (across-category expansion). Prior LLM studies test this observationally on pretrained vocabularies (color, causal order). We ask a sharper, causal question: can an arbitrary labeling scheme, introduced only in-context, dynamically rewarp what an already-trained LLM can discriminate and reason about? We construct continuous, controllable stimulus spaces (e.g., numeric magnitudes, HSL colors described in text, feature-vector 'creatures') and impose novel partitions via labels, including nonce labels with no pretraining meaning. Measuring representational distances in hidden states, we test whether presenting a labeling scheme compresses same-label pairs and expands different-label pairs relative to a no-label baseline, and whether the boundary location tracks the arbitrary partition we chose rather than any pretrained structure. We then test behavioral consequences: does the induced warp make the model worse at fine within-category discrimination and better/worse at across-boundary comparisons on identical items? Finally, we test the mechanism causally: we isolate a 'label-warp direction' and steer along it to reproduce or cancel the geometric warp and its behavioral signature, and compare it to an inference-time analog of coarse vs. fine labeling pressure. Across several open-weight models we quantify the compression/expansion index, boundary-placement fidelity to arbitrary partitions, the label-warp-to-behavior correlation, and steering controllability. This reframes linguistic relativity in LLMs from a fixed bias into a controllable, mechanistically-grounded lever on machine discrimination.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (Setup - Continuous stimulus spaces and label schemes): Prerequisite. Data: three built spaces with ground-truth metric structure - (a) integer magnitudes 1-100, (b) colors specified as HSL text (hue 0-360), (c) synthetic 'creatures' defined by 4 continuous features; for each we prepare no-label, real-word-label, and nonce-word-label (e.g., 'blicket','dax') conditions plus multiple arbitrary boundary placements so a given item pair is same-label under one scheme and different-label under another, and a scrambled-label control (labels assigned randomly to items). ~600 item pairs per space, length/format-matched across conditions. Decisive metric first: verification that schemes are format-matched and that swapped partitions truly cross-classify the same pairs. Convincing result: every target pair appears as both same-label and different-label across schemes; else pairs are regenerated. Indecision/negative bands are design checks, not hypotheses.

Experiment 2 (H1 - Ad-hoc labels causally rewarp discrimination geometry, boundary follows the imposed partition, even for nonce labels): The central Whorfian-warp test. Data: the pairs above, used as is. Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, and a larger model (Qwen2.5-14B) for scale, all weights frozen. We prompt with the labeling scheme in-context, present item pairs, and extract each item's hidden state at matched positions per layer. Systems compared: no-label baseline, real-word labels, nonce labels, swapped arbitrary partitions, coarse vs. fine schemes, and scrambled-label control. Decisive metric first: the same_label coefficient in a regression of representational distance on true metric gap and a same-label indicator (distance ~ metric_gap + same_label + (1|layer) + (1|model)) - the Compression-Expansion Index. Convincing result: a significant negative same_label coefficient (within-label compression) with boundary-aligned across-label expansion, present even for nonce labels, that REVERSES when the same items are re-partitioned by a different arbitrary scheme (sign flip CI excluding zero), while the scrambled-label control shows no warp; coarse schemes converge items and fine schemes differentiate them, matching the labeling-geometry prediction. Indecision band: same_label coefficient CI spanning zero, or a warp that does not follow the swapped partition - in-context labels do not reliably rewarp geometry, so category structure looks rigidly pretrained rather than dynamically Whorfian. Negative result (positive same_label coefficient, or nonce labels show no effect while only real words do): no genuine categorical warp beyond lexical priming, refuting the causal claim.

Experiment 3 (H2 - The warp changes behavior and behavior tracks geometry): Tests downstream consequences. Data: the same items rendered as (i) fine within-category discrimination (which of two same-label items is larger/redder?), (ii) across-boundary comparison, (iii) odd-one-out and analogy tasks; item spacing calibrated to mid-range difficulty to avoid ceiling/floor. Models: same four, frozen; 5 samples/item, temperature 0.7, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: imposed scheme vs. no-label baseline. Decisive metric first: change in within-category discrimination accuracy under an imposed scheme; secondary: the mixed-effects correlation between per-pair behavioral change and per-pair measured geometric warp. Convincing result: within-category discrimination degrades and across-boundary judgments shift under an imposed scheme (accuracy-change CI excluding zero), and per-pair behavioral change correlates with geometric warp (Spearman CI excluding zero). Indecision band: behavioral-change CI spanning zero while geometry warps - the geometric warp has no behavioral teeth, so the phenomenon is representational-only. Negative result (no behavioral change or negative geometry-behavior correlation): warp does not shape discrimination.

Experiment 4 (H3 - A label-warp direction steers the warp and its behavior on and off): Tests causal controllability. Data: contrast pairs (same items, labeled vs. unlabeled) to compute a mid-layer difference-in-means 'label-warp direction'; 400 held-out pairs per space for evaluation. Models: same four, frozen; steering strength tuned on a dev split, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: +direction steering (induce warp without presenting labels), -direction steering (cancel a presented scheme's warp), random-direction steering (matched norm), and no-steer. Decisive metric first: fraction of the Compression-Expansion Index reproduced (by +steering) or cancelled (by -steering) relative to the label-presentation effect; secondary: matched fraction of the behavioral discrimination change. Convincing result: +steering reproduces and -steering cancels a substantial share of both the geometric and behavioral warp, significantly beyond random-direction steering (difference CI excluding zero). Indecision band: recovered/cancelled fraction under 20% and within the random-direction control's CI - the warp is not captured by a single steerable direction. Negative result (steering has no effect or destroys general output): no isolable causal mechanism. All quantities are planned evidence with bootstrap CIs over pairs, seeds, and models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) In-context labels may bias representations trivially via lexical priming rather than genuine categorical warping; mitigated by nonce labels, swapped arbitrary partitions of identical items, and scrambled-label controls that isolate the categorical (boundary-structured) component. (2) Hidden-state distances may reflect the prompt's surface tokens rather than the concept; we extract item representations at matched positions and control for true metric gap. (3) Warp effects may be small or layer-specific; we report multiple layers, models, and effect sizes with bootstrap CIs. (4) Behavioral discrimination tasks could be at ceiling/floor for some spaces; we calibrate item spacing to mid-range difficulty. (5) The label-warp direction may entangle with generic content shifts; random-direction and cancellation controls address this. (6) A null result (arbitrary in-context labels do not warp geometry) is itself informative, indicating LLM category structure is rigidly pretrained rather than dynamically Whorfian.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims needing novelty are: (1) arbitrary in-context labels can causally induce within-category compression and across-boundary expansion in a pretrained LLM within a single forward pass; (2) this holds for nonce labels, dissociating the effect from pretrained label semantics; (3) the induced boundary tracks an imposed partition and reverses under repartition of the same items; (4) the geometric warp changes downstream discrimination/relational reasoning on the same stimuli; (5) there exists a steerable 'label-warp direction' that can induce or cancel the effect. Relative to the search summary, categorical warping in hidden states is already established in LLMs, and in-context compression/expansion dynamics are also known. The actual defendable delta is the causal arbitrary-partition manipulation with nonce labels, repartition reversal, and steering. That is non-trivial and potentially novel if it works, but the very close 2026 digit-count paper already finds warping mainly at structural/format boundaries and not semantically arbitrary ones, which directly weakens the central surprise. So the proposal is novel in mechanism/setting/manipulation rather than in the broad phenomenon, with meaningful but narrowed originality.

impact.reasoning: The phenomenon under study is whether ad-hoc in-context labels can transiently reshape an LLM's discrimination geometry and reasoning over the same items. The audience includes interpretability, in-context learning, controllability, and LLM-cognition researchers. If true, the strongest case is that language prompts would not merely query latent structure but dynamically reconfigure representational discrimination, implying a new lever for steering and a stronger form of prompt-induced cognition. This could matter for theory of ICL, prompt design, and representation steering. The 'so what?' test is moderately favorable: a strong positive result with nonce labels, reversal, and behavioral consequences would change how researchers think about prompt effects and controllability; a null result would also matter by supporting rigidity of pretrained category structure, especially given prior mixed evidence. Real-world application impact is less immediate than scientific impact, and uptake depends heavily on whether the effect is robust beyond toy stimulus spaces.

review.reasoning: The proposal is testable and better specified than average, with concrete domains, controls, multiple model families, repartition manipulations, and a causal steering experiment. The hypotheses are reasonably falsifiable. However, there are important technical gaps. Related work positioning is incomplete relative to the closest prior art in the search summary, especially the paper showing CP effects at structural but not semantic boundaries; omitting that makes the proposal overclaim novelty and understate risk. The central construct 'categorical warp' risks conflation with token/position/lexical priming, generic ICL compression, or induced task heuristics. The current regression sketch is too thin to isolate these confounds. The behavior experiments are underspecified: exact prompting, response metrics, ceiling/floor avoidance, and how to disentangle strategic use of labels from changed item representation are not yet clear. The steering claim is ambitious and likely fragile; a difference-in-means direction may capture label token content or task state rather than a reusable warp subspace. Still, if executed with stronger controls and more precise analysis, this could be serious workshop/conference material and possibly venue-worthy depending on effect strength.

Name: private_speech_zpd
Title: Chain-of-Thought as Private Speech: Testing the Vygotskian Zone of Proximal Development in LLM Reasoning
Short Hypothesis: An LLM's chain-of-thought behaves like children's private (self-directed) speech: its amount follows an inverted-U over task difficulty (peaking at moderate difficulty), it shifts from overt to abbreviated/covert form as competence rises, and — the key falsifiable claim — it is beneficial only inside a 'zone of proximal development' (moderate difficulty), while being wasteful overhead on easy items and actively interfering on already-mastered ones, so reasoning should be self-regulated by difficulty rather than applied uniformly.
Related Work: Developmental psychology (Vygotsky; Fernyhough) establishes that private speech follows a developmental trajectory: it appears most at intermediate task difficulty, peaks and then internalizes/abbreviates as skill grows, forming a zone of proximal development. Recent cross-domain work shows GPT-4o produces child-like private speech (Private speech: similarities between an LLM and children, 2026) and reviews inner speech as a cognitive tool (Alderson-Day & Fernyhough, 2023). In ML, 'Scaling Competence, Shrinking Reasoning' (2025) reports reasoning-token length rises then falls over fine-tuning (an inverted-U over TRAINING), latent-reasoning work (Coconut, 2024) internalizes CoT, and 'Why think step by step?' (2023) explains WHEN reasoning helps via data locality. However, no prior work (a) tests the inverted-U of reasoning emission as a function of per-item DIFFICULTY (a within-model, inference-time developmental law, not a training-time one), (b) tests the Vygotskian ZPD prediction that forced reasoning hurts at difficulty extremes, or (c) links overt-to-covert abbreviation of CoT to per-item competence. We turn the developmental theory of private speech into concrete, falsifiable predictions about self-regulated inference-time reasoning.
Abstract: Children talk to themselves while solving hard problems, and developmental psychology gives a precise account of this 'private speech': its quantity follows an inverted-U over task difficulty, it is concentrated in a learner's zone of proximal development (ZPD), and it becomes abbreviated and covert as competence grows. We propose that an LLM's chain-of-thought (CoT) is a computational analog of private speech and obeys the same developmental laws — at inference time and per item, not merely over training. We make three falsifiable predictions. (1) Emission: when allowed to reason freely, a model's spontaneous CoT length forms an inverted-U over graded difficulty, peaking at intermediate difficulty rather than rising monotonically. (2) ZPD benefit: the accuracy gain from CoT over direct answering is largest at intermediate difficulty and small or negative at the extremes — forced reasoning is wasteful overhead on trivial items and can interfere on already-mastered items. (3) Abbreviation: as items move from moderate toward mastered, spontaneous CoT compresses (shorter, more elliptical), mirroring overt-to-covert internalization. We test these across difficulty-graded arithmetic, logic, and word-problem suites on several open-weight models with controlled per-item difficulty calibration. We then add a lightweight mechanistic component: a probe that reads a model's own competence/difficulty estimate from early hidden states, used to build a self-regulated 'ZPD-gated' reasoning controller that spends CoT only where it helps, and compare it to always-CoT and never-CoT baselines on accuracy and token cost. Confirming these predictions reframes CoT as difficulty-self-regulated private speech and yields a principled, training-free efficiency lever.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (Setup - Difficulty-graded task suites with calibrated per-item difficulty): Prerequisite. Data: built suites of ~300 items each - multi-digit arithmetic (operand size/carry count as the surface difficulty axis), propositional/multi-hop logic (number of inference steps), and GSM-style word problems (number of reasoning steps); 900 items. Per-item empirical difficulty = direct-answer error rate estimated from 20 samples/item per model, giving a continuous difficulty score independent of the surface axis. Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, all weights frozen, seeds 0/1/2. Decisive metric first: spread and reliability (split-half) of the calibrated difficulty score. Convincing result: difficulty spans a wide range with split-half reliability >=0.7, and is not confounded with item length (|correlation| < 0.3). Indecision band: reliability 0.5-0.7 - we increase samples/item. Negative result (difficulty not separable from length): the calibration is unusable and we redesign items.

Experiment 2 (H1 - Spontaneous reasoning emission forms an inverted-U over difficulty): Tests the emission law. Data: the 900 items, elicited under a permissive prompt that neither forbids nor mandates chain-of-thought. Models: same four, frozen. Systems compared: a quadratic vs. a monotonic model of CoT length over difficulty. Decisive metric first: the sign and significance of the quadratic coefficient in length ~ difficulty + difficulty^2 + (1|model) + (1|item), plus AIC/BIC preference of the quadratic over the monotonic model. Convincing result: a significant negative quadratic term (95% CI excluding zero) with an interior peak at intermediate difficulty, and AIC/BIC favoring the quadratic, in at least 3 of 4 models. Indecision band: quadratic-term CI spanning zero but AIC/BIC roughly tied - emission is not clearly inverted-U (could be monotone or flat), so the private-speech emission law is unsupported at this resolution. Negative result (positive quadratic or strictly monotone increasing length): reasoning emission does not follow the developmental inverted-U.

Experiment 3 (H2 - CoT benefit is a zone-of-proximal-development function of difficulty): Tests the ZPD-benefit claim. Data: the 900 items, each evaluated under forced-direct (no CoT), forced-CoT, and free conditions; 10 samples/condition/item. Models: same four, frozen. Decisive metric first: the per-item CoT benefit = accuracy(CoT) - accuracy(direct), fitted as benefit ~ difficulty + difficulty^2. Convincing result: benefit peaks at intermediate difficulty, is within +/-2 points of zero on easy items, and is significantly negative (interference) on a subset of already-mastered-but-nontrivial items (negative-benefit CI excluding zero), with qualitative confirmation that forced CoT introduces errors the direct answer avoided. Indecision band: benefit rises monotonically with difficulty with no interior peak and no negative region (quadratic CI spanning zero) - CoT is simply more useful on harder items, the ordinary view, and the distinctive ZPD prediction (harm at extremes) fails. Negative result (benefit flat or U-shaped): no ZPD structure.

Experiment 4 (H3 - CoT abbreviates as items approach mastery): Tests the internalization prediction. Data: within a fixed surface-difficulty band, items split into 'newly-in-ZPD' vs. 'approaching-mastery' by per-item direct accuracy; ~300 items/band. Models: same four, frozen. Decisive metric first: spontaneous CoT length; secondary: number of explicit steps and an ellipsis/compression score (operator-to-filler token ratio). Convincing result: CoT shortens and becomes more elliptical as items approach mastery (length and compression CIs excluding zero) within the matched surface band. Indecision band: length difference CI spanning zero with |effect| below one step - no measurable abbreviation. Negative result (CoT lengthens toward mastery): contradicts overt-to-covert internalization.

Experiment 5 (H4 - A self-difficulty probe supports a ZPD-gated controller that beats uniform reasoning): Tests the self-regulation payoff. Data: question-only early-layer hidden states (before any reasoning) for the 900 items, 70/30 item-disjoint split; controller evaluated on 300 held-out items. Models: same four, frozen; trainable component is a lightweight linear probe predicting calibrated difficulty (seeds 0/1/2). Systems compared: always-CoT, never-CoT, random-gated (matched CoT budget), and ZPD-gated (emit CoT only when predicted difficulty is in the middle band). Decisive metric first: accuracy at matched token budget (and, jointly, the accuracy-vs-average-tokens frontier); secondary: probe AUROC/correlation for predicting difficulty. Convincing result: ZPD-gating matches or exceeds always-CoT accuracy (its 95% CI lower bound at or above always-CoT) at a fraction of the tokens, and beats random-gating at equal budget (difference CI excluding zero), with probe AUROC >=0.65. Indecision band: ZPD-gating within 1 accuracy point of random-gating at equal budget - the model's internal difficulty estimate adds no usable signal, so the controller is not justified even if the probe is weakly above chance. Negative result (ZPD-gating below never-CoT or below random-gating): self-regulated private speech is not a useful lever. All numbers are planned evidence with bootstrap CIs over items, seeds, and models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Instruction-tuned models may be strongly primed to always emit CoT, flattening the spontaneous inverted-U; we mitigate with permissive prompts, base/less-aligned models, and by measuring emission via willingness-to-abbreviate rather than raw presence. (2) 'Difficulty' calibrated from direct-answer error may conflate item difficulty with model-specific gaps; we calibrate per-model and also report the surface difficulty axis. (3) The inverted-U could be an artifact of length ceilings (max tokens) or format; we cap generously and length-control. (4) Interference (negative CoT benefit on mastered items) may be small or model-dependent; a monotonic (non-ZPD) result is itself informative, distinguishing LLM reasoning from human private speech. (5) The competence probe may capture surface features rather than genuine self-difficulty estimation; we test generalization across task families and use question-only (pre-reasoning) activations. (6) The developmental/private-speech framing is an analogy operationalized behaviorally, not a claim of human-like inner experience; we frame all findings behaviorally and mechanistically.

novelty.reasoning: Core novel claims are: (1) per-item difficulty vs spontaneous CoT emission has an inverted-U, (2) forced CoT can hurt already-mastered items, and (3) CoT abbreviates as competence rises within a matched difficulty band. The private-speech/ZPD framing itself is not new, and difficulty-adaptive reasoning controllers plus overthinking analyses are already well studied. The delta is mainly in the specific, falsifiable empirical laws at inference time, not the overall idea or mechanism.

Name: lexical_gap_resolution
Title: Mind the Gap: Do Lexicalization Gaps in the Latent Pivot Language Blur an LLM's Concepts?
Short Hypothesis: LLMs route non-English inputs through a largely English-shaped 'concept space.' We hypothesize that a concept's internal representational resolution is bottlenecked by whether it is *lexicalized* (has a compact, single-/few-token word) in the model's latent pivot language: concepts that fall in a lexical gap of the pivot language are represented more diffusely, are harder to separate from neighbors, and yield systematically worse fine-grained reasoning — and providing an ad-hoc lexicalization (a coined single token/name) in-context sharpens both the geometry and the behavior.
Related Work: A cluster of work establishes that multilingual LLMs form a shared, largely English-pivoted concept space in middle layers (Semantic Hub Hypothesis 2024; Do Llamas Work in English 2024; Separating Tongue from Thought 2024; Tracing Multilingual Representations with Cross-Layer Transcoders 2025; When Meanings Meet 2026). These works show a shared space *exists* and can be causally patched, and that averaging concept representations across languages helps translation. Concept Space Alignment (2024) and High-Dimensional Interlingual Representations (2025) show alignment quality varies by typology and abstractness. XCOMPS (2025) shows conceptual understanding degrades for low-resource and morphologically complex languages. Crucially, all this work treats concepts holistically or averages across languages; none isolates *lexicalization gaps* — concepts that are compactly lexicalized in some languages but not the pivot — as a natural, controllable experiment on whether the pivot language's vocabulary sets a resolution limit on non-linguistic conceptual discrimination and reasoning. We uniquely (1) predict a lexicalization-gap penalty on representational resolution and downstream fine-grained reasoning, (2) contrast this with mere frequency/abstractness confounds, and (3) test a causal, training-free 'ad-hoc lexicalization' intervention that closes the gap.
Abstract: Multilingual language models process the world through a shared internal concept space that is disproportionately shaped by their dominant (often English) latent pivot language. We ask a simple question with deep implications for how language bounds machine intelligence: does the *vocabulary* of the pivot language set a resolution limit on what the model can finely discriminate and reason about? Human languages differ in which concepts they lexicalize — some have a single compact word for a notion (e.g., a specific kinship relation, an emotion, a color category, a shade of taste) that other languages must express periphrastically. We hypothesize a lexicalization-gap penalty: concepts that lack a compact lexicalization in the pivot language are represented more diffusely (lower cluster tightness, poorer separability from neighbors) and are correspondingly harder for the model to reason about at fine grain, even when the content is expressed identically. We assemble concept sets that are lexicalized in some languages but constitute lexical gaps in English, matched to lexicalized controls on frequency and abstractness, and measure (i) representational resolution via probing and cluster geometry across layers, and (ii) fine-grained behavioral discrimination and relational reasoning. We then test causality two ways: introducing an ad-hoc single-token lexicalization (a coined name) in-context should sharpen geometry and improve reasoning about gap concepts, while artificially 'de-lexicalizing' control concepts (forcing periphrastic reference) should blur them. Across several open-weight models we quantify the gap penalty, its dissociation from frequency/abstractness, and the effectiveness of ad-hoc lexicalization. Our work reframes the shared concept space from a uniform interlingua into a vocabulary-limited one, revealing a concrete channel by which language shapes AI intelligence.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (Setup - Lexicalization-gap concept sets with matched controls): Prerequisite. Data: a built set of ~120 target concepts that are compactly lexicalized in at least one non-English language but are English lexical gaps requiring periphrasis (e.g., Portuguese 'saudade', German 'Schadenfreude', fine kinship distinctions, specific color/material/taste/texture and social-relation terms), each paired with a control concept that IS compactly lexicalized in English, matched on estimated corpus frequency (from a reference corpus) and on human abstractness rating; each concept supplied with a cross-lingual definition (English plus 2-3 other languages, back-translation checked) and a set of minimally-different neighbor concepts. Gap status set by multiple annotators plus cross-linguistic dictionaries. Decisive metric first: inter-annotator agreement on gap status and match quality on frequency/abstractness. Convincing result: substantial agreement (kappa >=0.6) and no significant frequency/abstractness difference between target and control sets. Indecision band: kappa 0.4-0.6 - ambiguous items are dropped. Negative result (targets and controls differ on frequency/abstractness): the confound is unresolvable and sets are rebuilt.

Experiment 2 (H1 - Lexicalization-gap penalty on representational resolution): Central representational test. Data: for each concept, multiple paraphrased descriptions in English and 2-3 other languages (back-translation checked), hidden states extracted at matched positions in middle layers. Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, Aya-23-8B, all weights frozen; trainable component is a linear neighbor-discrimination probe (seeds 0/1/2). Systems compared: gap concepts vs. matched controls. Decisive metric first: per-concept representational resolution measured three ways - cluster tightness (within-concept variance across paraphrases), neighbor separability (silhouette vs. minimally-different neighbors), and probe AUROC distinguishing the concept from neighbors - entered as resolution ~ lexical_gap_status + frequency + abstractness + language + (1|model). Convincing result: a significant negative lexical_gap coefficient (resolution lower for gap concepts) with 95% CI excluding zero beyond frequency and abstractness, consistent across the three resolution measures and in at least 3 of 4 models. Indecision band: lexical_gap coefficient CI spanning zero once frequency/abstractness are controlled - any raw gap penalty is a frequency/abstractness artifact, so pivot-vocabulary does not set a resolution limit. Negative result (gap concepts show higher resolution): refutes the lexicalization-gap penalty.

Experiment 3 (H2 - Behavioral fine-grained penalty that tracks representational resolution): Tests downstream consequences. Data: for each concept, built discrimination and relational items - odd-one-out among near-neighbors, 'does description X match the concept better than its neighbor?', and analogy/relational-ordering - all expressed via descriptions so the surface never contains a compact English word; ~5 items/concept. Models: same four, frozen; 5 samples/item, seeds 0/1/2. Decisive metric first: accuracy with the lexical_gap coefficient controlling for frequency/abstractness; secondary: per-concept Spearman correlation between the behavioral penalty and the Experiment-2 resolution penalty. Convincing result: a significant behavioral gap penalty (coefficient CI excluding zero) that correlates with the representational penalty (Spearman CI excluding zero). Indecision band: behavioral-penalty CI spanning zero - representational diffuseness, if any, does not reach behavior. Negative result (no penalty or negative resolution-behavior correlation): the resolution limit does not affect reasoning.

Experiment 4 (H3 - Ad-hoc lexicalization sharpens, forced de-lexicalization blurs): Causal test holding the concept fixed. Data: for gap concepts, an in-context coined single-token name ('Let X = <definition>') then the same discrimination/relational items using X, vs. a no-name baseline and a matched-length inert-preamble control and a random-name control; conversely, for control concepts, forced periphrastic reference (never the compact word, only its definition). Models: same four, frozen; seeds 0/1/2. Decisive metric first: change in accuracy for gap concepts under naming (and change in cluster tightness/separability); secondary: change for control concepts under de-lexicalization. Convincing result: naming significantly improves gap-concept accuracy and sharpens geometry beyond the inert-preamble and random-name controls (difference CI excluding zero), and forced de-lexicalization degrades control-concept resolution/accuracy toward gap levels. Indecision band: naming effect within the inert-preamble control's CI - any benefit is a generic anchor-token effect, not lexicalization per se, leaving causality unestablished. Negative result (naming does not help or de-lexicalization does not hurt): lexicalization is not the causal factor.

Experiment 5 (H1 - Pivot-language crossover): Directly ties the penalty to the pivot language's vocabulary. Data: the concept sets re-scored for lexicalization in a non-English pivot language. Models: an available non-English-pivot model (e.g., a Japanese-continued-pretraining Llama variant) plus the English-pivot models as comparison, all frozen. Decisive metric first: whether the gap penalty tracks lexicalization in the model's pivot language rather than English (interaction of gap-status-in-pivot x model-pivot). Convincing result: the penalty follows the model's own pivot vocabulary (interaction CI excluding zero). Indecision band: interaction CI spanning zero - the penalty does not clearly relocate with the pivot, so the pivot-vocabulary mechanism is only weakly supported and we lean on Experiments 2-4. Negative result (penalty stays English-shaped regardless of pivot): the effect is not pivot-vocabulary-driven. If no suitable non-English-pivot model is available, this experiment is reported as not run and the causal Experiment 4 carries the mechanism claim. All quantities are planned evidence with bootstrap CIs over concepts, seeds, and models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Frequency and abstractness are hard to fully control and may drive apparent gap penalties; we match controls on both and include them as covariates, and use the causal naming/de-lexicalization interventions (which hold the concept fixed) to isolate lexicalization per se. (2) 'Lexical gap' status is fuzzy and language-dependent; we rely on multiple annotators and cross-linguistic dictionaries and report robustness to concept-set choices. (3) Extracting clean per-concept representations is noisy given surface-token contamination; we use many paraphrases, matched positions, and multiple layers. (4) Ad-hoc naming might help simply by adding a stable anchor token regardless of concepts, so we include inert-preamble and random-name controls. (5) The pivot-language crossover test depends on availability of a non-English-pivot model; if unavailable we rely on the English-pivot evidence plus the causal interventions. (6) A null result (no lexicalization-gap penalty) is itself informative, indicating the shared concept space is genuinely vocabulary-independent and that periphrastic descriptions fully recover fine-grained conceptual resolution.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims requiring novelty: (1) lexical gaps in the model's latent pivot language create a representational-resolution bottleneck for concepts; (2) this bottleneck is measurable via cluster tightness, neighbor separability, and probe AUROC beyond frequency/abstractness effects; (3) the representational penalty propagates to fine-grained discrimination and relational reasoning; (4) a training-free ad-hoc lexicalization can causally sharpen representations, while de-lexicalization blurs them; (5) pivot-crossover should flip the effect in a non-English-pivot model. Relative to the search summary, the basic finding that lexical-gap concepts have weaker cross-lingual alignment is already partially pre-empted by the 2026 lexical-gap-embedding paper, so novelty cannot rest on merely detecting a representational signature. The actual delta is the pivot-vocabulary bottleneck framing, the geometry/behavior link, and the causal intervention. That is non-trivial and potentially novel, but still close to an obvious next step from prior multilingual concept-space and lexical-gap work unless the causal and crossover pieces are executed convincingly.

impact.reasoning: The phenomenon under study is whether absence of compact lexicalization in a model's pivot language degrades internal concept resolution and downstream reasoning. The audience is multilingual NLP, interpretability/concept-representation researchers, low-resource language communities, and adjacent cognitive-science-of-language work. If true, the result would matter because it would imply multilingual models are not just unevenly aligned across languages but structurally bottlenecked by pivot vocabulary, suggesting new evaluation and mitigation strategies. The strongest case is that a simple lexicalization intervention could reveal and partially repair concept-quality disparities for underrepresented linguistic categories. The 'so what?' test is moderately positive: if the result holds, researchers may add lexical-gap diagnostics and interventions; if null, that would support vocabulary-independent concept spaces. Impact is limited somewhat because the proposal focuses on a specific explanatory factor within multilingual representation rather than a broad capability or deployed application, but the phenomenon itself could be influential.

review.reasoning: The proposal is coherent and testable, with a reasonably falsifiable hypothesis and a decent experimental outline, but several technical gaps weaken confidence. The biggest issue is construct validity: 'latent pivot language' is asserted more than operationalized, and English lexicalization is used as a proxy for pivot lexicalization in most experiments. Gap status is fuzzy, annotator agreement threshold is low, and the concept set (~120) may be too small and heterogeneous for the breadth of claims. The behavioral tasks risk confounding general description difficulty, cultural familiarity, tokenization length, and paraphrase quality with lexicalization per se. The ad-hoc naming intervention is promising but may improve performance through generic labeling, memorability, or attentional anchoring rather than true concept sharpening; current controls help but may not fully isolate mechanism. The non-English-pivot crossover is crucial yet underdeveloped and contingent on model availability. If executed well, this could be a respectable workshop or conference submission, but for a serious ML venue it needs tighter operational definitions, stronger controls, and a more decisive causal design.

Name: grammatical_evidentiality_calibration
Title: Grammar of Knowing: Does Obligatory Evidential Marking Make LLMs Track Their Sources and Calibrate Better?
Short Hypothesis: Some human languages grammatically force speakers to mark HOW they know something (firsthand perception vs. inference vs. hearsay). We hypothesize that when an LLM reasons in, or is scaffolded by, an evidentiality-marking grammar, it more sharply separates the provenance of its beliefs internally and becomes better calibrated — assigning lower confidence to hearsay/inference-derived claims and higher to firsthand-supported ones — than when reasoning in a language (like English) that leaves evidence-source grammatically optional.
Related Work: Two literatures meet here but have never been connected. (1) LLM calibration/verbalized uncertainty: models can verbalize calibrated confidence (Teaching Models to Express Uncertainty, 2022), verbal uncertainty is a single linear feature only moderately aligned with semantic uncertainty (Calibrating Verbal Uncertainty as a Linear Feature, 2025), verbalized confidence often mimics superficial certainty cues rather than being content-grounded (TracVC, 2026), and epistemic-modal sensitivity grows with depth (Mapping Clinical Doubt, 2025). All of this is essentially monolingual (English) and treats confidence as a scalar, ignoring information SOURCE. (2) Linguistic evidentiality: cross-linguistic studies show grammatical evidential markers change perceived certainty and psychological distance (Evidentiality & Construal Level Theory, 2014; Source vs. Stance, 2018; Perceiving Speaker's Certainty, 2025), and that grammatical (Turkish) vs. lexical (English) evidentiality is processed differently. No prior work asks whether an LLM's calibration and its internal representation of knowledge PROVENANCE depend on whether the operative grammar obligatorily encodes information source. We uniquely (a) decompose confidence by source-type (firsthand/inference/hearsay) rather than as a scalar, (b) test whether an evidentiality-marking grammar improves source-conditioned calibration and source separability in representation space, and (c) causally test evidential scaffolding as a training-free calibration intervention.
Abstract: Human languages differ in whether they grammatically force speakers to mark how they came to know something: evidentiality-marking languages (e.g., Turkish, Quechua, Japanese to varying degrees) obligatorily distinguish firsthand perception, inference, and hearsay, whereas English marks this only optionally through lexical hedges. Cognitive science shows these grammatical markers systematically shift perceived certainty and psychological distance. We ask whether this feature of language shapes machine intelligence: does reasoning under an evidentiality-marking grammar make a large language model track the provenance of its own beliefs and calibrate its confidence more faithfully? We introduce a source-decomposed view of calibration in which each claim is tagged by its evidence type, and we measure whether confidence is appropriately graded by source (lower for hearsay/inference, higher for firsthand-supported). We test three conditions on identical questions: reasoning in evidentiality-marking languages, reasoning in English, and reasoning in English with an explicit evidential scaffold that requires the model to name its information source before answering. We predict that evidential grammar (native or scaffolded) yields better source-conditioned calibration, sharper internal separability of source types, and reduced overconfident hallucination on hearsay/inference claims. Mechanistically, we test whether an 'evidential-source direction' exists in representation space, whether evidentiality-marking grammars increase its use, and whether steering along it improves calibration. Across several open-weight multilingual models we quantify source-conditioned calibration error, source separability, and steering controllability. Our work reframes calibration as a partly grammar-dependent capacity and offers a simple, training-free intervention grounded in linguistic typology.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (Setup - Source-tagged QA construction): Prerequisite. Data: a built set of ~600 questions, each with a short context passage engineered so the answer's support is one of three evidence types - firsthand/direct (fact stated explicitly and verifiably in context), inference (must be logically derived), and hearsay/unreliable (reported only by an unreliable in-context source or absent, so the correct stance is low confidence); plus a no-context internal-knowledge variant tagged by whether the model actually knows the answer (measured via repeated sampling). Ground-truth correctness known for all items. Multiple annotators tag evidence type. Decisive metric first: inter-annotator agreement on evidence-type tags. Convincing result: kappa >=0.6; ambiguous items dropped. Indecision band: kappa 0.4-0.6 - items adjudicated or removed. Negative result (kappa <0.4): the evidence-type construct is too unstable and items are redesigned.

Experiment 2 (H1 - Evidential grammar improves source-conditioned calibration): The central calibration test. Data: each item translated (back-translation checked) into English (optional evidentiality) and 2-3 evidentiality-marking languages (e.g., Turkish, Japanese, and Quechua or Bulgarian per model coverage), plus a fourth condition, English + Evidential Scaffold (the model must first output an evidential tag - 'I saw this stated' / 'I inferred this' / 'this is only reported/unknown' - before answering and giving confidence), and a fifth control condition, English + length-matched non-evidential reflection scaffold. Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Aya-23-8B, Gemma-2-9B, all weights frozen; verbalized confidence and log-prob confidence both elicited, 5 samples/item, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: the five conditions. Decisive metric first: source-conditioned Expected Calibration Error (ECE computed within each evidence-type stratum, then averaged) and a Source-Grading Score = degree to which mean confidence is correctly ordered firsthand > inference > hearsay; analyzed as ECE/Source-Grading ~ condition + per_language_accuracy + (1|model) + (1|item). Convincing result: evidentiality-marking grammar (native OR scaffolded) lowers source-conditioned ECE and raises the Source-Grading Score relative to plain English AND relative to the length-matched non-evidential reflection scaffold (95% CI on both contrasts excluding zero), after controlling for accuracy, in at least 3 of 5 models. Indecision band: the evidential-vs-control-scaffold contrast CI spanning zero - any gain is generic reflection/prompt structure, not source-marking, so grammar per se does not improve calibration. Negative result (evidential conditions worsen source-conditioned calibration): refutes the grammar-calibration link.

Experiment 3 (H2 - Evidential conditions reduce overconfident hallucination): Tests the abstention prediction. Data: the hearsay/unknown items where correct behavior is low confidence or abstention. Models: same five, frozen. Decisive metric first: confident-error rate (high-confidence wrong answers) per condition. Convincing result: evidential conditions significantly lower the confident-error rate vs. plain English and vs. the non-evidential reflection control (CI excluding zero). Indecision band: confident-error-rate difference CI spanning zero - evidential marking does not curb overconfidence. Negative result (higher confident-error rate under evidential conditions): contradicts the prediction.

Experiment 4 (H3 - Sharper internal source separability and an evidential-source direction): Mechanistic test. Data: mid/late-layer hidden states on matched items across conditions. Models: same five, frozen; trainable component is a linear probe classifying the three evidence types (seeds 0/1/2, item-disjoint split); a difference-in-means 'evidential-source direction' (firsthand vs. hearsay) is also extracted. Systems compared: source separability across conditions; magnitude of use of the evidential-source direction across conditions. Decisive metric first: probe AUROC (macro over the three evidence types) for source separability. Convincing result: evidentiality-marking grammars/scaffold significantly raise separability AUROC vs. plain English (CI excluding zero) and increase use of the evidential-source direction. Indecision band: AUROC difference CI spanning zero - grammar does not sharpen internal source representation, so the calibration effect (if any) is not mechanistically localized here. Negative result (lower separability under evidential conditions): no internal source-tracking benefit.

Experiment 5 (H4 - Steering the evidential-source direction improves calibration): Causal test. Data: 400 held-out plain-English items (item-disjoint from probe training). Models: same five, frozen; steering adds the evidential-source direction at inference in the plain-English condition; strength tuned on a dev split, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: no-steer, random-direction steering (matched norm), the linear verbalized-uncertainty-feature baseline from prior work, and evidential-source steering. Decisive metric first: change in source-conditioned ECE; secondary: confident-hallucination rate and fluency. Convincing result: evidential-source steering lowers source-conditioned ECE and confident-hallucination more than random-direction steering and the verbalized-uncertainty baseline (difference CI excluding zero) without harming fluency. Indecision band: steering effect within the random-direction control's CI - the direction is not a usable causal calibration lever. Negative result (steering worsens calibration or collapses fluency): no causal control. All calibration analyses are accuracy-stratified so improvements reflect calibration not competence; every number is planned evidence with bootstrap CIs over items, seeds, and models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Evidentiality-marking languages may be lower-resource for these models, confounding grammar effects with competence; mitigated by accuracy-stratified calibration metrics, back-translation checks, and by the English+scaffold condition which isolates evidential structure without changing language resource level. (2) The scaffold could improve calibration simply by adding a reflection step; we include a length-matched non-evidential reflection scaffold as a control to isolate the source-marking contribution. (3) Verbalized confidence may mimic surface certainty cues (per TracVC 2026) rather than content; we cross-check with log-prob confidence and the internal source-separability probe. (4) Constructing clean firsthand/inference/hearsay items is hard and somewhat subjective; we use multiple annotators and report robustness to item-set choices. (5) The 'evidential-source direction' may entangle with generic sentiment/certainty; random-direction controls and the linear-VUF baseline from prior work help disentangle. (6) A null result (grammar does not affect source-conditioned calibration) is still informative, showing calibration is grammar-independent and that any gains from evidential scaffolding are purely prompt-structural rather than typological.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims needing novelty: (1) source-decomposed calibration as a construct, measuring confidence separately for firsthand/inference/hearsay rather than a scalar; (2) obligatory evidential grammar, or an English evidential scaffold, causally improves source-conditioned calibration and reduces confident hallucination; (3) this effect is not just generic reflection, as shown against a length-matched non-evidential scaffold; (4) there exists an internal evidential-source direction that is strengthened by evidential marking and can be steered; (5) source-direction steering can outperform or complement scalar verbal-uncertainty-feature baselines. Relative to the search summary, this is not wholly new territory: Turkish source-sensitive reasoning under trust manipulation is a very close behavioral neighbor, and verbal-uncertainty calibration/steering already exists as the main baseline. The real delta is the decomposition by evidence source, the grammar-vs-scaffold causal contrast, and the mechanistic source-direction claim. That delta is meaningful and non-trivial, but somewhat fragile: if scaffold effects reduce to generic reflection or multilingual prompting artifacts, the typological novelty collapses.

impact.reasoning: The problem under study is trustworthy confidence assignment conditioned on evidence provenance: whether models know when a claim is firsthand-supported, inferred, hearsay-like, or unsupported. People who would care include calibration/hallucination researchers, multilingual NLP, and RAG/source-attribution practitioners. The strongest case is that if grammatical/source-structured prompting materially reduces overconfident unsupported claims, it offers a cheap intervention for trustworthiness. This matters beyond the method because provenance-sensitive calibration is a real need, not a mere linguistic curiosity. The main limitation is that the proposal's direct practical reach depends on effect size and portability: if gains appear only in a few evidential languages or only as a prompt artifact, uptake may be narrower. The result could influence how researchers think about uncertainty representation, but probably not dramatically unless the causal typology claim is strong and robust.

As written, this could become a solid workshop or conference submission if executed well, but for a serious ML venue it needs sharper operationalization and stronger controls.

Name: future_tense_present_bias
Title: Does Grammar Make an LLM Impatient? Testing the Linguistic Savings Hypothesis Inside Language Models
Short Hypothesis: The famous Linguistic Savings Hypothesis (grammatically obligatory future-time reference makes speakers more present-biased) can be tested causally inside LLMs: framing the same intertemporal choice with strong future-tense grammar (a) increases the model's present-bias (steeper discounting) and (b) increases the internal represented psychological distance between 'now' and the future outcome, and steering along a latent future-distance direction reproduces or cancels this present-bias — providing the first mechanistic, causally-controlled test of whether grammatical future marking shapes machine intertemporal choice.
Related Work: Chen's Linguistic Savings Hypothesis (2013, 712 cites) correlated weak grammatical future-time reference (FTR) with higher savings; follow-up lab studies (2017, 2019) and a psycholinguistic framework (2023) find inconclusive/contested effects, limited by imperfect control over framing and confounds in human populations. Separately, interpretability work shows LLMs encode time as linear/curvilinear representations (Language Models Represent Space and Time, 2023; Time Travel Engine, 2026), exhibit human-like log-compressed temporal distance around a subjective 'now' (The Other Mind, 2025), and encode grammatical tense/aspect as steerable orthogonal directions (Steering Tense and Aspect, 2025). No prior work connects the FTR grammar hypothesis to LLM intertemporal CHOICE behavior, nor tests whether grammatical future framing causally alters the internal represented distance-to-future that drives discounting, nor uses latent-direction steering to isolate grammar's effect from content. We are the first to (1) operationalize FTR-strength as a within-item, content-matched framing manipulation, (2) link behavioral present-bias to internal temporal-distance geometry, and (3) causally steer a future-distance direction to reproduce/cancel the effect, converting a contested socioeconomic correlation into a controlled mechanistic experiment.
Abstract: One of the most striking claims about language and thought is Chen's Linguistic Savings Hypothesis: languages that grammatically force speakers to mark the future as distinct from the present (strong future-time reference, FTR) foster more present-biased, impatient behavior. Human studies of this claim are contested because grammar cannot be cleanly separated from culture and economics. Large language models offer a controlled testbed: we can hold content constant and vary only grammatical future framing. We test whether the way an LLM is asked to talk about the future causally changes how impatiently it chooses. We construct matched intertemporal-choice items (sooner-smaller vs. later-larger rewards over money, health, and effort) and render each in weak-FTR framing (present-tense/futureless phrasing) versus strong-FTR framing (obligatory, explicit future marking), plus a native cross-lingual variant across languages spanning the FTR spectrum (Chinese/German=weak, English/Spanish=strong). Behaviorally, we estimate each model's discount rate and present-bias per framing and test whether strong-FTR framing steepens discounting. Mechanistically, using probes on temporal representations we measure the internal 'psychological distance' the model assigns to the future outcome and test whether strong-FTR framing inflates it, correlating this distance with behavioral impatience. Finally, we isolate a latent future-distance direction and steer along it to causally induce or cancel present-bias, comparing against random-direction and content-matched controls. Across several open-weight models we quantify the FTR present-bias effect, its dissociation from mere accuracy, the distance-to-behavior link, and steering controllability, delivering the first mechanistic adjudication of a famous linguistic-relativity claim.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (Setup - Intertemporal-choice battery): Prerequisite. Data: a built battery of ~400 base items, each a binary choice between a sooner-smaller and a later-larger reward, spanning three domains (money, health, effort) and a grid of delays (1 week to 5 years) and reward ratios, enabling per-model discount-rate estimation via hyperbolic/exponential fits. Decisive metric first: coverage of the delay x ratio grid sufficient to fit a stable discount curve (bootstrap SE on the discount rate). Convincing result: the grid yields discount-rate fits with tight SEs and choices spanning both options (no ceiling/floor). Indecision band: many items at ceiling/floor (one option always chosen) - we widen the ratio/delay grid. Negative result: choices are option-invariant, and the battery is redesigned to avoid saturation.

Experiment 2 (H1 - Strong future-time-reference framing steepens discounting): The central behavioral test, holding content constant. Data: each of the 400 items rendered in (a) weak-FTR framing (present-tense/futureless phrasing, e.g., 'you receive X in a year') and (b) strong-FTR framing (obligatory explicit future marking, e.g., 'you WILL receive X, one year from now, in the future'), verified by an independent FTR-strength rating; content, numbers, and delays held identical and framings length-matched. Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, Aya-23-8B, all weights frozen; choices and a separately-elicited indifference point collected, 5 samples/item, temperature 0.7, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: strong- vs. weak-FTR framing within item. Decisive metric first: the FTR-strength coefficient on discounting/present-bias in a mixed-effects model (choice/discount ~ FTR_strength + delay + ratio + domain + (1|model) + (1|item)), stratified by decision consistency. Convincing result: strong-FTR framing yields significantly steeper discounting / more sooner-smaller choices (FTR coefficient 95% CI excluding zero) in at least 3 of 5 models, not explained by decision-consistency differences. Indecision band: FTR coefficient CI spanning zero with a standardized effect below 0.1 - grammatical future framing does not measurably move impatience, the cleanest evidence to date against a mechanistic reading of the Linguistic Savings Hypothesis in this controlled setting. Negative result (strong-FTR framing makes the model more patient): the hypothesized direction is reversed.

Experiment 3 (H1 - Native cross-lingual FTR variant): Tests that native grammatical FTR reproduces the within-item framing effect. Data: the items translated (back-translation checked) into languages spanning the FTR spectrum (Chinese, German = weak-FTR; English, Spanish = strong-FTR). Models: same five, frozen; all cross-lingual analyses accuracy/consistency-stratified. Decisive metric first: the FTR-strength coefficient across native languages, controlling for a resource-level covariate. Convincing result: native strong-FTR languages show steeper discounting than weak-FTR languages after stratification (coefficient CI excluding zero), converging with Experiment 2. Indecision band: coefficient CI spanning zero once resource level is controlled - cross-lingual differences are competence-driven, so the within-item framing test (Experiment 2) remains the primary evidence. Negative result (reversed cross-lingual ordering): the native-grammar prediction fails.

Experiment 4 (H2 - Strong-FTR framing inflates internal represented future-distance, which tracks impatience): Mechanistic representational test. Data: hidden states on the future-outcome mention across framings. Models: same five, frozen; trainable component is a temporal-distance probe (following prior space-and-time representation work) validated on held-out delays (seeds 0/1/2), matched positions, multiple layers. Decisive metric first: represented distance-from-now for the delayed outcome, tested for inflation under strong-FTR framing; secondary: per-item Spearman correlation between represented distance and behavioral impatience. Convincing result: strong-FTR framing significantly inflates represented future-distance (CI excluding zero) and per-item distance correlates with impatience (Spearman CI excluding zero). Indecision band: distance-inflation CI spanning zero - framing does not move the internal distance representation, so any behavioral effect is not mediated by represented distance. Negative result (strong-FTR compresses represented distance): contradicts the mediation account.

Experiment 5 (H3 - Steering a future-distance direction induces or cancels present-bias): Causal test. Data: 300 held-out items (disjoint from probe validation). Models: same five, frozen; a 'future-distance' direction computed via difference-in-means between near- and far-future outcome representations (and between weak- vs. strong-FTR framings of identical items); strength tuned on a dev split, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: +direction steering (increase represented distance), -direction steering (decrease it), no-steer, random-direction steering (matched norm), and a content-matched reward-magnitude-direction control. Decisive metric first: induced change in present-bias (beta) parameter; secondary: fraction of the FTR framing effect reproduced (+) or cancelled (-). Convincing result: +steering increases present-bias and -steering cancels the strong-FTR framing effect, significantly beyond random-direction and reward-magnitude controls (difference CI excluding zero). Indecision band: steering effect within the control directions' CIs - present-bias is not controllable via this direction, so the mechanistic link is unproven even if Experiments 2 and 4 hold. Negative result (steering has no effect or destroys coherent choice behavior): no causal handle on grammar-induced impatience. All quantities are planned evidence with bootstrap CIs over items, seeds, and models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Instruction-tuned models may answer intertemporal choices in a rigid, framing-insensitive way, yielding null behavioral effects; we mitigate with graded reward ratios/delays to avoid ceiling/floor, multiple models including base variants, and per-item indifference elicitation. (2) Strong- vs weak-FTR framings may differ in length/emphasis rather than grammar per se; we length-match, use independent FTR-strength ratings, and rely on the native cross-lingual variant plus content-matched steering to isolate grammar. (3) Cross-lingual differences confound grammar with training-data resource level; all cross-lingual analyses are accuracy/consistency-stratified and the English within-item framing manipulation (same language, only grammar varies) is the primary test. (4) Temporal-distance probes may capture surface delay tokens rather than psychological distance; we use held-out probe validation, matched positions, and multiple layers. (5) The future-distance steering direction may entangle with reward magnitude or generic content; random-direction and reward-magnitude-direction controls address this. (6) A null result (grammatical framing does not shift LLM present-bias) is itself informative — it would provide the cleanest evidence to date against a mechanistic reading of the Linguistic Savings Hypothesis, since human confounds are absent here.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) test the Linguistic Savings Hypothesis inside LLM intertemporal choice; (2) strong-FTR framing should increase present-bias and internal future-distance; (3) a latent future-distance steering direction can induce/cancel that bias; (4) cross-lingual FTR variants provide a native-language setting. The setting is genuinely new (LLMs, causal framing, latent steering), but the mechanism is mostly an adaptation of existing temporal-representation and tense-steering work. Relative to prior work, the delta is real but incremental: first behavioral test of FTR/LSH in LLM choice plus a causal probe, not a new theory. The headline sign claim is also not novel in the broader human literature because recent causal work points the opposite way, so the novelty is in the LLM test and causal decomposition rather than the hypothesized direction.
