Name: codeswitch_executive_control
Title: Code-Switching as a Cognitive Tool: Does Inducing Language Mixing Boost an LLM's Inhibitory Control?
Short Hypothesis: In humans, code-switching trains and transiently boosts executive control (inhibition and conflict monitoring), with different switch types (insertion vs. alternation vs. dense) modulating different control modes. We hypothesize the same functional relationship holds inside LLMs: deliberately inducing code-switching in the reasoning trace improves the model's performance on conflict/inhibition-demanding tasks (distractor resistance, misleading-premise resistance, override of intuitive lures) beyond monolingual reasoning of equal length, that the beneficial switch TYPE dissociates by control demand (reactive vs. proactive), and that this benefit is mediated by a locatable conflict-monitoring component whose engagement rises under induced switching.
Related Work: Recent LLM work treats language mixing as a symptom of latent pivot-language preferences to be controlled away: 'Language Mixing in Reasoning LMs' (2025) shows mixing increases with difficulty and that forcing a Latin/Han script helps; 'When Less Language is More' (2025) and MRRE (2025) improve multilingual reasoning by suppressing/aligning language-specific components; 'Cross-Lingual Knowledge-Free Reasoners' (2024) shows reasoning transfers across languages. All of these frame language identity as noise to remove. Separately, a large human cross-domain literature shows the OPPOSITE valence: code-switching TRAINS executive control (inhibition, goal-monitoring; e.g., Language athletes 2023; Training in Language Switching 2019) and that switch TYPE selectively modulates reactive vs. proactive control via a dual-control-mode account (2020), with fast context effects on non-verbal conflict tasks (2013). No LLM work has transferred this: none asks whether deliberately INDUCING code-switching functions as a cognitive tool that improves conflict/inhibition reasoning, whether switch type dissociates control mode, or whether a conflict-monitoring internal component mediates the effect. We uniquely reframe language mixing from symptom-to-suppress into a controllable executive-control resource, and give it a mechanistic (Location + Causal Intervention) test.
Abstract: Multilingual interpretability work treats an LLM's tendency to mix languages while reasoning as a nuisance symptom of its internal pivot language, best suppressed. Yet decades of bilingualism research show the reverse for humans: code-switching trains and transiently boosts executive control, sharpening inhibition and conflict monitoring, with distinct switch types tuning distinct control modes. We ask whether this functional relationship transfers to LLMs: can deliberately inducing code-switching in a model's chain-of-thought act as a cognitive tool that improves performance on tasks demanding inhibition and conflict resolution? We assemble a battery of conflict/inhibition-heavy reasoning tasks (linguistic-Stroop-style distractor items, misleading-premise math, cognitive-reflection lures, and irrelevant-context word problems) and compare monolingual reasoning against three induced switch regimes drawn from the psycholinguistic taxonomy: insertion (single foreign content words), alternation (whole-clause switches between languages), and dense switching (frequent intra-sentence switching). Crucially we control for confounds by matching reasoning length and adding a same-language 'switch-token' scramble control, so any gain reflects switching rather than extra tokens or translation. We predict induced switching improves conflict-resolution accuracy over length-matched monolingual reasoning, that alternation aids reactive (distractor) control while dense switching aids proactive (sustained-monitoring) control, mirroring the human dual-control dissociation, and that these gains dissociate from ordinary (non-conflict) reasoning. Mechanistically, we locate a conflict-monitoring direction/component (via probing on high- vs low-conflict trials) and test whether induced switching raises its engagement and whether steering it reproduces the switching benefit. Across several open-weight models we quantify the switching-benefit effect, its type-by-control-mode dissociation, and mechanistic mediation, reframing language mixing as a controllable executive-control resource.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - Does induced code-switching cut conflict errors beyond length-matched monolingual reasoning?): Tests whether deliberately inducing code-switching in the chain-of-thought improves performance on inhibition/conflict tasks over monolingual reasoning of equal length, and whether the benefit is specific to conflict rather than ordinary reasoning. Data: a conflict battery of ~1000 items, 250 per family - (a) linguistic-Stroop distractor items (constructed; a salient distractor word/number must be suppressed), (b) misleading-premise math sampled and adapted from GSM-IC (Shi et al. 2023, ~58k released problems) by tagging the tempting irrelevant number as the labeled lure, (c) Cognitive-Reflection-Test-style lures (only ~7 canonical CRT items exist, so we template 250 items preserving the intuitive-lure structure), (d) irrelevant-context word problems drawn directly from GSM-IC; plus a matched NON-CONFLICT control set of 250 plain arithmetic/logic items of equal surface difficulty. We use 250 per family rather than the full GSM-IC pool to balance families and keep 5 models x 5 regimes x 4 decoding passes within a single-lab compute budget. Each conflict item carries a labeled correct answer AND a labeled lure answer so lure-error rate is scorable. Models: five frozen open-weight instruction-tuned models spanning families/scales - Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Aya-23-8B, Mistral-7B-Instruct; inference only, no weights trained; decoding at temperature 0.7 with sampling seeds {0,1,2} plus one greedy pass (four traces per item). Regimes, all length-matched to the same reasoning-token budget and format-enforced: monolingual baseline; insertion; alternation; dense switching; a same-language switch-token scramble control (foreign-looking nonce tokens injected at the switch positions); and a pure-translation control (reason fully in the second language). The second language is one of each model's strong languages (English<->Chinese or English<->Spanish). We verify switch compliance and analyze only compliant traces. Decisive metric: lure-error rate on conflict items (fraction of responses equal to the labeled lure), in a mixed-effects model lure_error ~ regime*conflict_level + (1|model) + (1|item); secondary: accuracy. Convincing result: alternation and/or dense switching lower lure-error rate versus both length-matched monolingual and the switch-token scramble control with 95% bootstrap CIs excluding zero, AND a regime x conflict interaction showing the reduction is larger on conflict than on non-conflict items. Indecision band: if the switching-minus-monolingual lure-error difference has a 95% CI contained within +/-2 percentage points (thus overlapping zero), or the regime x conflict interaction CI lies within +/-2 pp, the measurement cannot decide and H1 is treated as unsupported at this power. Negative result (switching no better, or worse, than length-matched monolingual and scramble) would mean LLM language mixing is a nuisance symptom rather than an executive-control tool, cleanly separating LLMs from the human bilingualism finding.

Experiment 2 (H2 - Does switch TYPE dissociate by control mode, alternation for reactive and dense for proactive?): Tests the predicted crossover between switch type and control demand. Data: the same conflict battery re-labeled by control demand - reactive (transient single-distractor suppression: linguistic-Stroop and CRT items, ~500) vs proactive (sustained monitoring across distractor-laden context: irrelevant-context and misleading-premise word problems, ~500). Models, seeds and decoding as Experiment 1, restricted to monolingual, alternation and dense regimes. Decisive metric: the regime x control_mode interaction coefficient on accuracy (and, secondarily, lure-error rate) in the mixed-effects model. Convincing result: a crossover in which alternation's advantage over monolingual is larger on reactive items while dense switching's advantage is larger on proactive items, with the interaction's 95% CI excluding zero and the two simple effects ordered as predicted. Indecision band: if the interaction coefficient's 95% CI lies within +/-2 pp of zero, the type-by-mode dissociation is undecided and we retreat to the weaker claim that switching helps without dissociating by mode. Negative result (no crossover, or the reverse ordering) leaves H1 intact but refutes the human dual-control-mode analogy for LLMs.

Experiment 3 (H3 - Is there a locatable conflict-monitoring component whose engagement rises under induced switching?): Location plus mediation. Data: hidden states cached from the monolingual runs of Experiment 1 on the conflict battery, split into high-conflict vs low-conflict (and lure-resolved vs lure-failed) trials, with a 70/15/15 train/validation/test split over items. Model: the same five models, frozen; the only trainable parameters are per-layer logistic-regression linear probes trained with 5-fold cross-validation over seeds {0,1,2}. Decisive metric: held-out probe AUROC for high- vs low-conflict trials (per layer; report best-layer AUROC). Then mediation: the Spearman correlation between the per-item increase in projection onto the conflict-monitoring direction (switching minus monolingual, at the critical resolution step) and the per-item accuracy gain. Convincing result: best-layer held-out AUROC clears 0.70 and generalizes to held-out items, induced switching raises the projection onto this direction versus monolingual, and the projection-gain-to-accuracy-gain Spearman rho is positive with a 95% CI excluding zero. Indecision band: probe AUROC in [0.55, 0.65] means no reliable conflict-monitoring direction was located; a mediation rho whose 95% CI lies within +/-0.1 of zero means engagement change does not track behavior. Either leaves the mechanism undecided. Negative result (no decodable direction, or switching does not raise its engagement, or engagement does not predict benefit) would show any behavioral benefit from Experiment 1 is not mediated by a conflict-monitoring component, undercutting the mechanistic half of the hypothesis while leaving the behavioral claim standing.

Experiment 4 (H3 - Does steering the conflict-monitoring direction reproduce and cancel the switching benefit?): Causal test. Data: a held-out 200-item conflict subset disjoint from the probe-training items of Experiment 3. Model: the same five frozen models; no weights trained; the difference-in-means conflict-monitoring direction from Experiment 3 is added or subtracted at the located layer across a dose sweep (coefficients spanning 0 to a few times the natural projection norm), each over seeds {0,1,2}. Systems compared: +direction during monolingual reasoning; -direction during dense-switch reasoning; random-direction steering; and no-steer. Decisive metric: change in lure-error rate (and accuracy) under steering versus no-steer, with a specificity check on the non-conflict control set. Convincing result: +direction under monolingual reproduces at least 50% of the alternation/dense switching benefit from Experiment 1 with a monotone dose-response, -direction under dense switching cancels it, both exceed the random-direction control (95% CIs excluding it), and off-target non-conflict accuracy stays within +/-2 pp of no-steer. Indecision band: if the steering effect's 95% CI overlaps the random-direction control, or reproduces less than 25% of the behavioral benefit with no dose-response, the causal claim is undecided. Negative result (steering does not shift behavior, or is indistinguishable from random) would mean the conflict-monitoring direction is correlational at best, not the causal mediator the hypothesis requires.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Induced switching may simply add tokens/'thinking time'; mitigated by strict length-matching, the switch-token scramble control, and testing the conflict-vs-non-conflict INTERACTION rather than raw gains. (2) Switching may degrade fluency or cause the model to lose the thread, hurting rather than helping; a null or negative result is still informative (it would show LLM language mixing is a symptom, not a tool, cleanly separating LLMs from the human executive-control literature). (3) The second-language choice confounds switching with translation quality; the pure-translation and random-direction controls plus multiple language pairs isolate switching per se. (4) The 'conflict-monitoring' direction may entangle with generic difficulty rather than genuine inhibition; mitigated by matched high/low-conflict contrasts, held-out probe validation, random-direction steering controls, and specificity checks on non-conflict tasks. (5) Reactive/proactive task labels are hypotheses; a flat (non-crossover) result would still test the core switching-benefit claim and is publishable. (6) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (7) The human-cognition framing (executive control, dual control modes) is an operationalized analogy, not a claim of human-like cognition; all findings are framed behaviorally and mechanistically.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) deliberately induced code-switching in LLM reasoning can improve performance on inhibition/conflict tasks beyond length-matched monolingual reasoning; (2) switch type (insertion/alternation/dense) dissociates by reactive vs proactive control demands; (3) a locatable conflict-monitoring component mediates the effect and can be causally steered; (4) the novelty is mainly in the mechanism/interpretive framing and switch-type/control-mode crossover, not the general idea that mixing may help. Closest prior work already pre-empts the broad 'mixing helps reasoning' claim and even shows monolingual enforcement hurts math accuracy. The actual delta is a human bilingual executive-control mapping plus a specific, testable switch-type-by-control-mode and mediation/steering hypothesis, which is meaningfully new if it holds.

Name: answer_deferral_typology
Title: Think Verb-Last: Does Answer-Deferring Word Order Delay an LLM's Commitment and Reduce Premature-Answer Errors?
Short Hypothesis: Human psycholinguistics shows head-final (verb-late, SOV) languages defer the pivotal predicate, forcing the parser to keep multiple hypotheses open, whereas head-initial (SVO) languages front the verb and encourage early prediction. We hypothesize the same trade-off governs LLM reasoning: when a model reasons in (or is scaffolded into) an answer-deferring, verb-final structure, it commits to a final answer later in its chain-of-thought and keeps competing candidate answers alive longer, which reduces premature-commitment errors on problems that require revising an initially tempting wrong answer — and this delayed commitment is readable and steerable via an internal 'answer-commitment' direction.
Related Work: Human work shows head-initial SVO languages afford more prediction while head-final SOV languages rely on rich pre-verbal structure building and holding hypotheses open until the verb (Prediction in SVO and SOV, 2023; Hyper-active gap filling, 2015; Hindi verbal-prediction limits, 2021; Word order affects formulation time course, Tzeltal 2015). In LLMs, word-order studies focus on training-time inductive biases via synthetic/artificial languages (Ravfogel 2019; White & Cotterell 2021) or on representation of grammatical role (BERT word order, 2022) and incremental garden-path processing (2024). BICAUSE (2025) shows LLMs internalize language-specific causal-order attention biases. None of this connects word-order typology to WHEN an LLM commits to a reasoning answer, to whether verb-final/answer-deferring structure keeps its candidate-answer space open longer, or to premature-commitment errors on revision-requiring problems. We uniquely (1) transfer the human prediction-vs-deferral finding into LLM reasoning behavior, (2) operationalize word order as a within-item, content-matched reasoning-structure manipulation (answer-early vs answer-late), and (3) locate and causally steer an internal answer-commitment signal, distinguishing our claim from purely observational typology-bias work.
Abstract: Languages differ in where they place the verb: head-initial languages (English, SVO) front the predicate and let listeners predict early, while head-final languages (Japanese, Hindi, SOV) defer the verb, forcing the comprehender to keep multiple interpretations open until it arrives. We ask whether this typological trade-off shapes how large language models reason: does an answer-deferring, verb-final reasoning structure make a model commit to its answer later and hold competing candidate answers alive longer, thereby avoiding premature-commitment errors on problems that require overriding a tempting-but-wrong first guess? We construct reasoning items with a strong intuitive lure and manipulate, within-item and content-matched, whether the reasoning trace is structured answer-early (conclusion/predicate stated up front, then justified) versus answer-late (all evidence marshalled first, conclusion deferred to the end), plus a native cross-lingual variant across SVO and SOV languages. Behaviorally, we measure the token position of first answer commitment, the persistence of the lure answer as a live candidate across the trace (via next-token answer probabilities), and lure-error rate on revision-requiring vs. non-revision problems. We predict answer-late structure defers commitment, sustains multiple candidates longer, and selectively reduces lure errors where revision matters, while offering no benefit (or a cost) on problems where the first guess is correct. Mechanistically, we locate an 'answer-commitment' direction from hidden states contrasting pre- vs post-commitment steps, test whether answer-late structure lowers its early engagement, and steer it to delay or force commitment, causally reproducing or cancelling the behavioral effect. Across several open-weight models we quantify the commitment-timing effect, its revision-specificity, and steering controllability, reframing word-order typology as a controllable lever on reasoning commitment.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - Does answer-deferring, verb-final structure delay commitment and keep candidates alive longer?): Tests whether an answer-late reasoning structure defers first answer-commitment and sustains competing candidates longer than an answer-early structure. Data: a lure battery of ~1000 items, 250 per family - (a) misleading-premise math adapted from GSM-IC (Shi et al. 2023, ~58k released problems), (b) Cognitive-Reflection-Test-style traps (templated, since only ~7 canonical CRT items exist), (c) multi-hop logic where an early sub-conclusion is superseded by later evidence (constructed), (d) belief-bias syllogisms (constructed from standard belief-bias templates). Each item carries a labeled correct answer AND a labeled lure answer and is tagged revision-requiring (intuitive first guess wrong) vs non-revision (first guess correct). We use 250 per family to keep 5 models x 3 structures x 4 decoding passes affordable. Models: five frozen open-weight instruction-tuned models - Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Aya-23-8B, Mistral-7B-Instruct; inference only; temperature 0.7 with seeds {0,1,2} plus one greedy pass. Structures (within-item, content- and length-matched, format-enforced): answer-early (state the tentative conclusion first, then justify), answer-late (marshal all evidence, defer the conclusion to the final tokens), and a free baseline. We verify structure compliance and analyze only compliant traces. Measurement: at each reasoning step read the implicit answer via next-token probabilities on constrained answer slots for the correct vs lure candidate; define first-commitment position = earliest step (as a fraction of trace length) where the eventual answer's probability crosses a dominance threshold of 0.5 and stays, and candidate persistence = number of steps both correct and lure remain above a 0.2 liveness threshold. Decisive metric: first-commitment position (fraction of trace) in a mixed-effects model controlling trace length; secondary: candidate persistence. Convincing result: answer-late yields a later first-commitment position than answer-early (difference 95% CI excluding zero and exceeding 0.10 of the trace) and longer candidate persistence. Indecision band: if the first-commitment-position difference has a 95% CI within +/-0.05 of the trace fraction, or trace-length matching is imperfect enough that the effect is confounded, the timing claim is undecided. Negative result (no shift in commitment timing) would indicate LLM reasoning commitment is independent of surface reasoning-order structure.

Experiment 2 (H2 - Does deferred commitment selectively reduce lure errors where revision is needed?): Tests the revision-specific behavioral benefit, plus a native cross-lingual variant. Data: the same battery from Experiment 1, using the revision-requiring vs non-revision tags. Cross-lingual variant: translate the items into SVO languages (English, Spanish) and SOV languages (Japanese, Hindi, Turkish), back-translation checked, to test whether native verb-final grammar reproduces the answer-late effect; all cross-lingual analyses are stratified on per-language task accuracy to separate structure from language-resource competence. Models, seeds and decoding as Experiment 1. Decisive metric: the structure x revision-status interaction on lure-error rate. Convincing result: answer-late reduces lure-error rate on revision-requiring items significantly more than on non-revision items (interaction 95% CI excluding zero), may slightly raise errors on non-revision items (a deferral cost), and native SOV framing shows the same direction after competence stratification. Indecision band: if the structure x revision interaction has a 95% CI within +/-2 percentage points, the selective-benefit claim is undecided. Negative result (answer-late does not selectively cut revision errors) would show deferral buys no genuine revision benefit, weakening the functional analogy to head-final comprehension.

Experiment 3 (H3 - Is there a locatable answer-commitment direction whose early engagement answer-late structure lowers?): Location plus mediation. Data: hidden states cached on the traces of Experiment 1, contrasting pre-commitment vs post-commitment steps (defined by the first-commitment crossing), 70/15/15 train/validation/test over items. Model: the same five frozen models; only per-layer logistic-regression linear probes are trainable, 5-fold CV over seeds {0,1,2}. Decisive metric: held-out probe AUROC for pre- vs post-commitment steps (best layer). Then: whether answer-late structure lowers early-trace projection onto this answer-commitment direction versus answer-early, and the Spearman correlation between per-item projection timing and per-item first-commitment position. Convincing result: best-layer AUROC clears 0.70 and generalizes, answer-late lowers early projection (CI excluding zero), and projection timing tracks first-commitment position (rho CI excluding zero). Indecision band: AUROC in [0.55, 0.65], or a projection-timing rho whose 95% CI is within +/-0.1 of zero, leaves the mechanism undecided. Negative result (no decodable commitment direction, or its timing does not track structure) would sever the behavioral timing effect from any internal commitment signal.

Experiment 4 (H3 - Does steering the commitment direction delay or force commitment and reproduce or cancel the behavioral effect?): Causal test. Data: a held-out 200-item revision-requiring subset disjoint from probe training. Model: the same five frozen models; no weights trained; the difference-in-means commitment direction from Experiment 3 is added or subtracted at the located layer over a dose sweep, seeds {0,1,2}. Systems compared: -commitment-direction during answer-early reasoning (to delay commitment), +commitment-direction during answer-late reasoning (to force early commitment), random-direction, and no-steer. Decisive metric: change in lure-error rate on revision items under steering versus no-steer, with a specificity check that non-revision accuracy is preserved. Convincing result: -direction under answer-early reduces revision lure errors (reproducing the answer-late benefit) with a monotone dose-response, +direction under answer-late cancels the benefit, both exceed random-direction (CIs excluding it), and non-revision accuracy stays within +/-2 pp of no-steer. Indecision band: if the steering effect's 95% CI overlaps random-direction, or shows no dose-response, the causal claim is undecided. Negative result (steering does not move commitment timing or lure errors) would mean the commitment direction is correlational, not the causal lever the hypothesis claims.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Answer-late structure may simply give the model more evidence before answering (a 'more deliberation' effect) rather than a genuine deferral/open-hypothesis effect; mitigated by strict length/content matching, by testing the revision-specific interaction rather than raw accuracy, and by the native cross-lingual variant. (2) Instruction-tuned models may resist the imposed structure or emit the answer regardless of placement; we enforce format, verify structure compliance, and analyze only compliant trials. (3) Reading implicit commitment via answer-slot probabilities is approximate for free-form traces; we use constrained answer slots and multiple liveness thresholds, reporting robustness. (4) Cross-lingual SVO/SOV differences confound grammar with training-data resource level; the within-language answer-early/answer-late manipulation is the primary clean test and all cross-lingual analyses are accuracy-stratified. (5) The commitment direction may entangle with generic confidence/difficulty rather than answer commitment per se; mitigated by matched pre/post-commitment contrasts, held-out validation, random-direction steering, and non-revision specificity checks. (6) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (7) A null result (word-order structure does not shift commitment timing or revision errors) is itself informative, indicating LLM reasoning commitment is independent of surface reasoning-order typology. (8) The head-initial/head-final framing is an operationalized analogy to human prediction-vs-deferral, not a claim of human-like parsing; findings are framed behaviorally and mechanistically.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) answer-deferring/verb-final reasoning structure delays an LLM's commitment relative to answer-early structure; (2) this reduces premature-commitment errors on revision-requiring items; (3) the effect can be measured and causally steered via an internal answer-commitment direction; (4) the within-item content-matched structure manipulation is the main novel lever, with a cross-lingual SVO/SOV framing as a secondary setting. The mechanistic 'commitment direction is decodable/steerable' piece is substantially pre-empted by recent commitment-boundary work. The potentially novel delta is the specific intervention on reasoning structure and its interaction with revision errors. That is non-trivial, but it is closer to a smart application/setting shift than a new mechanism or theory.
revision_notes: State explicitly that the novelty is the structure intervention on reasoning traces, not the commitment probe/steering mechanism.

impact.reasoning: The problem under study is whether reasoning format can reduce premature-answer errors by keeping alternatives alive longer. Who cares: prompt/CoT practitioners, interpretability researchers, and people studying reasoning faithfulness and error modes. If true, it could yield a cheap prompt-structure knob for reducing revision mistakes; if false, it would still inform limits of format-based control. But the real-world reach is moderate: it is mostly about model behavior on a niche class of lure/revision tasks, not a broad capability advance. The 'so what' is credible for research practice, less so for end-user applications unless the effect is robust and generalizable.

Name: articulated_rule_repair
Title: Say-Do Gap: Can an LLM's Own Correctly-Articulated Rule Repair Its Rule-Violating Behavior?
Short Hypothesis: LLMs frequently state a linguistic or symbolic rule correctly (articulation) while violating that same rule during free generation (execution), and this say-do gap reflects a representational dissociation between an articulation pathway and an execution pathway rather than a lack of knowledge; therefore the model's own correctly-articulated rule can be causally injected into the execution stream to close the gap, improving compliance without external supervision.
Related Work: Prior work established the say-do / comprehension-competence gap only behaviorally and treats it as a limitation. Hu & Levy (2023) and Language Models Fail to Introspect (2025) show metalinguistic prompt responses diverge from and underperform direct probability measurements, concluding LLMs lack privileged self-access. Comprehension Without Competence (2025) frames a 'computational split-brain' where instruction and execution pathways are geometrically dissociated, and Large Language Models as Neurolinguistic Subjects (2024) distinguishes performance from competence. On the reasoning side, When Less Language is More (2025) and On Representational Dissociation of Language and Arithmetic (2025) show reasoning/arithmetic occupy regions separable from language. All of these DOCUMENT a gap or dissociation but none (a) test whether the articulation and execution pathways can be jointly located and causally manipulated, (b) ask whether the model's OWN correctly-articulated rule can be causally read out and injected to repair execution, or (c) turn the dissociation from a diagnosed weakness into a self-supervised, training-free repair intervention. We uniquely propose a Location + Causal Intervention account that converts a well-documented deficit into a controllable lever, distinguishing our work from purely descriptive introspection studies and from language-ablation reasoning work.
Abstract: Large language models routinely state a rule correctly yet break the very same rule when they generate freely: they will explain that a sentence should use the subjunctive, avoid a repeated word, respect an order-of-operations convention, or obey a stated constraint, and then produce output that violates it. Prior work documents this say-do gap and concludes that metalinguistic self-report should not be trusted as evidence of a model's generalizations. We take the opposite stance: if the model can articulate the correct rule, the knowledge exists somewhere in the network, and the failure is a dissociation between an articulation pathway (used when asked to state a rule) and an execution pathway (used when generating) rather than an absence of knowledge. We test three claims. First, the gap is real and graded: across linguistic (grammar, style, morphology) and symbolic (arithmetic conventions, format constraints) rule families, models articulate rules they systematically violate in generation, with a measurable say-do gap per rule. Second, articulation and execution are representationally dissociated: a probe can decode the correct rule from hidden states even on trials where the generated output violates it, and the components carrying articulation differ from those driving execution. Third, and most importantly, the dissociation is exploitable: we read out the model's own articulated-rule representation and inject it (via activation patching / steering) into the execution stream, causally increasing rule compliance without any external label or fine-tuning. We compare this self-supervised Articulated-Rule Repair against no-intervention, random-direction, and explicit-rule-prompting baselines across several open-weight models, reporting compliance gains, dose-response, specificity, and fluency cost. Confirming these claims reframes a diagnosed weakness of LLMs as a controllable bridge between what a model knows and what it does.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - Is the say-do gap real and graded across rule families?): Tests whether models articulate rules they systematically violate in generation. Data: a battery of ~15 rules across five families - (a) grammatical (subjunctive, agreement, negative-polarity) using minimal pairs sampled from BLiMP (Warstadt et al. 2020, 67 paradigms x 1000 = 67k pairs; we draw ~500 pairs per selected paradigm), (b) stylistic/discourse (avoid repeating a specified word, maintain a required register), (c) morphological (produce a required inflection), (d) symbolic conventions (order-of-operations formatting, specified numeral base or separator), (e) explicit instruction constraints (do not use the letter e; answer in exactly N words). For each rule we build an ARTICULATION test (forced-choice grammaticality judgment or explicit rule statement scored against ground truth) and an EXECUTION test (free generation where the rule applies, automatically compliance-checked), ~200 items each. We use ~15 rules to span families while keeping five-model coverage affordable. Models: five frozen open-weight instruction-tuned models - Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B; inference only; temperature 0.7 with seeds {0,1,2} plus one greedy pass. Decisive metric: per-rule Say-Do Gap = articulation accuracy minus execution compliance. Convincing result: at least 5 rules show a Say-Do Gap whose 95% bootstrap CI excludes zero while articulation accuracy is near ceiling (knowledge present, execution fails), and the gap tends to grow with rule complexity/output length. Indecision band: rules whose gap 95% CI lies within +/-5 percentage points are counted as no-gap; if fewer than 3 rules clear the band, the premise (a real, exploitable gap) is undecided. Negative result (no reliable gap anywhere) would remove the phenomenon the rest of the hypothesis depends on: articulation and execution would be equally (in)competent, not dissociated.

Experiment 2 (H2 - Are articulation and execution representationally dissociated?): Tests whether the correct rule is decodable from hidden states on trials whose output violates it, and whether articulation-driving and execution-driving components differ. Data: execution trials from Experiment 1 for the rules with a confirmed gap, split 70/15/15 over items, including a labeled subset whose final output violates the rule. Model: the same five frozen models; only per-layer logistic-regression linear probes are trainable (5-fold CV, seeds {0,1,2}); component localization uses activation patching, no weights trained. Decisive metric: held-out probe AUROC for whether the correct rule is satisfied, computed specifically on rule-VIOLATING trials (best layer). Secondary: the Jaccard overlap between components that causally drive the articulation response and those that drive execution compliance, from activation patching. Convincing result: probe AUROC on violated trials clears 0.70 (the rule is internally represented yet not enacted) and the articulation/execution component overlap is low (Jaccard below 0.5), evidencing two pathways. Indecision band: probe AUROC in [0.55, 0.65] on violated trials, or Jaccard in [0.5, 0.7], leaves dissociation undecided. Negative result (rule not decodable on violated trials) would indicate the gap reflects genuinely absent/inaccessible knowledge in the execution context rather than a representational dissociation, predicting the repair in Experiment 3 should fail.

Experiment 3 (H3 - Can the model's own articulated rule be injected to close the gap without supervision?): Tests Articulated-Rule Repair (ARR). Data: a held-out 150-item execution set per gap-rule, disjoint from probe training. Model: the same five frozen models; no weights trained. ARR runs the ARTICULATION prompt, caches the correctly-articulated-rule representation (and, as a more transferable alternative, a difference-in-means rule-active direction from articulation-correct vs articulation-absent contexts), then injects it at mid layers during EXECUTION over a dose sweep, seeds {0,1,2}. Systems compared: no intervention; explicit-rule prompting (restate the rule in the generation prompt); random-direction steering; patching from an INCORRECT articulation; and single-prompt self-consistency (ask-then-generate). Decisive metric: execution compliance gain (percentage points) under ARR versus no intervention. Convincing result: ARR closes at least 30% of the say-do gap, exceeds both the random-direction and incorrect-articulation controls (95% CIs excluding them) - showing it transfers the model's own correct rule, not generic follow-the-rule pressure - shows a monotone dose-response, preserves off-target rules and fluency (external-LM perplexity and unrelated-task accuracy within +/-3 pp of baseline), and rules with a larger probe-decodable-but-violated signal from Experiment 2 benefit more (Spearman rho CI excluding zero). Indecision band: an ARR compliance gain whose 95% CI lies within +/-3 pp of zero, or overlaps the random-direction control, means the repair is undecided. Negative result (ARR fails, or only matches random) would support the alternative that the say-do gap reflects a deeper execution-pathway limitation (an architectural split-brain) rather than a retrievable, injectable dissociation.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The say-do gap may be small or near-zero for some rules once articulation is measured carefully; we include many rule families and report the distribution, and any rules with a genuine gap suffice for the repair test. (2) Articulation scoring can be noisy (open-ended rule statements); we favor forced-choice / minimal-pair articulation where possible and use automatic compliance checkers for execution. (3) The cached articulation representation may not be cleanly transferable across the articulation→execution context shift; we test difference-in-means directions as a more robust alternative and report both. (4) ARR could improve compliance simply by generic 'follow-the-rule' pressure rather than transferring the specific rule; the incorrect-articulation and random-direction controls isolate this. (5) Explicit-rule prompting is a strong, cheap baseline that may match ARR; a finding that ARR only matches it is still informative (it shows the gap is representational and closable internally), and ARR's value is in cases where the rule cannot be conveniently prompted (implicit/self-discovered rules). (6) Effects may be model- or rule-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes. (7) A null repair result is still publishable as evidence that the say-do gap reflects a deeper execution-pathway limitation (consistent with the 'architectural split-brain' hypothesis) rather than a retrievable-knowledge dissociation.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims requiring novelty: (1) LLMs exhibit a graded say-do gap across linguistic/symbolic rule families; (2) this gap reflects representational dissociation between articulation and execution pathways, with rule information decodable even on violating trials; (3) articulation- and execution-relevant components are distinct enough to localize and compare; (4) the model's own articulated-rule representation can be read out and causally injected to repair execution without labels or fine-tuning; (5) the repair is specific to the articulated rule rather than generic compliance pressure. Per the search summary, claims (1)-(2) are already substantially established by recent work on computational split-brain and metalinguistic dissociation, so the descriptive phenomenon is not novel. The actual nontrivial delta is claim (4)-(5): converting the diagnosed dissociation into a training-free causal repair lever via activation patching/steering using the model's own articulated rule. That is meaningfully different from prior descriptive work and not entirely obvious, though it is adjacent to standard activation steering/intervention methods. The closest prior family is say-do gap / split-brain work plus generic activation steering; the delta is self-supervised extraction of internally articulated rule representations and rule-specific injection into execution.
revision_notes: Narrow the claimed novelty explicitly: present the main contribution as a causal self-repair intervention, not discovery of the say-do gap or dissociation.
Add a sharper comparison to closest mechanistic baselines: generic activation steering, task-vector methods, activation patching, and ask-then-generate prompting.
Specify what is uniquely new about ARR relative to explicit-rule prompting: e.g., cases where the rule is internally recoverable but not externally restated in the execution prompt.
Include at least one setting where the rule is latent/implicit rather than explicitly restatable, to strengthen novelty beyond a prompt-engineering variant.
State whether the novelty lies in mechanism, finding, or setting; right now mechanism is strongest, while the rest reads partially pre-empted.

impact.reasoning: The phenomenon under study is failure of models to execute rules they can correctly articulate, and whether internal representations of the articulated rule can be used to repair instruction/rule compliance. Who cares: interpretability researchers, controllable generation and alignment/instruction-following researchers, and practitioners who want stronger compliance without fine-tuning. Strongest case: if internal rule representations can be causally reused to fix execution, this offers a self-supervised lever for improving behavior and a concrete test of whether the say-do gap is a tractable routing problem versus an architectural limit. This is a real problem rather than a niche curiosity, and even a negative result would matter because it supports the architectural-limit account. Follow-up work would likely cite it in interpretability and control circles. However, real-world reach depends heavily on effect size and whether ARR beats cheap baselines like explicit-rule prompting; if prompting matches ARR, practical impact drops. The result could shift direction modestly by reframing introspection from merely untrustworthy evidence to a manipulable internal resource, but only if the intervention is robust and specific.

review.reasoning: The proposal is testable and reasonably well scoped, with concrete experiments, controls, and success criteria. The central hypothesis is falsifiable: decodable-but-not-enacted rule representations should exist, and injecting them should improve compliance. The inclusion of random-direction, incorrect-articulation, and explicit-rule-prompt baselines is good. Still, there are notable logical and methodological gaps. The proposal overinterprets articulation as evidence that 'the knowledge exists' and dissociation as the explanation, when alternative explanations include decoding artifacts, prompt-format mismatch, search failures, or weak articulation measures. Jaccard overlap of 'components' from activation patching is underspecified and may not be a stable or meaningful measure of pathway dissociation. Probe AUROC >0.70 on violating trials does not by itself establish a causally relevant representation. ARR may simply add generic steering toward shorter/safer/more constrained outputs unless stronger off-target and specificity controls are added. The experiment plan also leaves key details open: how compliance is scored across heterogeneous rule families, where/when activations are cached and injected, how layer/site selection is chosen without leakage, and how to prevent contamination between articulation and execution contexts. Feasibility is plausible on open-weight models, but the current story is mechanistically stronger than the evidence plan can cleanly support. If executed very well it could be workshop/TMLR/interpretability-paper material; for a stronger ML venue it needs tighter causal design and sharper baseline positioning.

Name: iconic_naming_bootstrap
Title: Names That Help You Think: Does Sound-Symbolic Iconicity Bootstrap In-Context Learning and Referent Binding in LLMs?
Short Hypothesis: Iconicity (sound-meaning congruence, e.g. 'kiki' for spiky) is not merely something LLMs passively recognize; it functions as a cognitive scaffold: when novel entities, variables, or categories are given iconic rather than arbitrary or anti-iconic names, an LLM learns them faster in-context, binds them to their referents more reliably, and makes fewer errors on downstream reasoning about them, and this facilitation is mediated by a locatable binding/association component whose engagement rises under iconic naming.
Related Work: A large recent cluster establishes that LLMs and VLMs can *recognize* sound symbolism: they exhibit bouba-kiki-like preferences (Kiki or Bouba?, 2023; With Ears to See, 2024; LEX-ICON, 2025; Adversarially Probing Cross-Family Sound Symbolism, 2025), can generate iconic pseudowords humans decode (Iconicity in LLMs, 2025), and encode iconicity as a psycholinguistic feature in embeddings (Word Meanings in Transformer LMs, 2025; Where meaning lives, 2026). Neuron-level work (Unveiling Language Competence Neurons, 2024) finds GPT-2-XL lacks specialized sound-shape neurons. Crucially, ALL of this treats iconicity as a perceptual/associative fact to be detected, never as an instrumental resource that changes reasoning or learning performance. Meanwhile human developmental science shows sound symbolism *facilitates* infant word learning (Miyazaki et al., 2013; Imai & Kita's sound-symbolism-bootstrapping hypothesis) and the physics-rooted account (2022) explains why iconic mappings are learnable. We are the first to transfer the bootstrapping hypothesis into LLMs: does iconic naming causally improve in-context learning, referent binding, and reasoning, and is there an internal binding mechanism that iconicity strengthens? This distinguishes us from all recognition-only prior work.
Abstract: Human infants learn words tagged with iconic sounds (round meanings for round-sounding words) faster than arbitrary ones, a phenomenon known as the sound-symbolism bootstrapping hypothesis. Large language models are known to *recognize* iconicity, but no work asks whether iconicity is functionally useful to them: does giving an LLM a sound-symbolically congruent name for a new entity help it actually learn and reason about that entity? We test whether iconic naming acts as a cognitive scaffold. We construct in-context learning and reasoning tasks in which novel entities, categories, or variables (defined only by their properties in context) are assigned names drawn from three regimes: iconic (name's phonology matches the entity's property, e.g. a spiky object named 'kikith'), arbitrary (phonologically neutral names), and anti-iconic (name mismatches the property, e.g. a spiky object named 'boumo'). Holding all content identical, we measure whether name regime changes (1) in-context learning speed (accuracy vs. number of examples), (2) referent-binding reliability (do models keep the right name attached to the right entity across a long context and under distractors), and (3) downstream reasoning accuracy about the entities. We predict an iconicity gradient: iconic > arbitrary > anti-iconic, with anti-iconic names causing systematic binding errors. Mechanistically, we locate a binding/association signal (via probing name-to-referent linkage in hidden states and attention) and test whether iconic naming increases its strength and whether steering it reproduces or cancels the naming benefit. Across several open-weight models we quantify the iconicity-facilitation effect, its dissociation from mere name memorability/length, and its mechanistic mediation, reframing iconicity from a recognized association into a controllable lever on machine learning and reasoning.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - Does iconic naming speed learning, tighten binding, and cut reasoning errors in a graded way?): Tests the predicted iconicity gradient (iconic > arbitrary > anti-iconic), including a systematic anti-iconic cost. Data: iconicity-graded pseudoword name banks built from validated cross-linguistic phoneme-to-meaning mappings (Bouba-Kiki shape/spectral cues; LEX-ICON size/speed/brightness dimensions) across four semantic dimensions (shape, size, speed, brightness); for each dimension we build iconic, arbitrary (phonologically neutral, length- and frequency-matched), and anti-iconic name sets, with iconicity validated by an independent classifier and human ratings on a sample. Three tasks, ~250 items per dimension each (content held identical across name regimes): (a) in-context category learning with learning curves over k labeled examples, (b) referent binding over N novel named entities with intervening distractor context, (c) downstream multi-step reasoning (comparison, sorting, relational inference) where the property matters. Controls: length/frequency matching, a scrambled-iconic control (same phonemes, wrong dimension), an orthographic-only vs IPA-provided variant, and a name-recall-alone memorability check. Models: five frozen open-weight instruction-tuned models - Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B; inference only; temperature 0.7 with seeds {0,1,2} plus greedy. Decisive metric: name-regime effect on referent-binding accuracy (primary), plus in-context learning-curve AUC and reasoning accuracy, in a mixed-effects model outcome ~ name_regime + dimension + task + (1|model) + (1|item). Convincing result: a monotone gradient with iconic > arbitrary (95% CI excluding zero) AND anti-iconic < arbitrary (the sharpest signature that phonology is used, not ignored), surviving the scrambled-iconic and memorability controls and present under the IPA variant. Indecision band: if BOTH the iconic-minus-arbitrary and arbitrary-minus-anti-iconic differences have 95% CIs within +/-3 percentage points, the gradient is undecided. Negative result (no gradient, or gains explained by memorability/length) would show LLMs recognize iconicity but cannot exploit it as a learning scaffold, dissociating them from the human bootstrapping account.

Experiment 2 (H2 - Is there a locatable binding component whose engagement rises under iconic naming?): Location plus mediation. Data: binding trials from Experiment 1, 70/15/15 train/validation/test over items. Model: the same five frozen models; only per-layer logistic-regression linear probes are trainable (5-fold CV, seeds {0,1,2}); name-token to entity-token attention is read out without training. Decisive metric: held-out probe AUROC for decoding which entity a name is currently bound to (best layer); secondary: name-to-referent binding attention magnitude. Convincing result: best-layer AUROC clears 0.70, iconic naming yields higher probe-decodable binding and stronger binding attention than arbitrary while anti-iconic degrades both (CIs excluding zero), and per-item behavioral facilitation correlates with per-item binding-signal increase (Spearman rho CI excluding zero). Indecision band: AUROC in [0.55, 0.65], or a mediation rho whose 95% CI is within +/-0.1 of zero, leaves the mechanism undecided. Negative result (no binding signal, or it does not track naming) would sever any behavioral iconicity benefit from a binding mechanism.

Experiment 3 (H3 - Does steering a binding-strength direction reproduce or cancel the iconicity benefit?): Causal test. Data: a held-out 200-item binding/reasoning subset disjoint from probe training. Model: the same five frozen models; no weights trained; a difference-in-means binding-strength direction (correctly-bound vs mis-bound trials) is added or subtracted at the located layer over a dose sweep, seeds {0,1,2}. Systems compared: +direction under arbitrary/anti-iconic naming (to recover the iconic-level benefit), -direction under iconic naming (to cancel it), random-direction, and no-steer. Decisive metric: change in binding accuracy (and mis-binding rate) under steering versus no-steer, with a specificity check that off-target reasoning is preserved. Convincing result: +direction under arbitrary/anti-iconic recovers a substantial share of the iconic advantage with a monotone dose-response, -direction under iconic cancels it, both exceed random-direction (CIs excluding it), and off-target reasoning stays within +/-2 pp of no-steer. Indecision band: a steering effect whose 95% CI overlaps random-direction, or shows no dose-response, leaves causal mediation undecided. Negative result (steering does not move binding) would mean the binding direction is correlational, not the causal scaffold the hypothesis requires.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Iconicity effects may be washed out by tokenization (pseudowords split unpredictably), muting phonological signal; mitigated by testing IPA-provided variants, spelled-out phoneme forms, and multiple tokenizers/models, and by reporting whether any facilitation survives. (2) The effect could be pure memorability rather than binding facilitation; the name-recall-alone control and the anti-iconic *cost* prediction isolate genuine dimension-congruence effects. (3) Arbitrary/anti-iconic classification of pseudowords is imperfect; we use validated cross-linguistic mappings, an independent iconicity classifier, and human-rated samples, plus the scrambled-iconic control. (4) Instruction-tuned models may be robust binders, yielding ceiling effects that hide differences; we increase entity count, add distractors, and lengthen context to avoid ceiling. (5) The binding direction may entangle with generic difficulty; random-direction and specificity controls address this. (6) Effects may be small or model/dimension-specific; we test multiple models and dimensions and report effect sizes. (7) A null result (iconic naming gives no learning/reasoning advantage) is itself highly informative: it would show LLMs recognize iconicity but cannot *exploit* it as a learning scaffold, cleanly dissociating them from the human bootstrapping account. (8) The developmental bootstrapping framing is an operationalized analogy, not a claim of human-like acquisition; findings are framed behaviorally and mechanistically.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) iconic vs arbitrary vs anti-iconic novel names causally affect in-context learning speed, referent binding, and reasoning in LLMs; (2) the effect is directional/graded, not just a detection of bouba-kiki preferences; (3) the benefit is mediated by an internal binding/association signal and can be causally steered; (4) the setting is novel-word learning/reasoning in LLMs rather than human infant learning or model recognition. This is meaningfully different from prior recognition-only work and from MAGNIFICo-style novel-word learning without iconicity. The delta is strong and non-obvious, though the underlying phenomenon is adjacent to existing sound-symbolism and in-context learning literature.

Yes, serious researchers would care either way because the result distinguishes recognitional iconicity from functional utility; practitioners only modestly so.

Name: counterfactual_marker_reasoning
Title: Mood Matters: Does a Grammatical Counterfactual Marker Unlock an LLM's Counterfactual Reasoning?
Short Hypothesis: Bloom's contested claim that languages lacking a dedicated counterfactual/irrealis marker impair counterfactual reasoning can be tested cleanly inside LLMs: framing an identical problem with an explicit counterfactual mood marker (subjunctive/irrealis) versus an unmarked indicative causally improves the model's counterfactual reasoning and more strongly engages an internal 'irrealis mode' that keeps the actual world and the hypothetical world distinct; steering along this irrealis direction reproduces or cancels the marker's behavioral benefit.
Related Work: Bloom (1981) argued Chinese speakers reason counterfactually less because Chinese lacks a distinct subjunctive marker; this is contested (Exploring counterfactuals in English and Chinese, 2023, shows Chinese uses lexical/contextual cues). Recent LLM linguistic-relativity work is observational: BICAUSE (Under the Shadow of Babel, 2025) shows LLMs internalize language-specific causal-order attention biases; the Sapir-Whorf reproduction study (2025) probes behavioral alignment; grammatical-concept work (LLMs Share Representations of Latent Grammatical Concepts, 2025; Naturalistic Causal Probing for Morpho-Syntax, 2022; A Geometric Notion of Causal Probing, 2023) shows number/gender/tense are shared, linearly-encoded, causally manipulable directions but never links a grammatical MOOD marker to a REASONING capability. My prior proposals covered evidentiality, future-tense present-bias, word-order commitment, and dual-process gears, but none address counterfactual/irrealis mood or counterfactual reasoning. This work is the first to (1) turn Bloom's famous counterfactual-marker claim into a controlled within-item grammatical manipulation in LLMs, (2) test whether the marker causally changes counterfactual-reasoning accuracy dissociated from language resource level, and (3) locate an 'irrealis mode' representation that separates actual from hypothetical worlds and steer it to reproduce/cancel the effect.
Abstract: A landmark and still-contested claim in the language-and-thought literature (Bloom, 1981) holds that speakers of languages lacking a dedicated counterfactual/irrealis marker reason counterfactually less readily than speakers of languages with an explicit subjunctive. Human tests are confounded by culture and education; large language models offer a clean testbed where content can be held fixed and only grammatical mood varied. We ask whether the presence of a counterfactual mood marker causally changes how well an LLM reasons about hypothetical, contrary-to-fact worlds. We construct counterfactual-reasoning items (contrary-to-fact conditionals requiring the model to compute what would follow in a hypothetical world without contaminating it with actual-world facts) and manipulate, within-item and content-matched, whether the antecedent is grammatically marked as counterfactual (subjunctive/irrealis) versus stated in unmarked indicative form, plus a native cross-lingual variant across strong-marker (English, Spanish) and weak-marker (Chinese, Indonesian) languages. Behaviorally, we measure counterfactual-reasoning accuracy and a diagnostic 'actual-world intrusion' error rate (importing real-world facts the hypothetical explicitly overrides). We predict the counterfactual marker improves accuracy and reduces intrusion errors, selectively on genuinely contrary-to-fact items. Mechanistically, we locate an 'irrealis mode' direction from hidden states contrasting counterfactual versus factual framings, test whether the marker increases its engagement and whether items with stronger engagement suffer fewer intrusions, and causally steer it: adding the direction under unmarked framing should recover the benefit, subtracting it under marked framing should cancel it. Across several open-weight models we quantify the marker effect, its dissociation from language resource level, and steering controllability, delivering the first mechanistic adjudication of Bloom's hypothesis.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - Does a counterfactual mood marker causally improve counterfactual reasoning and cut actual-world intrusions?): Tests whether an explicit counterfactual/irrealis marker raises counterfactual accuracy and lowers actual-world intrusion errors, selectively on genuinely contrary-to-fact items. Data: ~400 counterfactual-reasoning items, each a contrary-to-fact scenario with a question requiring reasoning in the hypothetical world; each is paired with a matched FACTUAL (indicative, real-world) control and includes an 'already-true' subset where the hypothetical coincides with reality (selectivity control). Each item carries a labeled correct counterfactual answer AND a labeled actual-world-intrusion lure (the answer following from reverting to real-world facts). We use 400 items to fit the marker x item-type interaction with adequate power while keeping five-model coverage affordable. Marked and unmarked forms are content-, entity-, and length-matched; marker strength is validated by independent grammaticality ratings. Manipulation (within-item): MARKED form with an explicit subjunctive/irrealis marker (If A had been Q...; were A to be Q...) vs UNMARKED indicative conveying the same hypothetical content lexically (Assume A is Q now; then...). Cross-lingual variant (secondary): translate items into strong-marker (English, Spanish) and weak-marker (Chinese, Indonesian) languages, back-translation checked, accuracy-stratified. A length-matched non-mood reflection preamble is added as a control against generic extra structure. Models: five frozen open-weight instruction-tuned models - Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Aya-23-8B, Gemma-2-9B; inference only; temperature 0.7 with seeds {0,1,2} plus greedy. Decisive metric: actual-world intrusion rate (primary) and counterfactual accuracy, in a mixed-effects model outcome ~ mood_marker*item_type + (1|model) + (1|item). Convincing result: MARKED framing lowers intrusion and raises accuracy selectively on contrary-to-fact items (marker x item_type interaction 95% CI excluding zero) with little effect on factual/already-true controls, the non-mood reflection control does not reproduce it, and native strong-marker languages track the effect after competence stratification. Indecision band: a marker x item_type interaction whose 95% CI lies within +/-2 percentage points is undecided. Negative result (no marker benefit, intrusions unchanged) would be the cleanest evidence to date AGAINST Bloom's mechanistic reading, since cultural confounds are absent.

Experiment 2 (H2 - Is there a locatable irrealis-mode direction the marker more strongly engages?): Location plus mediation. Data: hidden states on matched marked-vs-unmarked and counterfactual-vs-factual contrasts, 70/15/15 over items. Model: the same five frozen models; only per-layer logistic-regression probes are trainable (5-fold CV, seeds {0,1,2}); a difference-in-means irrealis direction is derived without training. Decisive metric: held-out probe AUROC for hypothetical/irrealis vs factual mode (best layer); then whether the marker increases projection onto the irrealis direction and whether per-item irrealis engagement correlates with fewer intrusion errors (Spearman). Convincing result: best-layer AUROC clears 0.70, MARKED framing raises projection onto the irrealis direction (CI excluding zero), and engagement predicts fewer intrusions (rho CI excluding zero). Indecision band: AUROC in [0.55, 0.65], or a mediation rho within +/-0.1 of zero, leaves the mechanism undecided. Negative result (no irrealis direction, or it does not track the marker) would detach any behavioral marker benefit from an internal actual-vs-hypothetical separation.

Experiment 3 (H3 - Does steering the irrealis direction reproduce or cancel the marker's benefit?): Causal test. Data: a held-out 200-item counterfactual subset disjoint from probe training. Model: the same five frozen models; no weights trained; the irrealis direction is added or subtracted at the located layer over a dose sweep, seeds {0,1,2}. Systems compared: +irrealis-direction during UNMARKED reasoning (to recover accuracy / cut intrusions), -irrealis-direction during MARKED reasoning (to cancel the benefit), random-direction, and no-steer. Decisive metric: change in actual-world intrusion rate (and accuracy) under steering versus no-steer, with a specificity check that factual-item accuracy and fluency are preserved. Convincing result: +direction under UNMARKED reproduces a substantial fraction of the marker benefit with a monotone dose-response, -direction under MARKED cancels it, both exceed random-direction (CIs excluding it), and factual-item accuracy stays within +/-2 pp of no-steer. Indecision band: a steering effect whose 95% CI overlaps random-direction, or shows no dose-response, leaves causal mediation undecided. Negative result (steering does not move counterfactual behavior) would mean the irrealis direction is correlational, not causal, weakening the mechanistic adjudication of Bloom's hypothesis.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Unmarked indicative framings may still convey counterfactuality lexically well enough that the model reasons correctly, muting the marker effect; a null result is itself informative (it would provide the cleanest evidence to date AGAINST Bloom's mechanistic reading, since cultural confounds are absent) and we sharpen sensitivity with intrusion-error metrics and difficulty-calibrated items. (2) Cross-lingual differences confound grammar with training-data resource level; the within-language marked/unmarked manipulation is the primary clean test and cross-lingual analyses are accuracy-stratified. (3) Marked vs unmarked forms may differ in length/emphasis rather than mood per se; we length-match, use independent marker-strength ratings, add a non-mood reflection control, and rely on content-matched steering to isolate mood. (4) The irrealis direction may entangle with generic difficulty or hedging rather than a genuine actual-vs-hypothetical world separation; mitigated by matched contrasts, held-out probe validation, random-direction steering, and factual-item specificity checks. (5) Instruction-tuned models may reason counterfactually robustly regardless of marking, yielding ceiling effects; we calibrate item difficulty, include harder multi-step hypotheticals, and test multiple models. (6) Effects may be small or model-specific; we report effect sizes with CIs across models. (7) Bloom's hypothesis framing is operationalized behaviorally/mechanistically, not as a claim about human-like cognition.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims needing novelty: (1) explicit grammatical counterfactual/irrealis marking improves LLM counterfactual reasoning on content-matched items; (2) the effect specifically reduces actual-world intrusion by helping separate actual vs hypothetical worlds; (3) an internal 'irrealis mode' representation can be identified and is more engaged by marked prompts; (4) causal steering along that direction can reproduce/remove the marker effect; (5) this serves as a confound-reduced adjudication of Bloom's marker->reasoning hypothesis. Relative to prior work, the probe/steer mechanism is standard and the general idea of grammatical-feature directions is well-trodden. The real novelty is the specific phenomenon: connecting grammatical mood marking to reasoning behavior via within-item manipulations and a causal interpretability test. That is meaningfully different from prior grammatical-concept papers and from human Bloom-style debates, but it is also an obvious member of a broader template family applying the same recipe to another grammatical feature. So novelty is moderate: new finding/setting/problem operationalization, not a new method or theory.

impact.reasoning: The actual problem under study is whether grammatical packaging of counterfactuals changes a model's ability to keep actual and hypothetical worlds distinct. Who cares: cognitive science/linguistic relativity researchers, multilingual NLP, and interpretability researchers interested in language-conditioned reasoning. Strongest case: if true, small grammatical cues can causally alter reasoning fidelity, implying prompt formulation and multilingual evaluation may systematically bias measured reasoning. This is more than a niche curiosity because counterfactual reasoning is important, but the practical effect size and downstream consequences are uncertain, and the search context suggests a likely null. If the result is positive, it could influence prompt design, multilingual benchmarking, and theories of internal world modeling; if null, it still provides a clean negative test of a famous claim. The "so what" test is partially passed: serious researchers would likely update how they think about grammatical framing effects and multilingual reasoning evaluation, though everyday practitioners may not change much unless effects are sizable and robust.

review.reasoning: The proposal is reasonably precise and falsifiable, with concrete hypotheses, controls, and mixed-effects analyses. It is stronger than many early-stage proposals because it specifies primary metrics, directional predictions, steering controls, and major risks. However, several logical gaps remain. The central causal claim may be undermined if 'unmarked' prompts still lexically encode counterfactuality, making the manipulation weak or ambiguous. The cross-lingual component is underpowered conceptually because marker strength is entangled with pretraining/resource differences despite stratification. The probe evidence risks circularity: framing differences may reflect stylistic/hedging/difficulty signals rather than a clean world-separation variable, and mediation by projection is correlational. Steering success would not by itself prove the naturally used representation is specifically counterfactual rather than generic uncertainty. Related work is adequate but not fully specific about the closest probe/steer baselines. Overall, if executed very well it could be workshop/findings-worthy and possibly a solid main-venue empirical paper if effects are clean and robust, but as written it needs tighter operationalization and stronger controls to support the headline causal interpretation.
