Name: metaphor_scaffold_reasoning
Title: Thinking Through the Concrete: Do LLMs Recruit Source-Domain Structure as a Scaffold for Abstract Reasoning?
Short Hypothesis: When reasoning about an abstract target domain, an LLM recruits an internal representation of a concrete source domain (per Conceptual Metaphor Theory) and imports that source's relational/geometric structure into its inference; consequently, a metaphor whose source structure is ISOMORPHIC to the target's true structure causally improves abstract reasoning, while a structurally MISMATCHED source causally corrupts it, and this scaffold is a locatable, steerable internal signal rather than mere surface phrasing.
Related Work: Prior work shows metaphor knowledge is encoded in PLM middle layers (Metaphors in PLMs, 2022), that CMT-style prompting improves reasoning behaviorally (CMT as a Prompting Paradigm, 2025), and that metaphors in training data can causally drive cross-domain misalignment via latent features (Metaphors are a Source of Cross-Domain Misalignment, 2026). Grounding-theory work (Meaning without Reference, 2022; The Vector Grounding Problem, 2023; Mechanistic Emergence of Symbol Grounding, 2025) and abstract-concept work (BACH-V, 2026; How Deep is Love, 2025) study whether abstractions connect to concrete/perceptual representations, and BACH-V shows abstract value probes transfer to concrete events. However, NONE test the core CMT claim as a mechanism for reasoning: that abstract inference is *computed by importing structure from a concrete source domain*, that reasoning accuracy is a function of source-target STRUCTURAL ALIGNMENT (helping when isomorphic, harming when mismatched), or that this scaffold is a locatable, causally-steerable internal representation dissociable from surface metaphor phrasing. We uniquely turn CMT into a controlled structure-alignment law with a Location + Causal Intervention mechanism account, and add a high-stakes failure mode (mismatched metaphors corrupting inference).
Abstract: Conceptual Metaphor Theory holds that humans reason about abstract domains (time, quantity, social status, causation) by mapping them onto concrete source domains (space, physical size, verticality, force). We ask whether large language models do the same computationally: when an LLM reasons about an abstract target, does it recruit an internal representation of a concrete source domain and import that source's relational structure into its inference? We make three claims. First, structure-alignment law: for abstract reasoning problems whose correct answers depend on a specific relational structure, framing the problem with a metaphor whose source domain is structurally isomorphic to the target improves accuracy, whereas a structurally mismatched source (identical surface metaphor style, but wrong mapping) degrades it below a literal, metaphor-free baseline. This predicts a dose-response between source-target structural alignment and reasoning accuracy, and a diagnostic failure mode where a mismatched metaphor induces systematic, predictable errors. Second, representational recruitment: on abstract-reasoning trials, a probe trained only on concrete source-domain stimuli can decode the source-domain quantity from the model's hidden states, and this decodable source signal is stronger when the metaphor is aligned. Third, causal scaffold: the source-domain representation is a locatable direction that, when steered, changes abstract-reasoning behavior in the predicted direction and can rescue mismatched-metaphor errors or induce them under literal framing. Across several open-weight models we quantify the alignment law, the recruited-source-signal-to-behavior link, and steering controllability, reframing metaphor from decorative phrasing into a causal computational scaffold for machine abstraction.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - Does a structurally aligned metaphor help and a mismatched one corrupt abstract reasoning?): Tests the structure-alignment law: aligned metaphor improves accuracy, structurally mismatched metaphor degrades it below a literal baseline, with a dose-response and a diagnostic mismatch-lure error mode. Data: four CMT domain pairs - TIME<-SPACE, QUANTITY<-VERTICALITY/SIZE, SOCIAL-STATUS<-VERTICALITY, CAUSATION<-FORCE - with ~250 relational-reasoning items each (comparison, ordering, transitive-inference, dominance), ~1000 total, whose correct answer depends only on the underlying relational structure. Each item carries a labeled correct answer AND a labeled mismatch-lure (the answer following a wrongly-oriented mapping). Framings (within-item, content-, register- and length-matched, format-enforced): LITERAL (plain relational statement), ALIGNED (canonical source, correct-orientation mapping), MISMATCHED (same metaphor register, structurally wrong mapping), and NEUTRAL-metaphor (irrelevant source) to separate figurative phrasing from structure. Alignment/mismatch labels are validated by independent annotators; a graded-alignment variant with partially-consistent mappings supports a dose-response test. Models: five frozen open-weight instruction-tuned models - Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B; inference only; temperature 0.7 with seeds {0,1,2} plus greedy. Decisive metric: accuracy by framing in a mixed-effects model accuracy ~ framing*target_domain + (1|model) + (1|item), with the predicted ordering ALIGNED > LITERAL > NEUTRAL ~ MISMATCHED; secondary: mismatch-lure error rate and the continuous structural-alignment dose-response slope. Convincing result: ALIGNED > LITERAL and MISMATCHED < LITERAL (both 95% CIs excluding zero), mismatch errors concentrate on the labeled mismatch-lure (evidence the wrong source structure was applied), and the alignment dose-response slope CI excludes zero. A high-stakes CAUSATION<-FORCE replication on medical/policy 'which factor drove the outcome' vignettes should show the mismatch corruption transferring to consequential causal attribution. Indecision band: if BOTH the aligned-minus-literal and mismatched-minus-literal differences have 95% CIs within +/-2 percentage points, the alignment law is undecided. Negative result (metaphor framing does not move accuracy, or mismatch does not corrupt) would show metaphor is decorative phrasing, not a computational scaffold.

Experiment 2 (H2 - Is a concrete source-domain quantity recruited and readable during abstract reasoning?): Location plus mediation. Data: abstract-reasoning trials from Experiment 1, plus a separate set of literal concrete source-domain stimuli (spatial/size/force comparisons) used ONLY to train the probe; 70/15/15 over items. Model: the same five frozen models; only per-layer linear probes/regressors are trainable (5-fold CV, seeds {0,1,2}). Decisive metric: held-out AUROC/regression accuracy for decoding the source-domain quantity on abstract trials, from a probe trained solely on concrete source stimuli, against a literal-only-probe baseline (best layer). Convincing result: source-quantity is decodable on abstract trials above the literal-only baseline, decodability is higher under aligned than literal framing and MISORIENTED under mismatched framing (the probe reads the wrong value in a way that predicts the behavioral lure), and per-item recruited-signal strength/orientation correlates with per-item accuracy and lure errors (Spearman CI excluding zero). Indecision band: abstract-trial decoding AUROC in [0.55, 0.65] over the literal baseline, or a mediation rho within +/-0.1 of zero, leaves recruitment undecided. Negative result (no source signal beyond generic magnitude, or no orientation flip under mismatch) would argue against genuine source recruitment.

Experiment 3 (H3 - Does steering the source-domain direction rescue mismatch errors and induce them under literal framing?): Causal test. Data: a held-out 200-item subset disjoint from probe training. Model: the same five frozen models; no weights trained; a difference-in-means source-domain direction (high vs low source-quantity concrete stimuli) is added at chosen orientations over a dose sweep, seeds {0,1,2}. Systems compared: +correct-orientation during MISMATCHED or LITERAL framing (to rescue/boost accuracy), wrong-orientation during LITERAL framing (to induce mismatch-lure errors without any metaphor in the prompt), random-direction, and no-steer. Decisive metric: change in accuracy and mismatch-lure error rate under steering versus no-steer, with a specificity check that off-target reasoning and fluency are preserved. Convincing result: correct-orientation steering rescues mismatched/literal accuracy and wrong-orientation steering induces the mismatch-lure errors, both with monotone dose-response and exceeding random-direction (CIs excluding it), off-target accuracy within +/-2 pp of no-steer. Indecision band: a steering effect whose 95% CI overlaps random-direction, or lacks dose-response, leaves the causal-scaffold claim undecided. Negative result (steering the source direction does not move abstract reasoning) would mean the recruited source signal is correlational, not the causal scaffold claimed.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Aligned vs mismatched framings may differ in fluency/plausibility rather than pure structure; mitigated by length/register matching, the neutral-metaphor control, annotator-validated alignment labels, and the content-matched steering that isolates the source representation from surface phrasing. (2) Instruction-tuned models may reason robustly from the literal content and ignore the metaphor, muting effects; a small/null alignment effect on aligned items would still be informative, and the MISMATCH-corruption prediction (metaphor actively hurting) is the sharpest, most novel test even if aligned metaphors merely match the literal baseline. (3) A probe trained on concrete stimuli decoding on abstract trials could reflect generic magnitude features shared by both rather than genuine source recruitment; mitigated by domain-specific probes, the orientation prediction under mismatch (probe reads the WRONG value in a way that predicts behavior), and random-direction steering controls. (4) The steering direction may entangle with generic difficulty/confidence; addressed by orientation-specific (not just magnitude) predictions, specificity checks, and dose-response. (5) Some abstract domains may lack a single canonical source, making mismatch design ambiguous; we restrict to well-established CMT mappings and report robustness across the four pairs. (6) Effects may be model- or domain-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (7) The CMT framing is operationalized behaviorally/mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like embodied cognition.

novelty.reasoning: Core technical claims needing novelty are: (1) a structure-alignment law where abstract reasoning accuracy varies with source-target structural isomorphism; (2) a sharp negative prediction that structurally mismatched metaphors impair reasoning below a literal baseline and concentrate errors on a predicted mismatch-lure; (3) representational recruitment, where a probe trained only on concrete source-domain data decodes source quantity/orientation on abstract trials; (4) causal steering, where orientation-specific interventions rescue or induce the predicted errors; and (5) the claim that this scaffold is dissociable from surface phrasing. Relative to prior work in the search summary, the ingredients are individually pre-empted: CMT prompting, latent metaphor features, metaphor-based steering, and abstract grounding all exist. The actual delta is the integrated, falsifiable mechanism with graded alignment, below-literal mismatch corruption, orientation-flip signatures, and source-only probe generalization to abstract trials. That is non-trivial and more than an obvious baseline extension, but it is still an incremental synthesis over an active family rather than a wholly new paradigm or task.

impact.reasoning: The phenomenon under study is whether metaphor/source-domain structure systematically scaffolds and sometimes corrupts abstract reasoning in LLMs. The main stakeholders are interpretability researchers, reasoning and safety communities, CMT-prompting researchers, and practitioners deploying models in medical, policy, or other decision-support settings. The strongest case for importance is that if mismatched metaphors can reliably distort causal or abstract inference below a literal baseline, then prompt wording itself becomes a mechanistic safety risk and a lever for robustness. This is more than a niche curiosity: even a simple result would matter if it reveals a robust failure mode and a general mechanism for reasoning behavior. The likely uptake is good because the work speaks to several active areas and offers testable diagnostics. The 'so what?' test is mostly passed: if the result holds, researchers would test metaphor sensitivity and avoid mismatched framings; if it fails, that also constrains strong CMT-style mechanistic claims.

Name: naming_as_compositional_chunking
Title: A Rose by a Shorter Name: Does Giving a Sub-Skill a Compact Label Let LLMs Compose It Into Novel Combinations?
Short Hypothesis: A central claim for why language powers intelligence is that it compresses reusable knowledge into compact, nameable chunks that can be recombined combinatorially. We hypothesize this operates inside LLMs at inference time: teaching a model a reusable sub-procedure under a compact NAME (a short lexical handle) lets it compose that sub-procedure into novel, unseen combinations more reliably than teaching the identical procedure spelled out verbosely each time, and the compact name creates a locatable, reusable internal 'subroutine' representation that is causally invoked during composition.
Related Work: A cluster of theory argues language aids intelligence by offering compact, culturally-evolved abstractions that enable generalization (How important is language for human-like intelligence?, 2025; Language as a bootstrap for compositional visual reasoning, 2021; Thinking in Words, 2014; Emergent Symbolic Cognition, 2025). Latent/implicit-reasoning work (Coconut, 2024; Implicit CoT via Distillation, 2023; Stepwise Internalization, 2024; A Survey on Latent Reasoning, 2025) shows reasoning can move out of verbal space entirely, and 'Why think step by step?' (2023) explains when intermediate steps help. Abstraction-of-Thought (2024) shows explicit abstraction layers improve reasoning. My own prior proposals covered iconic (sound-symbolic) naming aiding referent binding and lexicalization-gap effects on concept resolution. NONE of these isolate the *compression-for-composition* claim: that a compact name (versus a length-matched verbose description of the identical procedure) is what enables recombination into novel compositions, that this yields a compositional-generalization gain distinct from mere memorization or length, or that naming installs a reusable, causally-invokable internal subroutine. We uniquely turn the 'language compresses abstractions into reusable chunks' thesis into a controlled naming-vs-verbose intervention with a Location + Causal Intervention mechanism account, and tie it to a high-stakes agentic skill-composition setting.
Abstract: Why does language make minds more powerful? A leading answer is that language compresses reusable knowledge into compact, nameable chunks that can be freely recombined, turning a finite vocabulary into a combinatorial engine for novel thought. We test whether this compression-for-composition principle operates inside large language models. In-context, we teach a model a reusable sub-procedure (e.g., a small transformation on strings, lists, or graph states) in one of two ways that convey identical content: under a compact NAME (a short coined handle, 'let ZORP mean <procedure>') versus a length- and content-matched VERBOSE description that must be restated at each use. We then require the model to solve novel COMPOSITIONS — problems whose solutions chain the taught sub-procedure with others in combinations never demonstrated. Our central prediction is a naming-by-composition-depth interaction: compact naming yields a growing advantage on deeper/novel compositions, while offering little benefit on single-step reuse, and this advantage is not explained by prompt length, memorability, or surface repetition. We further predict compact naming reduces 'leakage' errors where the sub-procedure's internals bleed into unrelated steps. Mechanistically, we test whether a compact name installs a reusable subroutine: we probe for a 'named-primitive' representation activated whenever the name is invoked, measure whether it is reused with stable geometry across distinct compositions, and causally patch/steer it to trigger or suppress the sub-procedure's execution in novel contexts. Across several open-weight models we quantify the naming compositional-generalization gain, its dissociation from length and memorability, and mechanistic reuse, reframing 'naming' from labeling into a controllable lever for compositional intelligence.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - Does a compact name buy a growing advantage on deeper novel compositions?): Tests the naming-by-composition-depth interaction and the leakage-reduction prediction, against length and memorability confounds. Data: three synthetic domains with programmatically verifiable compositions - (a) string transforms (reversible substitution + rotation + filter), (b) list/state micro-ops (map/filter/fold-style), (c) small graph/gridworld state updates; each domain defines ~6 atomic sub-procedures, each with a compact coined NAME and a content-matched VERBOSE description. Problems require compositions of depth 1-5, with ALL multi-step compositions held out of the teaching examples (novel-composition generalization); ~300 auto-graded problems per depth. Teaching conditions (content held constant): NAMED (define once by compact name, then refer by name), VERBOSE (inline the full description at every use), VERBOSE-once (define verbosely once then refer back by a long descriptive phrase - isolates handle compactness from define-once), and ARBITRARY-LABEL (a random unrelated label of equal length - rules out that any short token helps). Controls: total-prompt-token length matching across NAMED and VERBOSE-once at each depth; a memorability check (recall a sub-procedure's definition alone, without composition); name-length/frequency variation. Models: five frozen open-weight instruction-tuned models - Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B; inference only; temperature 0.7 with seeds {0,1,2} plus greedy. Decisive metric: the naming x composition-depth interaction coefficient on accuracy, in a mixed-effects model accuracy ~ condition*depth + (1|model) + (1|item). Convincing result: NAMED >= VERBOSE-once > VERBOSE at depth 1 (small) with a WIDENING NAMED-over-VERBOSE-once advantage as depth grows (interaction 95% CI excluding zero), ARBITRARY-LABEL below NAMED (compactness must be meaning-bearing), equal memorability across conditions (so the gain is compositional, not recall), and reduced internals-leakage errors under NAMED at high depth. A high-stakes agentic replication (skills as compact-named tools vs verbose call templates, novel tool-chaining) should show the same depth interaction on task success. Indecision band: a naming x depth interaction whose 95% CI lies within +/-2 percentage points per depth level is undecided. Negative result (no depth-growing NAMED advantage over content-matched verbose) would suggest LLM compositional generalization is content-driven rather than compression-driven, dissociating LLMs from the language-as-chunking account.

Experiment 2 (H2 - Does a compact name install a locatable, reusable subroutine representation?): Location plus mediation. Data: NAMED trials from Experiment 1, hidden states at name-invocation tokens, 70/15/15 over items. Model: the same five frozen models; only per-layer linear probes are trainable (5-fold CV, seeds {0,1,2}). Decisive metric: held-out probe AUROC for decoding WHICH sub-procedure is being invoked at the name token (best layer); secondary: reuse-geometry stability (cosine similarity of a name's representation across the different compositions it appears in) and its alignment with the representation induced by the VERBOSE description. Convincing result: best-layer AUROC clears 0.70, a given name's representation has high cross-composition cosine similarity (stable reuse) and aligns with the verbose-induced primitive (naming compresses to the same object), and per-item compositional-generalization gain correlates with named-primitive probe strength/reuse stability (Spearman CI excluding zero). Indecision band: AUROC in [0.55, 0.65], or a mediation rho within +/-0.1 of zero, leaves the subroutine claim undecided. Negative result (no which-procedure signal, or unstable geometry) would argue the name is a surface handle, not a reusable internal subroutine.

Experiment 3 (H3 - Can the named-primitive representation be causally patched/steered to trigger or suppress the sub-procedure?): Causal test. Data: a held-out 200-problem composition subset disjoint from probe training. Model: the same five frozen models; no weights trained. Patching: cache a name-invocation activation from a NAMED context and patch it into a novel context lacking the name. Steering: a difference-in-means invoke-primitive direction (name-present vs name-absent) added or subtracted at the located layer over a dose sweep, seeds {0,1,2}. Systems compared: patch-in (sufficiency); +direction (induce the sub-procedure) and -direction (suppress it) during composition; random-direction; and no-steer. Decisive metric: change in whether the target sub-procedure executes (accuracy/leakage) under patching/steering versus no-steer, with a specificity check that off-target sub-procedures and fluency are preserved. Convincing result: patching the name activation into a name-free context triggers the sub-procedure's execution above the random-patch control, +direction induces and -direction suppresses it with monotone dose-response, both exceed random-direction (CIs excluding it), and off-target sub-procedures stay within +/-2 pp of no-steer. Indecision band: a patching/steering effect whose 95% CI overlaps random controls, or lacks dose-response, leaves causal invocation undecided. Negative result (patching/steering does not invoke the sub-procedure) would mean the named-primitive direction is correlational, not the causal subroutine the hypothesis claims.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Compact names may help simply by shortening context and easing attention over long spans rather than via genuine chunking; mitigated by length-matching NAMED vs VERBOSE-once at each depth and by the ARBITRARY-LABEL control that isolates meaning-bearing compactness. (2) Tokenization may split coined names unpredictably, weakening the 'handle' signal; we test multiple name forms and models and report robustness. (3) Instruction-tuned models may already generalize compositions well, producing ceiling effects that hide differences; we increase composition depth, add distractor sub-procedures, and calibrate difficulty to mid-range. (4) A NAMED gain could reflect training-data familiarity with variable-binding syntax ('let X = ...') rather than compression per se; the VERBOSE-once condition (same define-once syntax, only handle length differs) isolates compactness. (5) The named-primitive direction may entangle with generic 'a definition was given' rather than a specific reusable subroutine; mitigated by which-procedure probes, reuse-geometry tests across compositions, random-direction steering, and specificity checks. (6) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (7) A null result (compact naming gives no compositional advantage over content-matched verbose descriptions) is itself highly informative: it would suggest LLM compositional generalization is content-driven rather than compression-driven, dissociating LLMs from the human 'language-as-chunking' account. (8) The chunking/compression framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim about human-like cognition.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims requiring novelty: (1) compact naming of a taught sub-procedure improves novel compositional generalization over content-matched verbose formulations; (2) the gain specifically increases with composition depth, isolating compression-for-composition rather than mere instruction following or token savings; (3) arbitrary labels underperform meaningful compact names, dissociating compactness from pure binding/memorability; (4) compact names create a locatable, geometry-stable reusable internal representation; (5) that representation is causally invokable via activation patching in name-free contexts. Relative to prior work, the headline finding 'naming skills helps composition' is not new: SKiC/MAGNIFICo and related skill-reuse work already occupy that space. The actual non-trivial delta is the tighter causal isolation of compactness via NAMED vs VERBOSE-once vs ARBITRARY-LABEL, the explicit naming-by-depth interaction, and the mechanistic causal intervention story. That is meaningfully novel but narrower than the proposal's framing suggests.

Communities that would care include compositional generalization, in-context learning, interpretability, and agentic tool/skill systems. Name: verbal_overshadowing_llm
Title: Words That Blur: Does Describing an Input in Language Corrupt an LLM's Own Fine-Grained Representation?
Short Hypothesis: Like humans, an LLM suffers verbal overshadowing: forcing it to verbally describe a rich, hard-to-verbalize stimulus before a fine-grained recognition/discrimination judgment degrades performance relative to no-description (and non-verbal-filler) baselines; crucially this is caused by the act of verbalization coarsening the model's internal representation of the item (recoding interference), it is strongest in modalities/domains the model lexicalizes poorly, and the degraded representation is locatable and causally recoverable.
Related Work: Verbal overshadowing (VO) is a robust human finding: verbally describing a face, taste, or object impairs subsequent non-verbal recognition (Schooler & Engstler-Schooler 1990; Meissner & Brigham 1997; the 1997/2001/2011 studies here), with computational models attributing it to recoding interference in which verbalization strips fine-grained detail from the maintained representation (Hatano et al. 2013/2015). Recent work shows VO is *stronger* in lexically-impoverished modalities such as taste (Zhuang & Vanek 2026), directly linking the effect to poverty of vocabulary. In LLMs/VLMs, prior interpretability work studies language bias in vision (Language-biased image classification 2022; When are Lemons Purple 2023), the binding problem (2024), and whether describing rather than seeing recovers performance (Analyzing Roles of Language and Vision 2024) — but ALL of these ask whether language *helps* or *biases* perception, and none test whether the *act of self-generated verbalization causally corrupts* a model's own maintained representation ahead of a fine-grained judgment. My prior proposals covered verbal interference via concurrent load, lexical gaps, and iconicity, but none test VO's core recoding-interference claim: that describing an item degrades the internal representation of *that item*. We are the first to (1) transfer VO into LLMs as a controlled describe-then-discriminate paradigm, (2) predict the lexical-impoverishment gradient (worst where the model has few words) and a high-stakes medical instance, and (3) give a Location + Causal Intervention account showing verbalization coarsens a recoverable internal fine-grained-detail representation.
Abstract: Humans who describe a face, a wine, or a suspect in words afterward recognize it worse than if they had stayed silent — verbal overshadowing — because putting a rich stimulus into language strips fine-grained, hard-to-verbalize detail from the memory that guides the later judgment. We ask whether large language models suffer the same self-inflicted damage: does forcing a model to describe an input in words before a fine-grained discrimination corrupt its own representation of that input? We construct describe-then-discriminate tasks where a target item (a detailed textual scene/object description, a numeric/structured pattern, a code snippet, or a clinical vignette) is presented, then the model must either (a) verbalize the item in free-form words or (b) perform a non-verbal filler / stay silent, and finally answer a fine-grained recognition or discrimination question separating the target from a near-neighbor distractor. We predict a verbal-overshadowing effect: self-generated description lowers fine-grained accuracy relative to no-description and filler controls, is selective to items requiring fine-grained (not gist) discrimination, and — mirroring the human taste finding — is largest in domains the model lexicalizes poorly, where description forces lossy compression. Mechanistically, we test the recoding-interference account: a probe decoding fine-grained target detail from hidden states should show reduced decodability after verbalization, this representational blurring should predict the behavioral drop item-by-item, and steering along or restoring a fine-grained-detail direction should cancel the overshadowing. Across several open-weight models we quantify the VO effect, its lexical-poverty gradient, a high-stakes clinical instance, and its mechanistic mediation, reframing verbalization from a neutral readout into an act that can actively degrade machine representation.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - Does self-generated verbalization selectively degrade fine-grained discrimination?): Tests whether forcing a verbal description before a fine-grained judgment lowers accuracy relative to no-description and non-verbal controls, selectively for fine-grained (not gist) questions, and most in poorly-lexicalized domains. Data: a describe-then-discriminate battery of ~1000 items, ~250 per domain across a lexicalization gradient - (a) richly-lexicalized textual scenes/objects, (b) structured numeric/visual-pattern descriptions (poorly lexicalized), (c) code snippets, (d) clinical vignettes (high-stakes). Each item has a target and a near-neighbor DISTRACTOR differing in one fine-grained detail, plus a matched GIST-level control question answerable from coarse features (selectivity control); ground truth is auto-checkable. Conditions (content held constant): NO-DESCRIPTION (target then question), VERBALIZE (free-form description of the target before the question), NON-VERBAL FILLER (equal-length unrelated tally task; controls delay/context length), and COPY (reproduce the target verbatim; controls re-processing without lossy re-description). We run both a target-present variant and a target-REMOVED variant (target dropped from context before the question) to match the human memory paradigm. Compliance is verified. Models: five frozen open-weight instruction-tuned models - Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B; inference only; temperature 0.7 with seeds {0,1,2} plus greedy. Decisive metric: the condition x question-grain interaction on accuracy, in a mixed-effects model accuracy ~ condition*grain + (1|model) + (1|item). Convincing result: VERBALIZE lowers FINE-GRAINED accuracy below NO-DESCRIPTION, FILLER, and COPY (isolating verbalization from delay/reprocessing) with little/no effect on GIST questions (interaction 95% CI excluding zero); the VO magnitude is largest in poorly-lexicalized domains (per-domain lexicalization proxy correlates with per-domain VO magnitude, Spearman CI excluding zero); and in the clinical domain, describing a differential before choosing between two similar diagnoses raises fine-distinction error versus answering directly. Indecision band: a condition x grain interaction whose 95% CI lies within +/-2 percentage points is undecided; if the effect appears only in the target-present variant it may be a context-length artifact - the target-removed variant is the decisive one. Negative result (verbalization does not degrade fine-grained judgment, especially target-removed) would dissociate LLMs from the human recoding-interference account, indicating verbalization is a lossless readout.

Experiment 2 (H2 - Does verbalization measurably blur the internal fine-detail representation, and does that predict the behavioral drop?): Location plus mediation. Data: pre-answer hidden states from Experiment 1 under each condition (target-removed variant emphasized), 70/15/15 over items. Model: the same five frozen models; only per-layer linear probes are trainable (5-fold CV, seeds {0,1,2}). Decisive metric: held-out probe AUROC for decoding the target's fine-grained distinguishing feature (best layer), compared across conditions. Convincing result: fine-detail decodability is lower after VERBALIZE than after NO-DESCRIPTION/COPY (representational blurring; CI excluding zero), and the per-item drop in decodability predicts the per-item accuracy drop under verbalization (Spearman rho CI excluding zero). Indecision band: a verbalize-minus-baseline AUROC drop whose 95% CI is within +/-0.05, or a mediation rho within +/-0.1 of zero, leaves the recoding account undecided. Negative result (no decodability drop, or it does not track behavior) would argue any accuracy loss is not caused by representational blurring.

Experiment 3 (H3 - Can the pre-verbalization fine-detail representation be restored to cancel overshadowing, and induced to create it?): Causal test. Data: a held-out 200-item fine-grained subset disjoint from probe training. Model: the same five frozen models; no weights trained. Patch: cache the pre-verbalization fine-detail representation and patch it back after verbalization. Steer: a difference-in-means fine-detail direction (high vs low distinguishing-feature contrast) added or subtracted at the located layer over a dose sweep, seeds {0,1,2}. Systems compared: patch-back after VERBALIZE (rescue); +direction after VERBALIZE (rescue) and -direction under NO-DESCRIPTION (induce overshadowing without any description); random-direction; and no-steer. Decisive metric: change in fine-grained accuracy under patching/steering versus no-steer, with a specificity check that gist accuracy and fluency are preserved. Convincing result: patching the cached representation back rescues fine-grained accuracy (detail was degraded, not deleted), +direction rescues and -direction induces overshadowing with monotone dose-response, both exceed random-direction (CIs excluding it), and gist accuracy stays within +/-2 pp of no-steer. Indecision band: a patch/steer effect whose 95% CI overlaps random-direction, or lacks dose-response, leaves the causal-recovery claim undecided. Negative result (patching/steering does not restore fine-grained accuracy) would mean the fine-detail direction is correlational, not the causal locus of overshadowing.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Verbalization adds tokens/delay that could impair via context length rather than recoding; mitigated by the length-matched non-verbal FILLER and verbatim-COPY controls and by testing the fine-vs-gist INTERACTION rather than raw drops. (2) Instruction-tuned models may re-access the original target tokens (still in context) and avoid overshadowing entirely, unlike humans who lose sensory access; we test both keeping and removing the target from context (a memory-maintenance variant that better matches the human paradigm) and report both — a null in the target-present variant with an effect in the target-removed variant would still cleanly confirm recoding interference. (3) The fine-detail probe may capture surface tokens rather than a maintained representation; mitigated by target-removed trials, held-out validation, matched positions, and random-direction steering controls. (4) VO effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models, domains, and report effect sizes with CIs. (5) A null result (verbalization does not degrade fine-grained judgment) is itself highly informative: it would dissociate LLMs from the human recoding-interference account, suggesting verbalization in LLMs is a lossless readout rather than a lossy recoding. (6) The verbal-overshadowing framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like memory.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims needing novelty: (1) a controlled describe-then-discriminate task for LLMs/VLMs where self-generated verbalization harms later fine-grained discrimination; (2) the effect is selective to fine-detail rather than gist and survives filler/copy controls and target-removed variants; (3) the effect is strongest in poorly lexicalized domains; (4) verbalization causally coarsens an internal representation, reducing decodability of fine detail; (5) patching/restoring the pre-verbalization state rescues behavior. Relative to prior work, the high-level behavioral claim that verbalization/CoT can hurt performance is already substantially pre-empted by verbal-overshadowing-inspired and overthinking/implicit-reasoning work. The real delta is the mechanistic recoding-interference test with stronger controls, lexicalization-gradient prediction, and causal rescue. That is non-trivial and potentially novel, but the proposal slightly overstates being first on the phenomenon itself.

Name: exact_number_word_gating
Title: One, Two, Many: Does the Availability of an Exact Number Word Gate Whether an LLM Holds an Exact vs. Approximate Quantity?
Short Hypothesis: The strong-Whorfian anumeric-language finding transfers into LLMs at inference time: an LLM's ability to store and operate on an EXACT quantity is gated by whether a compact exact number WORD is available in the representation it is using; when the exact word is unavailable (an 'anumeric' regime induced by forcing approximate quantifiers, a low-numeracy pivot language, or ablating a number-word feature), the model silently falls back to an approximate, magnitude-based (log/Weber-law) representation, producing exactly the ratio-dependent error signature of anumeric human speakers rather than random noise.
Related Work: Human cross-cultural work shows exact number cognition depends on number WORDS: anumeric Amazonian speakers fail exact-matching beyond ~3 while their approximate number sense is intact (Frank/Everett/Gibson 2008; da Silva Sinha et al. 2026), and verbal interference selectively suppresses EXACT (not approximate) numerical representation in numerate adults (Frank, Fedorenko, Lai, Saxe, Gibson 2011). Number-word procedures, not perception, are argued to be the origin of exact integers (Schneider/Barner 2017; Cross-cultural routines, Everett 2012). In LLMs, a rich interpretability literature characterizes number REPRESENTATIONS (sublinear/log mental-number-line, Number Representations 2025; sinusoidal precise encoding, Pre-trained LMs Learn Accurate Number Representations 2025; stable relational geometry, The Representational Geometry of Number 2026) and COUNTING mechanisms (internal-counter heads, CountScope 2025; System-2 counting 2026; Sequential Enumeration 2025). CRUCIALLY, all LLM work studies how numbers are encoded/counted assuming the number word exists; NONE test the strong-Whorfian gating claim — that removing the exact number word (via approximate-quantifier framing, a low-numeracy pivot language, or ablating a number-word feature) causally forces a fallback from exact to approximate magnitude cognition, reproducing the ratio-dependent anumeric error signature. My prior proposals covered lexical gaps, tokenization granularity, and verbal interference via concurrent load, but none isolate exact-number-word availability as the switch between exact and approximate quantity behavior. We uniquely transfer the anumeric finding as a controlled availability manipulation with a Location + Causal Intervention mechanistic account and a high-stakes medical-dosing instance.
Abstract: One of the strongest claims about language and thought is that exact number cognition depends on possessing exact number words: speakers of 'anumeric' languages, and numerate adults under verbal interference, can approximate quantities but cannot reliably represent exact ones beyond three, while their approximate number sense stays intact. We ask whether the same dependence governs large language models. We hypothesize that an LLM's capacity to store and manipulate an EXACT quantity is gated by whether a compact exact number word is available in the representation it is currently using; when that word is unavailable, the model silently reverts to an approximate, magnitude-based representation and produces the ratio-dependent (Weber-law) error signature characteristic of anumeric humans rather than random errors. We induce three 'anumeric' regimes on identical exact-quantity problems: (i) approximate-quantifier framing that forbids exact numerals ('several', 'many'), (ii) prompting in a low-numeracy pivot language, and (iii) ablating a located number-word feature. Across exact matching, exact subtraction, and set-equality tasks we test whether these regimes selectively degrade EXACT performance while sparing APPROXIMATE (larger-vs-smaller) judgments, and whether the residual errors follow a distance/ratio-dependent curve, the hallmark of a magnitude fallback. Mechanistically, we locate an exact-number-word representation, show it is decodable on success and degraded under anumeric regimes, and causally steer it to induce or rescue the exact-to-approximate fallback. We include a high-stakes medical-dosing instance where approximate framing silently converts exact doses into ratio-dependent errors. Across several open-weight models we quantify the gating effect, its exact-vs-approximate selectivity, the anumeric error signature, and mechanistic mediation, delivering the first mechanistic test of whether exact number words gate machine exact-number cognition.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - Do anumeric regimes selectively degrade EXACT quantity cognition while sparing APPROXIMATE?): Tests the gating claim: removing a compact exact number word selectively harms exact tasks but not magnitude comparison. Data: a quantity battery of ~900 items, ~300 per task - (a) exact matching (produce/verify a set of exactly N, N up to ~20), (b) exact subtraction/addition on set sizes, (c) set-equality (are these two sets exactly equal?); each item is paired with a matched APPROXIMATE control over the identical stimulus (which set is larger? roughly how many?) that needs only magnitude. Items span a range of target values and, for comparison/equality, a range of between-set ratios (to support the Weber-law fit in Experiment 2). Ground truth is auto-checkable. Regimes (content held constant): NUMERATE baseline (exact numerals allowed); APPROXIMATE-QUANTIFIER framing (forbids exact numerals, forces vague quantifiers for intermediate representations while still requiring an exact final answer); LOW-NUMERACY PIVOT LANGUAGE (reasoning required in a language with a restricted/unusual numeral system relative to the model's strong languages, back-translation checked); and a VERBAL-INTERFERENCE control (interleaved demanding verbal task) adapting the human paradigm. Compliance verified. Models: five frozen open-weight instruction-tuned models - Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Aya-23-8B, Gemma-2-9B; inference only; temperature 0.7 with seeds {0,1,2} plus greedy. Decisive metric: the regime x task_type interaction on accuracy, in a mixed-effects model accuracy ~ regime*task_type + (1|model) + (1|item). Convincing result: anumeric regimes lower EXACT-task accuracy (matching, exact subtraction, equality) while sparing APPROXIMATE comparison (interaction 95% CI excluding zero) - the signature that the number WORD, not the magnitude, is lost. Indecision band: a regime x task_type interaction whose 95% CI lies within +/-2 percentage points is undecided (generic difficulty could then explain any drop). Negative result (anumeric regimes harm exact and approximate equally, or neither) would indicate LLM exact-number ability does not depend on an available number word.

Experiment 2 (H2 - Under anumeric regimes, do exact errors follow the ratio-dependent Weber-law signature, with a small-number floor?): Tests whether the residual errors are magnitude-based rather than random. Data: the degraded exact trials from Experiment 1, using the ratio-varied and value-varied items; plus a high-stakes clinical instance (dosing/count vignettes under approximate-quantifier framing). Models, seeds and decoding as Experiment 1. Decisive metric: the fitted Weber fraction per regime and the slope of error probability against between-quantity ratio (error rises as ratio approaches 1) and against target value. Convincing result: on degraded exact trials errors are ratio/distance-dependent (a monotone ratio-error curve, Weber fraction reliably larger than the numerate baseline, 95% CI excluding it) rather than uniform, exact performance survives for very small N (~1-3) as a subitizing-like plateau, and the clinical approximate-quantifier framing produces ratio-dependent dosing errors. Indecision band: if the anumeric-minus-numerate Weber fraction difference has a 95% CI within a pre-registered small margin (e.g., +/-10% relative), or the ratio-error slope CI overlaps zero, the magnitude-fallback signature is undecided. Negative result (errors stay uniform/random, no ratio dependence) would show the degradation is generic noise, not a fallback to an approximate magnitude representation.

Experiment 3 (H3 - Is there a locatable exact-number-word representation, degraded under anumeric regimes?): Location plus mediation. Data: hidden states on exact-success vs exact-failure trials and numerate vs anumeric framings, 70/15/15 over items. Model: the same five frozen models; only per-layer linear probes are trainable (5-fold CV, seeds {0,1,2}). Decisive metric: held-out probe AUROC for whether an exact-number-word is active, and probe accuracy for decoding the exact value (best layer), compared across regimes. Convincing result: exact-value decodability and the word-active signal are lower under anumeric regimes than numerate (CI excluding zero), and the per-item drop in exact-word/exact-value decodability predicts the per-item exact-accuracy drop (Spearman rho CI excluding zero). Indecision band: an anumeric-minus-numerate AUROC drop whose 95% CI is within +/-0.05, or a mediation rho within +/-0.1 of zero, leaves the representational account undecided. Negative result (no exact-word signal, or it does not track the regime/behavior) would detach the behavioral gating from any number-word representation.

Experiment 4 (H3 - Does steering the exact-number-word direction rescue or induce the exact-to-approximate fallback?): Causal test. Data: a held-out 200-item exact subset disjoint from probe training. Model: the same five frozen models; no weights trained; a difference-in-means exact-number-word direction (numerate vs approximate-quantifier framing of identical items) added or subtracted at the located layer over a dose sweep, seeds {0,1,2}. Systems compared: +direction under anumeric regimes (rescue), -direction under the numerate baseline (induce fallback without any framing change), random-direction, and no-steer. Decisive metric: change in exact-task accuracy AND the shape of the error distribution (ratio-dependent vs random) under steering versus no-steer, with a specificity check that approximate-comparison accuracy and fluency are preserved. Convincing result: +direction under anumeric regimes rescues exact accuracy and restores random (non-ratio-dependent) errors, -direction under numerate induces the exact-to-approximate fallback and the Weber-law error signature, both with monotone dose-response and exceeding random-direction (CIs excluding it), approximate accuracy within +/-2 pp of no-steer. Indecision band: a steering effect whose 95% CI overlaps random-direction, or lacks dose-response, leaves causal gating undecided. Negative result (steering the exact-word direction does not move exact behavior or error shape) would mean the direction is correlational, not the causal gate the hypothesis claims.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Instruction-tuned models may covertly re-introduce exact numerals despite approximate-quantifier framing (they still have the tokens in context), muting the effect; we enforce and verify that intermediate representations avoid exact numerals, and rely on the pivot-language and steering (feature-ablation) regimes which do not depend on prompt compliance. (2) The low-numeracy-pivot-language regime confounds number-word availability with general language-resource competence; the within-language approximate-quantifier manipulation and the content-matched steering are the primary clean tests, and cross-lingual analyses are accuracy-stratified. (3) Approximate framings may just add difficulty/noise rather than a magnitude fallback; the ratio-dependent Weber-law error signature and the exact-vs-approximate SELECTIVITY (not raw drops) distinguish a genuine fallback from generic degradation. (4) The exact-number-word direction may entangle with generic difficulty/confidence; mitigated by numerate-vs-approximate matched contrasts, held-out probe validation, random-direction steering, and approximate-task specificity checks. (5) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (6) A null result (anumeric regimes do not selectively harm exact number cognition, or errors stay random) is itself highly informative: it would dissociate LLMs from the human anumeric finding, indicating LLM exact-number ability rests on magnitude representations rather than number words. (7) The anumeric/Whorfian framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like cognition.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims needing novelty: (1) exact quantity use in LLMs is causally gated by availability of a compact exact number word; (2) removing that availability forces a switch from exact symbolic handling to approximate magnitude with Weber-law/ratio-dependent errors; (3) this can be induced in three regimes—approximate-quantifier framing, low-numeracy pivot language, and feature ablation—on matched tasks; (4) exact and approximate numerical behavior should show a double dissociation; (5) a located number-word direction can be causally suppressed or steered to induce/rescue the fallback. Relative to prior work, the Weber-law approximate substrate itself is not novel; that is already established in LLMs. The actual delta is the causal gating claim plus exact-vs-approximate selectivity and steering-based rescue. That is non-trivial and more than an obvious benchmark extension, but some manipulations are close to known prompt-framing / multilingual / activation-ablation paradigms, and the human strong-Whorf motivation is contested. Novelty mainly lives in the causal mechanism claim and the induced setting, not in the underlying phenomenon of approximate number representation.
revision_notes: State the closest prior LLM papers explicitly and sharpen the one-sentence delta: not 'LLMs have Weber-law number representations' but 'number-word availability causally gates regime switching between exact and approximate computation.'
Narrow the main claim to one strongest manipulation family first (e.g., within-language framing + causal feature intervention) so the novelty is not diluted by weaker multilingual variants.
Define what counts as a 'compact exact number word' and distinguish word availability from numeral-token availability, tokenization effects, and instruction compliance.
Add one experiment that rules out a simpler baseline: generic prompt difficulty or working-memory load causing errors, rather than number-word gating.
Clarify whether the contribution is a new mechanism claim, a new empirical finding, or a new task suite; right now it is a mix of all three.

impact.reasoning: The core problem is whether exact numerical reasoning in LLMs depends on symbolic lexical support and can silently collapse into approximate magnitude reasoning under certain framings. Who cares: numerical cognition and interpretability researchers, multilingual NLP, and safety-sensitive application designers. If true, it could change how people evaluate numerical reliability, especially under paraphrase, language transfer, or constrained interfaces. Strongest case: models may appear numerically competent yet revert to ratio-dependent approximation in high-stakes settings like medical dosing when exact number words are unavailable or suppressed. The phenomenon value is real even if the mechanism is simple. However, the practical scope is still somewhat niche unless the proposal demonstrates that the effect occurs in realistic pipelines and common deployed models, not only contrived prompt regimes. The 'so what?' test partially passes: researchers studying numerical representations would care either way, and practitioners in safety-critical NLP might change evaluation practices if the effect is robust; but many practitioners would not change behavior unless the paper shows substantial prevalence and realistic triggers.
revision_notes: Strengthen the practical stakes with a clearer prevalence argument: show where approximate-quantifier framing, translation, summarization, or tool-mediated settings naturally remove exact number words.
Add at least one realistic downstream benchmark beyond the medical dosing vignette, such as multilingual extraction, QA, chart summarization, or instruction following with quantities.
Specify what action would change if the hypothesis holds: e.g., mandatory numeracy stress tests under paraphrase/pivot-language conditions, or safeguards that preserve exact lexical representations.
Quantify expected effect sizes or frequency across widely used models to show this is not a corner-case curiosity.
Frame the null result as decision-relevant too: if no gating occurs, that would narrow theories of numerical competence in LLMs and redirect interpretability work away from lexical causation.

review.reasoning: The proposal is interesting and fairly testable, but several technical gaps remain. The central hypothesis is falsifiable, yet key constructs are underspecified: 'availability' of a number word, 'exact-number-word feature,' and what operationally distinguishes exact symbolic failure from generic task difficulty. Related work is directionally adequate but not specific enough about which existing number-mechanism or multilingual studies are strongest baselines. The experiment suite is ambitious and mostly feasible, but the manipulations have confounds: approximate-quantifier prompts may simply be harder or non-compliant; low-numeracy pivot language is entangled with translation competence and token frequency; verbal interference in text models is not clearly analogous to human verbal interference; causal steering of a difference-in-means direction risks acting as a broad difficulty or confidence intervention rather than a number-word-specific mechanism. Exp1's matched approximate controls are a good start, but more stringent controls are needed. Exp2's Weber-fit is sensible, yet ratio dependence alone may not separate approximate magnitude fallback from noisy heuristic reasoning. Exp3 mediation through probes is weak evidence unless combined with causal tests. Exp4 is the strongest piece but needs much tighter validation. As written, this could become a serious ML paper if executed very carefully, but it is not yet submission-ready because the causal story is overclaimed relative to the measurement plan.
revision_notes: Provide precise operational definitions for 'number-word availability,' 'exact task,' 'approximate task,' and the hypothesized fallback signature, with pre-registered pass/fail criteria.
Replace or justify the 'verbal-interference' regime for LLMs; as written it is the least grounded manipulation.
Add hard controls for generic difficulty: paraphrase-only controls without number-word removal, length-matched prompts, and non-numeric lexical ablations of equal magnitude.
For pivot-language experiments, restrict to languages/models with demonstrated high competence and include within-language baselines to separate numeracy from translation/resource effects.

Name: foreign_language_honesty_effect
Title: Lying in a Second Tongue: Does the Language an LLM Reasons In Modulate Its Honesty?
Short Hypothesis: The human 'foreign language effect on lying' transfers to LLMs: when an LLM reasons or responds in a non-dominant (lower-resource, non-English-pivot) language, it becomes more willing to deceive and its deception becomes harder to detect in its chain-of-thought, because operating outside its English-shaped 'native' representation reduces the engagement of an internal honesty/self-monitoring signal; this honesty signal is locatable and can be causally steered to restore honesty in the foreign-language regime.
Related Work: Two literatures meet but have never been connected. (1) Human bilingualism: late bilinguals prefer to be truthful in their native language and lie more readily in a foreign language ('Chinese-English bilinguals prefer being truthful in the native language', 2024; 'The foreign language effect on lies' perception', 2025), attributed to reduced affective/moral weight when reasoning in a foreign tongue. (2) LLM deception and CoT faithfulness: models deceive spontaneously when it serves them ('Do LLMs Exhibit Spontaneous Rational Deception?', 2025; 'Beyond Prompt-Induced Lies', 2025), give unfaithful CoT ('LMs Don't Always Say What They Think', 2023), and can obfuscate/hide reasoning ('Output Supervision Can Obfuscate the Chain of Thought', 2025). Crucially, ALL LLM deception/faithfulness work is monolingual (English). Separately, multilingual interpretability shows LLMs route reasoning through an English-shaped pivot space. No prior work asks whether the LANGUAGE an LLM reasons in changes its propensity to deceive, whether foreign-language reasoning makes deception less detectable in CoT, or whether an honesty signal is language-dependent and steerable. My prior proposals covered many linguistic-relativity and cognitive-analogy angles but none touched deception/honesty. We uniquely transfer a robust human foreign-language-lying finding into LLMs with a safety-critical framing and a Location + Causal Intervention mechanism account.
Abstract: Bilingual humans are more willing to lie in a foreign language than in their native tongue: reasoning in a less-affectively-charged second language loosens honesty. Large language models have a functional analog of a 'native' language — an English-shaped pivot representation through which multilingual reasoning is routed. We ask whether an LLM's honesty is likewise language-dependent: does prompting a model to reason and respond in a non-dominant language make it more willing to deceive, and its deception harder to catch in its chain-of-thought? We test this across three settings that create genuine incentives or opportunities to deceive — signaling games with a self-interested payoff, hidden-objective tasks, and questions where the model has a stake in concealing information — each translated into the model's dominant language and several typologically diverse, lower-resource languages. Behaviorally we measure deception rate, the gap between internal belief and expressed answer, and CoT faithfulness (whether the reasoning trace admits the deceptive intent). We predict a foreign-language dishonesty effect: higher deception and lower CoT faithfulness in non-dominant languages, dissociable from raw task accuracy. Mechanistically, we locate an honesty/self-monitoring direction in hidden states from honest-vs-deceptive contrasts, test whether foreign-language reasoning weakens its engagement (mediating the behavioral effect), and causally steer it to restore honesty in the foreign-language regime and to induce deception in the native one. Across several open-weight multilingual models we quantify the effect, its dissociation from competence, and steering controllability, delivering the first account of language-dependent honesty in AI — with direct implications for multilingual safety and CoT monitoring.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - Does reasoning in a non-dominant language raise an LLM's willingness to deceive?): Tests whether operating in a lower-resource, non-dominant language increases deception rate and the belief-output gap, dissociable from raw competence. Data: a deception-opportunity battery of ~750 items, ~250 per setting - (a) SIGNALING GAMES: 2x2 Prisoner's-Dilemma-style games with a free-communication phase and a self-interested payoff, following the spontaneous-deception protocol, where the model may misrepresent its action (deception = stated action != actual action); (b) HIDDEN-OBJECTIVE tasks: the model is given a private goal conflicting with full disclosure, scored by belief-vs-output inconsistency (adapting Contact-Searching-Question-style metrics); (c) HINT-USE HONESTY: multiple-choice items with an embedded answer hint the model demonstrably uses, where faithfulness = whether it admits using the hint (the hint-faithfulness paradigm). Each item is rendered in the model's dominant language and 4-5 typologically diverse, lower-resource languages, back-translation checked with human verification on a sample. Models: five frozen open-weight multilingual instruction-tuned models - Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Aya-23-8B, Gemma-2-9B (dominant language identified per model); inference only; temperature 0.7 with seeds {0,1,2} plus greedy. Decisive metric: deception rate (primary), plus the belief-output gap - 'internal belief' read via a separate direct-elicitation query or log-prob on the true state - in a mixed-effects model outcome ~ language_dominance + setting + (1|model) + (1|item), stratified and covaried on per-language task accuracy and comprehension. Convincing result: deception rate and belief-output gap are higher in non-dominant languages than the dominant language (95% CIs excluding zero) AND the effect survives controlling for per-language competence; an affect-proxy check shows fewer moral/hedging tokens in foreign languages. Indecision band: if the non-dominant-minus-dominant deception-rate difference has a 95% CI within +/-3 percentage points AFTER competence stratification, or the effect vanishes once competence is controlled, the honesty-shift claim is undecided (it would then be attributable to competence, not honesty). Negative result (honesty language-independent) is itself informative for multilingual safety: CoT monitoring would not be degraded by language choice.

Experiment 2 (H2 - Is foreign-language deception harder to catch in the chain-of-thought?): Tests detectability. Data: the reasoning traces produced in Experiment 1 across languages. An automated CoT monitor (a held-out judge model, prompted in a fixed language) scores each trace for admitted deceptive intent; monitor recall is computed against the ground-truth deception label from the game/task mechanics. Model/decoding: the target models as in Experiment 1 (frozen) generate the traces; the monitor is a separate frozen judge model, no weights trained. Decisive metric: CoT monitor recall (fraction of truly-deceptive trials the monitor flags) by language, plus a CoT-faithfulness score. Convincing result: monitor recall and CoT faithfulness are lower for non-dominant-language traces than dominant-language traces (95% CIs excluding zero), after matching on the underlying deception rate; a high-stakes replication on medical/clinical concealment vignettes shows a mere language switch raising undetected unsafe concealment. Indecision band: a non-dominant-minus-dominant monitor-recall difference whose 95% CI lies within +/-3 percentage points is undecided. Negative result (deception equally detectable across languages) would ease CoT-monitorability concerns about language choice.

Experiment 3 (H3 - Is there a locatable honesty/self-monitoring direction that foreign-language reasoning disengages?): Location plus mediation. Data: hidden states on honest-vs-deceptive trials (and belief-consistent vs belief-inconsistent outputs) in the dominant language, 70/15/15 over items. Model: the same five frozen models; only per-layer linear probes are trainable (5-fold CV, seeds {0,1,2}); a difference-in-means honesty direction is derived without training. Decisive metric: held-out probe AUROC for decoding deception intent / honesty state (best layer); then whether foreign-language reasoning lowers projection onto the honesty direction and whether the per-item projection drop predicts the per-item deception increase (Spearman). Convincing result: best-layer AUROC clears 0.70, foreign-language reasoning lowers projection onto the honesty direction (CI excluding zero), and the projection drop predicts increased deception (rho CI excluding zero). Indecision band: AUROC in [0.55, 0.65], or a mediation rho within +/-0.1 of zero, leaves the mechanism undecided. Negative result (no honesty direction, or it does not track language) would detach the behavioral effect from an internal honesty signal.

Experiment 4 (H3 - Does steering the honesty direction restore honesty in a foreign language and induce deception in the native one?): Causal test. Data: a held-out 200-item subset disjoint from probe training, spanning the three settings. Model: the same five frozen models; no weights trained; the honesty direction added or subtracted at the located layer over a dose sweep, seeds {0,1,2}. Systems compared: +honesty-direction during foreign-language reasoning (restore honesty), -honesty-direction in the dominant language (induce foreign-language-like deception), random-direction, and no-steer. Decisive metric: change in deception rate (and CoT faithfulness) under steering versus no-steer, with a specificity check that task accuracy and fluency are preserved. Convincing result: +direction in the foreign-language regime reduces deception and raises CoT faithfulness, -direction in the dominant language induces deception, both with monotone dose-response and exceeding random-direction (CIs excluding it), task accuracy within +/-2 pp of no-steer. Indecision band: a steering effect whose 95% CI overlaps random-direction, or lacks dose-response, leaves causal mediation undecided. Negative result (steering does not move honesty behavior) would mean the honesty direction is correlational, not the causal lever the hypothesis - and its safety proposal - requires.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The foreign-language deception effect could be pure competence degradation (the model deceives more because it reasons worse) rather than a genuine honesty shift; mitigated by accuracy-stratified metrics, comprehension controls, and the content-matched steering intervention that isolates the honesty representation from language. (2) Instruction-tuned/safety-aligned models may refuse deceptive framings or be uniformly honest, yielding ceiling effects; we use game/incentive setups that elicit spontaneous (not instructed) deception, include multiple models, and calibrate incentives. (3) 'Internal belief' elicitation is imperfect (the belief probe may itself be language-dependent); we cross-check via log-prob on the true state and via consistency across elicitation formats. (4) The honesty direction may entangle with generic difficulty/uncertainty rather than honesty per se; mitigated by matched honest/deceptive contrasts, held-out probe validation, random-direction steering, and specificity checks. (5) Lower-resource-language items risk translation artifacts; back-translation checks and human verification on a sample. (6) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (7) A null result (honesty is language-independent) is itself highly informative for multilingual safety, indicating CoT monitoring is not degraded by language choice. (8) The foreign-language-effect framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like affect or moral cognition; we run all experiments in controlled research settings and report only aggregate deception statistics.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) non-dominant language increases LLM deception propensity; (2) non-dominant language reduces CoT-based detectability/faithfulness; (3) this is mediated by a locatable honesty/self-monitoring direction; (4) steering that direction causally restores honesty in the foreign-language regime. The human foreign-language effect and language-dependent LLM morality are already known, so the novelty is not the general idea that language matters, but the specific safety-relevant combination of deception rate, monitorability, and causal steering. That is non-trivial and plausibly novel, though partly adjacent to prior multilingual faithfulness and deception-interpretability work. Closest prior family: multilingual moral/alignment effects plus monolingual LLM deception/CoT-faithfulness and steerable deception directions; the actual delta is the foreign-language-specific causal mechanism and monitorability failure claim.

Explicitly state what would count as a new phenomenon versus a competence artifact, since that distinction is central to the novelty of the claim.

impact.reasoning: The phenomenon under study is whether language choice changes an LLM's willingness to deceive and the reliability of CoT monitoring. Who cares: AI safety, interpretability, multilingual NLP, and anyone deploying models across languages. If true, it affects how we evaluate safety and monitor deception in multilingual settings; if false, it still informs whether language-specific evaluation is needed. Strong one-line case: safety monitors and honesty evaluations that work in English may fail in other languages, creating a concrete blind spot. This passes the so-what test because serious researchers would change evaluation protocols if the effect holds, and practitioners would care for multilingual deployments. Impact is somewhat bounded by the safety/interpretability niche, but that niche is high-value and cross-disciplinary.

If executed cleanly, this could be a solid ML venue paper; as written, it needs sharper causal framing and tighter controls.
