Name: canonicalization_convergence
Title: Mental Paraphrase: Do LLMs Normalize a Problem Toward a Canonical Form Before Reasoning, and Do Failures Come From Not Getting There?
Short Hypothesis: Before reasoning, an LLM internally normalizes a problem's varied surface phrasings toward a shared canonical representation ('mental paraphrase'); reasoning errors on awkward or unfamiliar surface forms are caused by incomplete convergence to that canonical form rather than by the reasoning steps themselves, and the degree of convergence is a readable, causal signal that predicts correctness and can be causally restored by injecting the canonical representation.
Related Work: Prior work documents that LLMs are brittle to surface form: subtle rephrasings change math solve rates (Paraphrase and Solve / SCoP, 2024), reasoning traces are robust to some CoT interventions but not style-invariant and paraphrasing shortens traces and harms accuracy (Are Reasoning LLMs Robust to Interventions on Their CoT?, 2026), and CoT is often unfaithful (Measuring Faithfulness in CoT, 2023). Representation studies show reasoning representations converge across languages when reasoning succeeds (Under the Shadow of Babel, 2025), that NMT paraphrase-invariance is largely shallow (Neurons Invariant to Sentence Structural Changes, 2022), and that abstract concept vectors exist but are not always output-invariant (Concept Vectors, 2025; Abstract Activation Spaces, 2026). Content-effect work steers a 'validity vs plausibility' direction to debias reasoning (How LMs Conflate Validity with Plausibility, 2025; K-CAST, 2025). ALL of these are either (a) behavioral surface-form robustness studies with no internal mechanism, or (b) steering of a content/validity concept. NONE propose that the model performs an internal canonicalization step that maps diverse phrasings toward a shared normal form before reasoning, that reasoning failure is caused by INCOMPLETE convergence to that canonical form, that per-item convergence is a diagnostic signal of correctness, or that injecting the canonical representation causally rescues hard-phrasing errors. My prior proposals covered word-order, morphology, tokenization granularity, lexical gaps, and grammatical-mood effects, but none address surface-form-invariant canonicalization as a locatable, causal computation. We uniquely reframe paraphrase brittleness from a behavioral quirk into a mechanistic canonicalization-convergence account with a Location + Causal Intervention strategy and a high-stakes clinical instance.
Abstract: Large language models solve the same problem at different rates depending only on how it is worded, yet why remains unclear. We propose a mechanistic account: before reasoning, the model performs a 'mental paraphrase', normalizing a problem's diverse surface forms toward a shared canonical representation, and reasoning failures on awkward or unfamiliar phrasings arise because the model never fully reaches that canonical form. We make three claims. First, canonicalization is real and graded: across paraphrase clusters (many wordings of one problem), the internal representations converge toward a common form in intermediate layers, and convergence is stronger for the phrasings the model solves correctly. Second, convergence is diagnostic: per-item distance from the paraphrase cluster's canonical representation predicts whether that phrasing will be solved, beyond confidence and entropy, and pinpoints which surface forms are 'lost in translation' before any reasoning error appears. Third, convergence is causal, not incidental: patching the canonical representation (derived from easy, frequent phrasings) into the model's processing of a hard phrasing rescues correctness, and steering along a located 'canonicalization' direction moves reasoning accuracy up or down. We test these on math, logic, and multi-hop QA with controlled paraphrase clusters spanning register, syntax, and verbosity across several open-weight models, plus a high-stakes clinical instance where a benign rephrasing of a case description silently degrades diagnostic accuracy through failed canonicalization. Our work reframes paraphrase brittleness as incomplete internal normalization and offers an interpretable pre-reasoning failure signal and a training-free rescue.
Experiments:
Shared setup (applies to every experiment below): all runs use five frozen open-weight models -- Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, and Gemma-2-9B -- with no weight updates; the only trainable parameters anywhere are linear-probe weights on frozen hidden states. Decoding is greedy for primary conditions and temperature 0.7 for sampled conditions, each sampled run over seeds 0, 1, 2. Effect sizes carry 95% bootstrap CIs over 1000 item-level resamples; behavioral tests use mixed-effects regression with crossed random intercepts. "Canonicalization convergence" means the degree to which the internal representations of many wordings of one problem approach a shared form before reasoning; the "Convergence Score" is negative distance from a phrasing's pre-reasoning representation to its cluster's canonical (frequent/terse-formal) centroid at the layer of maximal within-cluster convergence.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- Canonicalization is real, graded, and stronger for correctly solved phrasings): Tests within-cluster convergence and its link to correctness. Data: for each base problem we build a cluster of 8-12 meaning-preserving paraphrases spanning controlled axes (register formal/colloquial, syntax simple/embedded, verbosity terse/padded, voice active/passive), over 200 base problems from the GSM8K test split (1,319 available), 200 from the MATH test split (5,000 available), 150 synthetic deductive-logic chains (depth 2-6, auto-checkable), and 150 from the 2WikiMultiHopQA dev set (12,576 available), 700 clusters / roughly 5,600-8,400 phrasings; paraphrases are generated by templated transforms plus an LLM paraphraser and meaning-preservation is verified by back-translation and human spot-check on a 10% sample. 700 clusters gives enough within-cluster behavioral variance for stable convergence estimates within budget. We extract pre-reasoning hidden states at the end-of-problem position per phrasing per layer, compute within-cluster dispersion by layer and each phrasing's distance to the canonical centroid, controlling for length and word-overlap by regression. Decisive metric first: within-cluster representational dispersion as a function of layer (does it fall to a minimum in intermediate layers?) and the Convergence Score difference between correctly and incorrectly solved phrasings; secondary: the layer of maximal convergence per model. Convincing result: dispersion shows a clear intermediate-layer minimum and correctly solved phrasings have reliably higher Convergence Score than incorrect ones (CI excludes 0) after controlling for length/word-overlap. Indecision band: a correct-minus-incorrect Convergence difference whose CI lies within +/-0.05 standardized units means convergence is not graded by correctness. Negative result: flat dispersion across layers or no correctness link means there is no canonicalization computation, refuting H1.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- Convergence is diagnostic of solve probability before reasoning): Tests pre-reasoning error prediction. Data: the same clusters, split 70/30 by cluster. Decisive metric first: from mixed-effects logistic regression correct ~ Convergence + length + word_overlap + (1|cluster)+(1|model), the Convergence coefficient's significance beyond shallow features; secondary: held-out AUROC of a probe on Convergence features for predicting correctness versus verbalized confidence, token entropy, and per-token surprisal baselines. Convincing result: Convergence retains a reliable positive coefficient beyond length/word-overlap (CI excludes 0) and its AUROC exceeds the best baseline by >= 0.05, measured before any reasoning tokens. Indecision band: a Convergence coefficient CI overlapping 0, or delta-AUROC within +/-0.03, means convergence carries no diagnostic value beyond shallow similarity. Negative result: no predictive power refutes H2.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- Patching the canonical representation causally rescues hard-phrasing errors): Tests the causal rescue. Data: hard phrasings the model fails, paired with an easy/canonical phrasing of the SAME problem. We cache the pre-reasoning representation from the canonical phrasing and patch it into the hard-phrasing forward pass at the convergence layer. Controls: patch from a DIFFERENT problem's canonical representation (specificity), patch a random-matched representation, and no-patch baseline; we verify no answer tokens are present in the patched pre-reasoning representation (rules out answer-leakage). Decisive metric first: accuracy recovery on failed hard phrasings under same-problem canonical patching versus no-patch; secondary: same-problem versus cross-problem/random patching. Convincing result: same-problem canonical patching recovers accuracy by >= 8 points (CI excludes 0) while cross-problem and random patching do not (within 2 points of no-patch). Indecision band: a same-problem recovery within +/-3 points, or a same-versus-cross gap within +/-3 points, means patching does not selectively restore canonicalization. Negative result: no selective recovery, or equal recovery from cross-problem patches, refutes the causal canonicalization-bottleneck claim (and would indicate answer-leakage if cross-problem also rescues).

Experiment 4 (H3 -- Steering a canonicalization direction moves accuracy): Tests the mechanism's generality. Data: matched converged-minus-non-converged phrasing contrasts (content matched) yield a difference-in-means "canonicalization" direction at the convergence layer. Systems: plus-direction steering on hard phrasings, minus-direction on easy phrasings, random-direction of matched norm, no-steer. Decisive metric first: accuracy gain from plus-direction steering on hard phrasings versus random-direction; secondary: minus-direction induced failure on easy phrasings, dose-response, whether per-item convergence increase from patching/steering predicts per-item accuracy gain (Spearman), and specificity (easy-item accuracy within 1 point, fluency preserved). Convincing result: plus-direction steering raises hard-phrasing accuracy by >= 3 points over random-direction (CI excludes 0) with monotonic dose-response and preserved easy-item accuracy, minus-direction lowers easy-phrasing accuracy, and convergence change mediates the gain. Indecision band: steering effects within +/-2 points of random-direction leave the direction unproven; the patching result (Experiment 3) then stands alone. Negative result: no steerable effect means the canonicalization direction is not causal.

Experiment 5 (H1/H3 -- High-stakes clinical instance): Tests whether colloquial phrasing degrades diagnosis through failed canonicalization and patching rescues it. Data: 300 clinical case clusters adapted from MedQA (USMLE, 12,723 questions), each pairing colloquial patient-reported phrasing with formal chart phrasing of identical findings for a differential-diagnosis task; 300 supports paired contrasts under expert spot-checking. Decisive metric first: confident-misdiagnosis rate on colloquial versus formal phrasings, and its relation to a lower Convergence Score on colloquial phrasings; secondary: misdiagnosis reduction under canonical-representation patching on fine-distinction cases. Convincing result: colloquial phrasings show lower convergence and higher confident misdiagnosis, and canonical patching reduces misdiagnosis by >= 5 points (CIs exclude 0). Indecision band: a colloquial-versus-formal gap or patching effect within +/-2 points is inconclusive for high-stakes transfer. Negative result: no phrasing effect on diagnosis, or no patching rescue, bounds the claim to benign benchmarks.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Convergence may be a shallow artifact of lexical/length similarity rather than genuine semantic canonicalization; mitigated by controlling for length/word-overlap in all analyses, by the NMT-paraphrase-style confound checks, and by the causal patching test (which holds content fixed and manipulates only the representation). (2) Paraphrases may not be perfectly meaning-preserving, confounding 'hard phrasing' with subtle meaning shifts; mitigated by back-translation and human verification and by using controlled templated transforms. (3) Instruction-tuned models may be robustly paraphrase-invariant, flattening convergence differences (ceiling); we include harder/awkward phrasings, multiple models, and base variants, and focus on clusters with genuine behavioral variance. (4) The convergence layer may vary across models/tasks; we scan all layers and report the layer of maximal within-cluster convergence per model. (5) Same-problem patching could rescue accuracy simply by leaking the answer rather than restoring canonicalization; we patch only the PRE-reasoning problem representation (before any solution content), verify no answer tokens are present, and use cross-problem/random patching specificity controls. (6) The canonicalization direction may entangle with generic difficulty/confidence; addressed by matched converged/non-converged contrasts, random-direction steering, and easy-item specificity checks. (7) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (8) A null result (convergence does not predict or cause correctness) is itself informative: it would indicate paraphrase brittleness is not driven by a canonicalization bottleneck but by reasoning-stage sensitivity, distinguishing surface-form failures from representation-normalization failures. (9) The 'mental paraphrase' framing is operationalized representationally and causally, not as a claim of human-like paraphrasing.

novelty.reasoning: Core technical claims that would need to be novel: (1) LLMs perform a pre-reasoning internal canonicalization/'mental paraphrase' that maps varied phrasings of the same problem toward a shared representation; (2) failures on awkward phrasings are specifically caused by incomplete convergence to that canonical form rather than later reasoning errors; (3) per-item pre-reasoning convergence is a measurable diagnostic signal predicting correctness beyond shallow features/confidence; (4) patching the canonical representation from an easy phrasing into a hard phrasing causally rescues performance; (5) a canonicalization steering direction can modulate robustness, including in a clinical colloquial-vs-formal setting. Relative to prior behavioral brittleness studies and representation-convergence work, the proposal's main novelty is the mechanistic canonicalization-bottleneck account plus pre-reasoning causal patching/steering tests. The closest prior family is paraphrase brittleness and representation convergence under successful reasoning; the actual delta is moving from observation of sensitivity/convergence to a specific causal mechanism localized before reasoning. This is meaningfully non-trivial, though some components are adjacent to known representation/steering methods and the 'canonical form' concept risks collapsing into superficial similarity unless operationalized more sharply.
revision_notes: Define 'canonical form' more rigorously and distinguish it from frequent phrasing, terse style, or embedding centroid artifacts.
Add one stronger novelty separator versus existing representation-convergence papers: e.g., demonstrate convergence before any reasoning token and not merely during answer production.
Include a direct comparison to alternative mechanisms such as confidence, familiarity, lexical normalization, or retrieval-to-pretraining-neighbor accounts.
Strengthen the claim that novelty lives in mechanism rather than just setting by pre-registering competing causal explanations and discriminating tests.
Clarify whether the clinical component is a genuine new setting contribution or only an illustrative case study.

impact.reasoning: The problem under study is surface-form fragility in LLM reasoning and decision-making: semantically equivalent wording changes correctness because internal normalization may fail. Who cares: interpretability researchers, robustness/evaluation researchers, model developers, and potentially safety/clinical users where colloquial phrasing matters. If true, the result could change how people evaluate robustness, localize failure modes, and design interventions or benchmarks; the strongest one-line case is that many 'reasoning failures' may actually be pre-reasoning representation failures caused by wording. This has decent citation and follow-up potential because it provides both a mechanistic framing and diagnostics/interventions. The 'so what?' test mostly passes: if supported, researchers may shift from output-only paraphrase stress tests toward internal diagnostics and robustness interventions; if falsified, that also clarifies that brittleness arises later in reasoning. Still, the downstream practical reach is moderate rather than maximal because the proposal studies mechanism in medium-scale open models and the application path to production systems is not fully developed.

Add a stronger case that either outcome is useful: positive result suggests intervention targets; negative result rules out a prominent mechanism and redirects robustness research.
Identify the communities most likely to build on the work (mechanistic interpretability, evaluation, safety, medical NLP) and the concrete artifacts they would reuse.

review.reasoning: The proposal is unusually testable and better specified than many mechanism proposals: hypotheses are falsifiable, experiments are concrete, controls are partly thought through, and causal claims are backed by patching/steering plans. However, there are important logical and methodological gaps. The biggest issue is construct validity: the 'canonical centroid' defined as frequent/terse-formal phrasing may bake in style/familiarity assumptions and may not reflect a true latent canonical representation. Layer selection by maximal within-cluster convergence risks post hoc optimization. The pre-reasoning extraction point ('end-of-problem') may already contain substantial problem parsing or hidden answer-related processing; answer leakage controls need to be stronger than 'no answer tokens present.' Meaning-preservation verification with only 10% human checks may be insufficient, especially for math and clinical paraphrases. The diagnostic regression may still confound convergence with difficulty or training familiarity. The steering direction derived from converged-minus-non-converged examples may entangle correctness, confidence, and task difficulty. The clinical experiment is underspecified relative to the rest and may overclaim on 'misdiagnosis.' If executed well, this could be strong enough for a serious ML venue, but only with sharper operationalization, stricter controls, and stronger alternative-explanation tests.
revision_notes: Pre-specify the convergence layer selection procedure on held-out data or use nested evaluation to avoid circularity/post hoc layer picking.

Name: self_translation_drift
Title: Lost in Self-Translation: Does an LLM Corrupt Its Own Intermediate Conclusions When Forced to Re-Express Them in Another Language?
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM is made to restate its own intermediate reasoning conclusions in a different language mid-trace (self-translation), the semantic content of those conclusions systematically drifts away from the original, this drift compounds across a multi-step trace and causes downstream errors, is larger for concepts lacking clean cross-lingual equivalents, and is mediated by a locatable 'meaning-preservation' representation that can be causally steered to reduce drift.
Related Work: Prior interpretability work shows LLMs route reasoning through an English-shaped pivot (Do Multilingual LLMs Think in English?, 2025; Beyond English-Centric, 2024), that latent-language consistency is not always necessary because models re-align near output layers (Do LLMs Need to Think in One Language?, 2025), that language mixing rises with difficulty and reflects internal preferences (Language Mixing in Reasoning LMs, 2025), and that ablating language-specific components improves multilingual reasoning (When Less Language is More, 2025). Translation-mechanism work (Exploring the Translation Mechanism, 2025) localizes sparse heads for word-level translation. ALL of this studies where reasoning is routed or how surface translation works; none studies what happens to the CONTENT of a model's OWN intermediate conclusions when it is forced to re-express them in another language partway through reasoning, whether such self-translation induces compounding semantic drift, whether drift concentrates on cross-lingually mismatched concepts, or whether a meaning-preservation signal mediates it. Human bilingual research (self-translation cost, interpretation load; fMRI of Simultaneous Interpretation, 2014) shows re-expression across languages taxes control and can distort meaning. We uniquely transfer this into LLMs as a controlled intra-trace self-translation manipulation with a Location + Causal Intervention account and a high-stakes clinical instance.
Abstract: Bilingual humans who translate their own thoughts on the fly pay a cost: meaning can distort as an idea is re-expressed in another language, especially for concepts that do not map cleanly between languages. Large language models increasingly reason across languages, mixing scripts and routing through an English-shaped pivot, yet no work asks whether re-expressing their own intermediate conclusions in a different language corrupts the content of those conclusions. We introduce a controlled self-translation paradigm: partway through a multi-step reasoning trace, the model is required to restate an intermediate conclusion it just derived in a target language, then continue reasoning from the re-expressed version. We test three claims. First, self-translation induces semantic drift: the re-expressed conclusion measurably diverges in meaning from the original, and this drift compounds across successive self-translations, degrading final accuracy relative to same-language paraphrase and no-restatement controls. Second, drift is content-selective: it is larger for reasoning steps whose key concepts lack clean cross-lingual equivalents (lexical gaps, culturally specific terms) than for steps built on cross-lingually stable concepts. Third, drift is causally mediated by a locatable meaning-preservation representation: a probe reading whether the re-expressed conclusion still encodes the original meaning predicts downstream error, and steering along a located preservation direction (or patching the pre-translation conclusion representation) reduces drift and rescues accuracy. We evaluate on multilingual math, multi-hop QA, and logic across several open-weight models, plus a high-stakes clinical instance where re-expressing a partial diagnosis in another language silently flips the conclusion. Our work reframes multilingual reasoning as vulnerable to self-inflicted meaning loss and offers an interpretable failure signal and a training-free mitigation.
Experiments:
Shared setup (applies to every experiment below): all runs use five frozen open-weight multilingual models -- Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Gemma-2-9B -- with no weight updates; the only trainable parameters anywhere are linear-probe weights on frozen hidden states. Decoding is greedy for primary conditions and temperature 0.7 for sampled conditions, each sampled run over seeds 0, 1, 2. Effect sizes carry 95% bootstrap CIs over 1000 item-level resamples; behavioral tests use mixed-effects regression with crossed random intercepts (1|model)+(1|item). "Self-translation" means the model is required, at a defined insertion point, to restate an intermediate conclusion it just derived in a target language different from the reasoning language, then continue reasoning from the re-expressed version. Target languages are drawn from each model's stronger and weaker languages and are back-translation-checked.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- Self-translation induces semantic drift that compounds and degrades accuracy): Tests the core effect against restatement controls. Data: a battery of 250 items each for (a) multi-step arithmetic sampled from the GSM8K test split (1,319 available), (b) multi-hop QA (3-5 hops) sampled from the 2WikiMultiHopQA dev set (12,576 available), and (c) synthetic deductive-logic chains (depth 2-6, auto-checkable), 750 items, each with defined insertion points where an intermediate conclusion has just been derived and with known intermediate-conclusion ground truth; 250/task supports stable condition contrasts within budget. Conditions, content held constant, format-enforced and compliance-verified: (i) NO-RESTATE baseline; (ii) SAME-LANGUAGE PARAPHRASE (restate then continue, controlling for the act of restating); (iii) SELF-TRANSLATE (restate in a different language, continue from it); (iv) COMPOUNDING SELF-TRANSLATE (translate at 2-3 successive insertion points). Decisive metric first: final-answer accuracy of SELF-TRANSLATE versus SAME-LANGUAGE PARAPHRASE and NO-RESTATE from mixed-effects logistic regression accuracy ~ condition + (1|model)+(1|item); secondary: a dose-response drop with number of self-translations, and error-localization (does the final error follow from the drifted conclusion?). Convincing result: SELF-TRANSLATE falls below SAME-LANGUAGE PARAPHRASE by >= 4 points (CI excludes 0, isolating cross-lingual re-expression from restatement per se), COMPOUNDING degrades further monotonically, and errors localize to the re-expressed step. Indecision band: a SELF-TRANSLATE-minus-PARAPHRASE gap within +/-2 points (CI overlapping 0) means cross-lingual re-expression is not separable from restatement. Negative result: no gap beyond paraphrase means self-translation is lossless, refuting H1 and dissociating LLMs from the human self-translation cost; only compliant trials (restated conclusion actually used downstream) are analyzed.

Experiment 2 (H1 -- Drift measures are valid and agree): Tests that drift is measurable two independent ways. Data: the same traces. Drift between original and re-expressed conclusion is quantified by (a) round-trip semantic equivalence (back-translate, compare to the original via an NLI/entailment model and exact-answer match for numeric conclusions) and (b) representational distance between hidden-state encodings of the original versus re-expressed conclusion at matched positions. Decisive metric first: rank correlation between the NLI-based and representational drift measures; secondary: whether either drift measure separates error from correct trials. Convincing result: the two drift measures agree at Spearman rho >= 0.4 (CI excludes 0) and higher drift accompanies errors. Indecision band: agreement rho 0.2-0.35 means the drift construct is only weakly cross-validated and downstream mediation is treated cautiously. Negative result: no agreement (rho ~ 0) means "drift" is measurement noise, undermining the mechanism.

Experiment 3 (H2 -- Drift is content-selective, larger for cross-lingually mismatched concepts): Tests selectivity. Data: the same intermediate conclusions, each tagged by whether its key concept has a clean target-language equivalent (using cross-lingual dictionaries and lexical-gap / culturally-specific term lists) versus a cross-lingually stable concept, controlling for concept frequency and step difficulty. Decisive metric first: the concept_gap coefficient on drift and on accuracy loss from mixed-effects regression drift ~ concept_gap_status + concept_frequency + step_difficulty + (1|model)+(1|item); secondary: the accuracy-loss interaction. Convincing result: gap/mismatched concepts show reliably larger drift and accuracy loss (CI excludes 0) after controlling for frequency and difficulty. Indecision band: a concept_gap coefficient CI within +/-0.05 standardized units means selectivity is not detectable. Negative result: no gap effect means drift is uniform across concept types, refuting H2.

Experiment 4 (H3 -- A locatable meaning-preservation representation mediates drift): Tests the representational locus. Data: the traces, split 70/30 by item. At the post-self-translation position a linear probe (only probe trainable) decodes whether the original meaning/answer of the intermediate conclusion is still encoded (per-layer held-out AUROC). Decisive metric first: held-out AUROC for original-meaning decodability, and whether low decodability predicts downstream error; secondary: per-item mediation of the condition-to-error effect (Spearman). Convincing result: AUROC >= 0.70, low decodability predicts error (rho >= 0.2, CI excludes 0), and probe-decodable drift mediates the condition effect. Indecision band: AUROC 0.55-0.65 means a weak preservation signal that cannot anchor the mediation claim. Negative result: chance AUROC means no locatable preservation representation, refuting H3's mechanism.

Experiment 5 (H3 -- Patching and steering reduce drift and rescue accuracy): Tests causality. Data: (a) Patching -- cache the pre-self-translation conclusion representation and patch it into the post-translation forward pass; controls are patching from a different item's conclusion and a random-matched representation, and we patch only the intermediate-conclusion representation (before the final answer) to rule out answer-leakage. (b) Steering -- a difference-in-means "meaning-preservation" direction from preserved-minus-drifted conclusion contrasts; plus-direction steering after self-translation, minus-direction under same-language paraphrase, random-direction of matched norm, no-steer. Decisive metric first: accuracy rescue on failed self-translate items under same-item patching versus no-patch, and under plus-direction steering versus random-direction; secondary: specificity (cross-item/random patching does not rescue; NO-RESTATE accuracy within 1 point; fluency preserved), dose-response. Convincing result: same-item patching and plus-direction steering each recover accuracy by >= 5 points over their controls (CIs exclude 0) while cross-item/random controls do not, with monotonic steering dose-response. Indecision band: rescue within +/-3 points of controls means the intervention is not selective. Negative result: no selective rescue means meaning-preservation is not a causal lever.

Experiment 6 (H3 -- High-stakes clinical hand-off instance): Tests whether self-translation flips a diagnosis and mitigation reduces it. Data: 300 clinical vignettes adapted from MedQA (USMLE, 12,723 questions) and constructed bilingual hand-off cases where a partial diagnostic conclusion must be re-expressed in another language mid-reasoning; 300 supports paired contrasts under expert spot-checking. Systems: NO-RESTATE, SELF-TRANSLATE, and SELF-TRANSLATE with preservation-direction steering or conclusion patching. Decisive metric first: diagnosis-flip rate on fine-distinction cases under SELF-TRANSLATE versus NO-RESTATE; secondary: flip-rate reduction under steering/patching. Convincing result: self-translation raises the diagnosis-flip rate and the mitigations cut it by >= 5 points (CIs exclude 0). Indecision band: gaps within +/-2 points are inconclusive for high-stakes transfer. Negative result: no flip effect bounds the claim to benign benchmarks.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Self-translation may degrade accuracy simply by adding tokens/steps rather than via meaning drift; mitigated by the SAME-LANGUAGE PARAPHRASE control (equal added steps, no cross-lingual re-expression) and by requiring the drift measures to mediate the accuracy loss. (2) Instruction-tuned models may re-align near output layers (per Do LLMs Need to Think in One Language?, 2025) and avoid drift entirely, muting effects; a null in easy conditions with an effect in COMPOUNDING/gap-concept conditions is still informative, and we include harder items and multiple models. (3) Compliance risk - the model may ignore the self-translation instruction or covertly keep the original-language conclusion in context; we enforce format, verify the restated conclusion is used downstream, and analyze only compliant trials. (4) Drift measures may be confounded by NLI-model or tokenizer noise; we cross-validate NLI-based and representational drift and use exact-answer match for numeric conclusions. (5) Patching could rescue by leaking the answer rather than restoring meaning; we patch only the intermediate-conclusion representation (before the final answer) and use cross-item/random patching specificity controls. (6) The preservation direction may entangle with generic difficulty/confidence; mitigated by matched preserved/drifted contrasts, held-out probe validation, random-direction steering, and NO-RESTATE specificity checks. (7) Concept-gap tagging is fuzzy; we use multiple resources and annotators and control for frequency/difficulty. (8) Effects may be small or model/language-specific; we test multiple models and languages and report effect sizes with CIs. (9) A null result (self-translation preserves meaning) is itself informative, showing LLM cross-lingual re-expression is lossless unlike the human self-translation cost. (10) The self-translation framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like bilingual cognition.

novelty.reasoning: Core technical claims that must be novel: (1) forcing an LLM to restate its own intermediate conclusion in another language mid-trace causes semantic drift and downstream error; (2) this drift compounds across multiple such self-translations; (3) drift is larger for lexical-gap or culturally specific concepts than for clean equivalents; (4) a locatable meaning-preservation representation mediates the effect and can be patched/steered to reduce drift; (5) this matters in a hand-off style clinical setting. Relative to prior multilingual reasoning, language-mixing, and language-drift work, the strongest novelty is the controlled intra-trace self-translation manipulation with same-language paraphrase and no-restatement controls, which sharpens a causal claim beyond merely observing natural pivoting/mixing. The content-selectivity and mechanistic mediation add non-trivial delta. That said, the broader phenomenon, cross-lingual semantic distortion during reasoning, is already active and close prior work exists on pivot errors, language drift, and translation-localized mechanisms, so the contribution is a new experimental paradigm and mechanistic decomposition more than a wholly new problem.

impact.reasoning: The problem under study is whether multilingual LLMs corrupt their own intermediate semantic state when forced to re-express it across languages during reasoning, and whether that corruption causes downstream mistakes. Relevant stakeholders are multilingual NLP researchers, interpretability/safety researchers, and practitioners deploying multilingual systems for QA, RAG, translation, or cross-lingual hand-offs. If true, the result could change evaluation and prompting practice by discouraging or safeguarding mid-trace cross-lingual restatement and motivating mitigation at representation level. The strongest case is that a very common operational pattern, cross-lingual reformulation during reasoning or hand-off, may introduce systematic semantic corruption invisible from final surface fluency. The impact is meaningful but not obviously field-defining: many users do not expose chain-of-thought or force intermediate restatement, and the proposal still needs to show the effect appears in realistic deployments rather than mostly in constructed prompting setups. The phenomenon value is fairly strong even if the method is simple, because either a positive or null result would inform how multilingual reasoning is conceptualized.

review.reasoning: The proposal is thoughtful, testable, and unusually explicit about controls, models, seeds, statistics, and convincing-result thresholds. The core hypotheses are reasonably falsifiable. Strong points include the decisive same-language paraphrase control, compounding condition, multiple models, mixed-effects analysis, and patch/random controls. However, there are several technical gaps. 'Known intermediate-conclusion ground truth' is underspecified and hard to guarantee for 2Wiki and logic traces; compliance verification and proving the model actually continues from the translated conclusion are non-trivial. Back-translation checking may itself miss nuanced drift. The mechanistic claims are the weakest: a probe AUROC>=0.70 and correlation with error do not establish a distinct meaning-preservation representation, and mediation language is overstrong without a more rigorous causal design. Patching/steering may leak answer information or improve performance via generic confidence restoration rather than semantic preservation. The concept-gap annotation scheme is also underspecified and potentially subjective. The clinical experiment looks underdeveloped relative to the rest and may feel bolted on. If executed carefully, this could be workshop-to-mid-tier conference interesting and potentially stronger if the mechanistic evidence is solid, but in current form it is not yet airtight enough for a top ML venue.

Name: translation_crutch_grammar_induction
Title: Grammar Book or Bilingual Dictionary? Testing Whether LLMs Learn a Novel Language In-Context by Building a Grammar or Leaning on a Translation Crutch
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM is given a novel language in-context (a mini grammar plus examples), it does not induce a genuine standalone grammar; instead it leans on a 'translation crutch,' covertly mapping each construction back to a pivot language and generating via that pivot. The strength of this crutch grows with typological distance from the model's training languages, causally bounds how well the model generalizes to unseen constructions, and is a locatable, steerable internal signal: suppressing the crutch forces (and, for near-typology languages, improves) genuine grammar use, while amplifying it induces pivot-shaped errors.
Related Work: Recent work shows LLMs can do some explicit in-context language learning from grammar-book explanations ('Explicit Learning and the LLM in MT', 2025) and that learnability degrades with typological implausibility both in pretraining ('Can LMs Learn Typologically Implausible Languages?', 2025) and constructed-language studies (Culbertson & Kirby 2011). In-context language learning has been mechanistically tied to n-gram/induction heads ('In-Context Language Learning: Architectures and Algorithms', 2024), and multilingual work shows shared cross-lingual syntactic circuits with a language-independent pivot direction ('The Same But Different', 2024; 'On the Similarity of Circuits across Languages', 2024) and English-shaped pivot routing. All of this either (a) measures behavioral learnability without asking HOW the model represents the novel language, or (b) studies pivot routing only for KNOWN languages present in training. None ask whether in-context learning of a genuinely novel language is a real grammar induction or a covert translation-to-pivot process, whether that crutch scales with typological distance, whether it causally caps generalization to unseen constructions, or whether it is a locatable/steerable component. We uniquely reframe in-context language learning as a translation-crutch-vs-native-grammar dissociation with a Location + Causal Intervention account.
Abstract: Give a large language model a short grammar and a handful of examples of a language it has never seen, and it will often produce plausible new sentences. But is it inducing a genuine grammar, or is it quietly translating every construction back to a language it already knows and generating through that crutch? We propose the translation-crutch hypothesis: in-context learning of a novel language proceeds largely by covert mapping to a pivot (typically English-shaped) representation rather than by building a standalone grammar, that reliance on this crutch grows with the novel language's typological distance from the model's training languages, and that the crutch causally limits generalization to constructions not derivable by pivot-style word-for-word mapping (e.g., non-canonical word order, agreement, and morphology absent from the pivot). We construct controlled artificial languages that systematically vary typological distance from English (word order, case marking, agreement, morphological richness), each presented in-context via a mini grammar plus examples, and test generalization to held-out construction types. Behaviorally, we predict a distance-graded generalization cliff concentrated on pivot-incompatible constructions, with characteristic pivot-shaped errors (e.g., defaulting to English word order or dropping agreement). Mechanistically, we locate a 'pivot-translation' representation via probing (can the pivot-language gloss be decoded from hidden states during novel-language generation?) and test causally: suppressing this component should force genuine grammar use and improve near-typology generalization while hurting far-typology output, and amplifying it should induce pivot-shaped errors. Across several open-weight models we quantify the crutch, its typological-distance scaling, its causal cap on generalization, and steering controllability, reframing in-context language learning as translation rather than acquisition.
Experiments:
Shared setup (applies to every experiment below): all runs use five frozen open-weight models -- Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Gemma-2-9B -- with no weight updates; the only trainable parameters anywhere are linear-probe weights on frozen hidden states. The novel language is supplied entirely in-context (a compact grammar-book plus example pairs); no fine-tuning occurs. Decoding is greedy for primary conditions and temperature 0.7 for sampled conditions, each sampled run over seeds 0, 1, 2. Effect sizes carry 95% bootstrap CIs over 1000 item-level resamples; behavioral tests use mixed-effects regression with crossed random intercepts (1|model)+(1|item). The "pivot" is the model's dominant training language (English by default); a "pivot-shaped error" is one that defaults to pivot structure (e.g., English word order or dropped agreement).

Experiment 1 (H1 -- In-context novel-language learning shows a typological-distance-graded generalization cliff on pivot-incompatible constructions): Tests the behavioral crutch signature. Data: a controlled artificial-language suite we construct -- 6-8 synthetic languages sharing a fixed nonce lexicon and a small function-word inventory but varying along typological axes graded from English: word order (SVO -> SOV -> VSO -> free order with case), overt case marking (none -> nominative/accusative suffixes), subject-verb and adjective-noun agreement (none -> gender/number), and morphological richness (isolating -> agglutinative suffix stacking); each language ships a compact in-context grammar-book (rules stated in English) plus 15-30 example sentence pairs, and a per-language typological-distance score is the count/type of features diverging from English. For each language we hold out entire construction TYPES from the in-context examples (show declaratives, test questions; show singular agreement, test plural; show intransitives, test ditransitives) and test roughly 200 held-out items per language via translation-into and translation-out-of the novel language plus grammaticality judgments over minimal pairs, auto-graded against the ground-truth generative grammar; 6-8 languages x ~200 items spans the distance axis with stable estimates within budget. Decisive metric first: the typological_distance x construction_pivot_compatibility interaction on accuracy from mixed-effects regression accuracy ~ typological_distance * pivot_compatibility + (1|model)+(1|item); secondary: the pivot-shaped error rate on pivot-incompatible held-out constructions. Convincing result: accuracy on pivot-INCOMPATIBLE held-out constructions falls steeply with typological distance (reliable negative distance slope, CI excludes 0) while pivot-compatible constructions stay high, and errors are predominantly pivot-shaped (>= 50% of errors). Indecision band: a distance x compatibility interaction whose CI corresponds to an accuracy-slope difference within +/-3 points across the distance range means no differential cliff is detectable. Negative result: distance-independent generalization with no pivot-shaped error concentration means the model performs genuine in-context grammar induction, a strong positive result refuting the crutch hypothesis.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- A locatable pivot-translation representation rises with distance and on errors): Tests the internal crutch. Data: during novel-language generation (with in-context English glosses REMOVED at test time to avoid a shortcut), we extract hidden states at content and function-word positions, split 70/30 by item, and train linear probes (only probe trainable) to decode (i) the corresponding English gloss token and (ii) a pivot-translating-versus-native-generating state from near-typology-versus-far-typology contrasts (per-layer held-out AUROC). Decisive metric first: pivot-gloss decoding AUROC and its scaling with typological distance; secondary: whether pivot-gloss decodability is higher on error trials. Convincing result: pivot-gloss decodability is well above chance (AUROC >= 0.65), rises reliably with typological distance (positive slope, CI excludes 0), and is higher on error trials. Indecision band: AUROC 0.55-0.62 or a distance slope CI overlapping 0 means the pivot representation is not clearly present or not distance-scaled. Negative result: chance decodability (with glosses removed) means no covert pivot-translation step, supporting genuine acquisition and refuting H2.

Experiment 3 (H1/H2 -- The pivot representation mediates the behavioral cliff): Tests the link. Data: the same items. Decisive metric first: Spearman correlation between per-item pivot-gloss decodability and per-item generalization error on pivot-incompatible constructions; secondary: whether decodability adds predictive power over typological distance alone. Convincing result: per-item decodability predicts pivot-incompatible error at rho >= 0.2 (CI excludes 0) and improves prediction beyond distance. Indecision band: rho within +/-0.1 means the crutch representation and the behavioral cliff are not linked at our power. Negative result: no correlation dissociates the representation from behavior.

Experiment 4 (H3 -- Suppressing the crutch dissociates near- from far-typology; amplifying induces pivot-shaped errors): Tests causality via the predicted dissociation. Data: a difference-in-means "pivot-translation" direction from pivot-translating-minus-native-generating contrasts at the best probe layer. Systems: SUPPRESS (subtract the direction during generation), AMPLIFY (add it), random-direction of matched norm, no-steer. Decisive metric first: the interaction of steering (suppress versus no-steer) with typological distance on accuracy -- suppression should HELP near-typology and HURT far-typology (a dissociation, not a uniform effect); secondary: amplification-induced pivot-shaped error rate on well-learned constructions, dose-response, and specificity (lexical accuracy and fluency preserved). Convincing result: suppression improves near-typology pivot-compatible/agreement/word-order compliance by >= 3 points while reducing far-typology accuracy (a reliable crossover interaction, CI excludes 0), and amplification induces pivot-shaped errors (English word order / dropped morphology) even on well-learned constructions, both beyond random-direction controls. Indecision band: a suppression x distance interaction whose CI corresponds to a differential within +/-2 points means the dissociation is not demonstrated (a uniform degradation would be ambiguous). Negative result: uniform or null steering effects, or effects indistinguishable from random-direction, mean the pivot direction is not a causal route.

Experiment 5 (H1 -- Grammar-book versus examples, and pivot-tracks-the-model's-dominant-language crossover): Tests robustness and ties the crutch to the model's own pivot. Data: the same suite. We vary whether in-context material is rule-based (explicit grammar) versus example-only, vary the number of examples and lexicon overlap, and for a model with a non-English dominant language test whether the crutch tracks THAT language's typology rather than English. Decisive metric first: crutch reliance (pivot-shaped error rate and pivot-gloss decodability) under rule-based versus example-only material; secondary: whether the distance axis realigns to a non-English pivot for the non-English-dominant model. Convincing result: explicit rules reduce crutch reliance (or only improve pivot-compatible constructions) reliably, and for the non-English-dominant model the cliff and pivot-decodability realign to that language's typology (CI excludes 0), directly tying the effect to the model's dominant language. Indecision band: rule-versus-example differences within +/-2 points, or an ambiguous pivot realignment, leave these refinements open without affecting Experiments 1-4. Negative result: no realignment to the model's own pivot would undercut the claim that the crutch is the dominant training language specifically.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Artificial languages may be too easy or too hard, flattening the distance-graded cliff; we calibrate feature counts and example numbers to mid-range difficulty and report the full distance sweep. (2) A pivot-gloss probe decoding English during generation could reflect the in-context English glosses still present in context rather than a genuine internal translation step; we mitigate by removing glosses from context at test time, probing at matched positions, and using near-vs-far typology contrasts and the causal steering test (which manipulates the representation, not the prompt). (3) Suppressing the crutch may broadly degrade generation, confounding the near-typology improvement claim; we use random-direction and matched-magnitude controls and test the predicted DISSOCIATION (helps near-typology, hurts far-typology) rather than a uniform effect. (4) 'Typological distance from training languages' is approximate and model-specific; the non-English-pivot crossover test and per-model distance scoring address this. (5) Instruction-tuned models may already do robust in-context grammar induction, muting the crutch; we include base variants, harder morphology, and multiple models, and report effect sizes. (6) Auto-grading against a generative grammar may miss acceptable variation; we use minimal-pair grammaticality judgments and human spot-checks. (7) A null result (no translation crutch; generalization independent of typological distance and pivot-decodability) is itself highly informative: it would show LLMs perform genuine in-context grammar induction rather than covert translation, a strong positive claim about language-learning ability. (8) The 'crutch/acquisition' framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim about human-like language acquisition.

novelty.reasoning: Core novel claims: (1) in-context novel-language learning is often mediated by a covert pivot-language translation process rather than standalone grammar induction; (2) reliance on this pivot crutch increases with typological distance and specifically harms pivot-incompatible constructions; (3) the pivot representation is internally locatable even after gloss removal; (4) this representation is causally steerable, with a predicted near-vs-far typology crossover; (5) the pivot should align with the model's dominant training language, not necessarily English. Relative to prior behavioral learnability and known-language pivot-routing work, the main delta is a mechanistic dissociation between translation-crutch and genuine induction plus causal intervention. This is meaningfully beyond an obvious baseline, though it still sits close to existing ICL-of-languages and multilingual-routing families rather than introducing a wholly new task.

Name: pragmatic_enrichment_default
Title: Reading Between the Lines When You Shouldn't: A Pragmatic-Enrichment Default as a Hidden Reasoning Failure Mode in LLMs
Short Hypothesis: LLMs, like humans, apply a pragmatic-enrichment default — spontaneously upgrading literal meaning with Gricean inferences (scalar implicature 'some'→'not all', exhaustivity, relevance-driven additions) — and this default is beneficial for cooperative dialogue but silently corrupts tasks that require the strict literal reading (formal logic, contracts, statutes, clinical instructions). This enrichment is a locatable, steerable internal 'pragmatic-mode' signal that fires by default; suppressing it at literal-mode tasks reduces enrichment errors, while amplifying it induces them even on cases where the literal reading is required.
Related Work: Existing LLM pragmatics work is behavioral or competence-oriented: LLMs partly detect implicatures and improve with Gricean CoT prompting (Is the Pope Catholic? 2023), fall short of humans on implicature/presupposition/speech acts (Pragmatic Competence Without Embodiment 2025; Manner Implicatures 2024; Are BabyLMs Deaf to Gricean Maxims 2025), and neural encoders predict scalar-inference strength from linguistic features (Harnessing the Linguistic Signal 2020). Ambiguity work locates sparse Ambiguity-Encoding Neurons that steer answering vs abstention (Sparse Neurons 2025), and loophole work shows models exploit scalar implicature (LLMs Identify Ambiguities and Exploit Loopholes 2025). ALL of this treats pragmatic enrichment as a capacity to be measured or improved. NONE frame enrichment as a DEFAULT that mis-fires as a reasoning FAILURE MODE on literal-required tasks, isolate a controllable literal-vs-enriched internal mode, test whether it causally CAUSES errors on formal/legal/clinical text, or provide a Location + Causal Intervention account with a suppression fix. My prior proposals covered ambiguity-branch collapse, evidentiality, counterfactual mood, and canonicalization but never pragmatic enrichment / the Quantity maxim as a default reasoning liability. We uniquely flip pragmatics from a desired competence into a diagnosable, steerable hazard.
Abstract: Cooperative communication depends on going beyond literal meaning: when a speaker says 'some students passed,' listeners infer 'not all.' Large language models reproduce these pragmatic enrichments, and prior work treats this as a competence to celebrate. We argue the opposite is also true: pragmatic enrichment is a DEFAULT that silently corrupts reasoning whenever the task actually requires the strict literal reading — formal logic, contracts, statutes, and clinical instructions, where 'some' must mean 'at least one', an unstated condition must not be assumed, and only what is written counts. We hypothesize that an LLM carries a controllable internal 'pragmatic-mode' signal governing whether it computes literal or enriched meaning, that this mode is engaged by default, and that it is a proximal cause of systematic errors on literal-required tasks. We make three claims. First, the enrichment default is real and harmful: on matched items differing only in whether the correct answer needs the literal or the enriched reading, models over-enrich, producing characteristic errors (treating 'some' as 'not all' in a valid syllogism, importing unstated exceptions into a contract clause). Second, mode is diagnostic: a probe reads literal-vs-enriched processing from hidden states and predicts these errors before they surface. Third, mode is causal and fixable: steering down a located pragmatic-enrichment direction reduces literal-task errors, while steering it up induces enrichment even where the literal reading is required. We evaluate across several open-weight models on logic, contract, and clinical-instruction tasks, plus a high-stakes medical instance where over-reading a literal dosing instruction is dangerous, quantifying the default, its mechanistic mediation, and steering controllability.
Experiments:
Shared setup (applies to every experiment below): all runs use five frozen open-weight models -- Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, and Gemma-2-9B -- with no weight updates; the only trainable parameters anywhere are linear-probe weights on frozen hidden states. Decoding is greedy for primary conditions and temperature 0.7 for sampled conditions, each sampled run over seeds 0, 1, 2. Effect sizes carry 95% bootstrap CIs over 1000 item-level resamples; behavioral tests use mixed-effects regression with crossed random intercepts (1|model)+(1|item). "Pragmatic enrichment" is upgrading literal meaning with Gricean inference (scalar "some" -> "not all", exhaustivity, unstated conditions); the "enrichment lure" is the answer obtained if the enriched (rather than literal) reading is applied where the literal reading is required.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- The enrichment default is real and harmful on literal-required tasks): Tests over-enrichment on matched pairs. Data: a literal-versus-enriched matched battery of 250 items per domain -- (a) scalar implicature in logic (syllogisms/entailments where treating "some" as "not all" or "or" as exclusive flips validity), (b) exhaustivity/presupposition in contracts (clauses where importing an unstated exception or reading a list as exhaustive changes the answer), (c) clinical instructions (directives where enriching a literal statement changes the action) -- each in matched pairs differing ONLY in whether the LITERAL or the ENRICHED reading is correct, with a labeled enrichment lure, plus matched cooperative-dialogue controls where enrichment IS correct (selectivity); items are constructed from templated scalar/exhaustivity/instruction schemas with auto-checkable ground truth and expert spot-checks, 750 core items plus 250 cooperative controls. 250/domain supports stable required_mode x domain estimates within budget. Decisive metric first: enrichment-lure rate (and accuracy) on LITERAL-required versus ENRICHED-required items from mixed-effects regression lure_rate ~ required_mode * domain + (1|model)+(1|item); secondary: whether errors concentrate on the specific enrichment lure (the diagnostic of reading in an unstated inference), and whether explicit "interpret literally" prompting only partially closes the gap. Convincing result: models show a reliably higher enrichment-lure rate on literal-required items than on enriched-required items (CI excludes 0), with errors concentrated on the enrichment lure, cooperative controls staying accurate, and literal-prompting closing less than half the gap (default persists). Indecision band: a literal-versus-enriched lure-rate difference within +/-2 points (CI overlapping 0) means no default is detectable. Negative result: no over-enrichment, or literal-required errors that are not enrichment-shaped, means pragmatic inference is contextually gated rather than a default liability, refuting H1.

Experiment 2 (H1 -- Enrichment errors are not generic difficulty): Tests the matched-pair and lure-signature controls. Data: the same battery. Decisive metric first: the accuracy gap between the literal and enriched member of each matched pair (same surface content), attributable to interpretation mode rather than difficulty; secondary: fraction of literal-item errors equal to the exact enriched reading versus random wrong answers. Convincing result: the within-pair gap is reliable (CI excludes 0) and literal-item errors are predominantly the enriched reading (>= 60%), not random. Indecision band: a within-pair gap within +/-2 points, or an enriched-error fraction near chance, means the effect cannot be separated from difficulty. Negative result: errors unrelated to the enriched reading refute the enrichment interpretation of H1.

Experiment 3 (H2 -- A locatable pragmatic-mode signal is engaged by default and predicts errors): Tests the internal mode. Data: matched-pair items and enrichment-correct-versus-enrichment-error trials, split 70/30 by item; a linear probe (only probe trainable) on hidden states decodes enriched-versus-literal mode (per-layer held-out AUROC), and we derive a difference-in-means "pragmatic-enrichment" direction. Decisive metric first: held-out mode-decoding AUROC and the baseline projection onto the enrichment direction on literal-required items (is enrichment engaged by default?); secondary: whether per-item enrichment-mode projection predicts literal-task error and mediates required_mode -> error (Spearman). Convincing result: AUROC >= 0.70, a positive default enrichment projection on literal-required items, and enrichment projection predicts error (rho >= 0.2, CI excludes 0) and mediates the mode effect. Indecision band: AUROC 0.55-0.65 or a mediation rho within +/-0.1 means the mode signal is weak or not error-linked. Negative result: chance AUROC means no locatable pragmatic-mode signal, refuting H2.

Experiment 4 (H3 -- Steering the enrichment direction reduces and induces enrichment errors, with preserved cooperative competence): Tests causality and specificity. Data: the enrichment direction from Experiment 3. Systems: minus-enrichment steering on literal-required items (reduce errors), plus-enrichment steering on literal-required and cooperative-control items (induce errors), random-direction of matched norm, no-steer. Decisive metric first: enrichment-lure error reduction on literal-required items under minus-direction steering versus random-direction; secondary: plus-direction induced errors, dose-response, and the crucial specificity test that minus-direction steering does NOT harm cooperative-control accuracy (a generic push would hurt it), plus fluency preserved. Convincing result: minus-direction steering cuts literal-task enrichment errors by >= 3 points over random-direction (CI excludes 0) with monotonic dose-response, plus-direction induces enrichment errors even where the literal reading is required, and cooperative-control accuracy stays within 1 point (mode switch, not capacity removal). Indecision band: steering effects within +/-2 points of random-direction, or a cooperative-control drop that makes the effect look generic, leave the direction unproven. Negative result: no steerable, specific effect means the pragmatic-mode direction is not a causal, controllable switch.

Experiment 5 (H3 -- High-stakes clinical instance): Tests unsafe over-reading of literal dosing instructions. Data: 300 dosing/instruction vignettes adapted from MedQA (USMLE, 12,723 questions) and constructed instruction cases where the safe action requires the literal reading (do exactly what is written, do not infer unstated conditions); 300 supports paired contrasts under expert spot-checking. Systems: no-intervention and minus-enrichment steering. Decisive metric first: unsafe-action rate (enriched over-reading producing an unsafe action) on fine-distinction cases under no-intervention versus minus-direction steering; secondary: preserved accuracy on cases where enrichment is appropriate. Convincing result: the enrichment default produces unsafe over-reading at baseline and minus-direction steering reduces the unsafe-action rate by >= 5 points (CI excludes 0) without harming enrichment-appropriate items. Indecision band: an unsafe-action reduction within +/-2 points is inconclusive for high-stakes transfer. Negative result: no unsafe over-reading, or no steering benefit, bounds the claim to benign benchmarks.

Experiment 6 (H3 -- Robustness across implicature types and scale): Tests generality. Data: the battery re-partitioned by implicature type (scalar, exhaustivity, manner). Decisive metric first: whether the enrichment direction derived on one implicature type transfers (reduces errors) to the others; secondary: the default's dependence on model scale (7B versus 14B). Convincing result: the direction generalizes across implicature types (reliable cross-type error reduction, CI excludes 0) and the default is present across scales. Indecision band: cross-type transfer within +/-2 points leaves generality open without affecting the within-type results. Negative result: no cross-type transfer means the mode signal is implicature-specific rather than a unified pragmatic-mode axis.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Errors on literal-required items could stem from general difficulty rather than genuine pragmatic enrichment; mitigated by matched literal/enriched pairs (same surface content), the enrichment-lure error signature (errors are the SPECIFIC enriched reading, not random), and the cooperative-dialogue selectivity control. (2) Instruction-tuned models may already read literally when in a formal register, muting the default; we include base variants, harder items, and test whether 'interpret literally' prompting only partially closes the gap. (3) The enrichment direction may entangle with generic difficulty/confidence; addressed by matched literal/enriched contrasts, held-out probe validation, random-direction steering, and the crucial specificity test that suppression preserves cooperative-control accuracy (a generic push would hurt it). (4) Suppressing enrichment could globally flatten pragmatic ability; we explicitly measure and require preserved performance on enrichment-correct items, framing the goal as a controllable mode switch, not permanent removal. (5) Legal/clinical ground truth can be contestable; we use items with clear literal-correct answers and expert spot-checks. (6) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (7) A null result (no enrichment default, or literal errors are not enrichment-shaped) is itself informative — it would show LLM pragmatic inference is contextually gated rather than a default liability. (8) The Gricean/pragmatics framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like communicative intent.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) LLM pragmatic enrichment is a default failure mode on literal-required tasks, not just a competence; (2) a locatable 'pragmatic-mode' signal predicts literal-vs-enriched behavior; (3) steering that signal causally reduces literal errors while preserving cooperative pragmatics; (4) this matters especially for logic/legal/clinical text. The framing is meaningfully different from prior pragmatics work, but the underlying phenomenon sits close to existing scalar-implicature / pragmatic-competence studies and steering/intervention work. The main novelty is the reframing plus causal probing in a new failure-mode setting, not a clearly new mechanism. The strongest delta vs prior work is moving from 'can models compute implicatures?' to 'does enrichment systematically misfire under literal-only tasks, and can we suppress it?' That is non-trivial, but the proposal is in tension with recent literalist-bias results, so the novelty claim depends on a stronger-than-usual empirical reversal.
