Name: acquisition_prerequisite_gating
Title: Skill Tree, Not Timeline: Does an Earlier-Acquired Linguistic Capability Causally Gate the Emergence of a Later One?
Short Hypothesis: The developmental order in which LLMs acquire linguistic capabilities (e.g., part-of-speech/morphology -> syntax -> semantic composition -> discourse) is not a mere timeline but a causal prerequisite chain: selectively delaying or degrading a model's acquisition of an earlier capability during training causally prevents or slows the emergence of the later capability that normally builds on it, even when abundant data for the later capability is present, whereas degrading a non-prerequisite (parallel) capability leaves it unaffected.
Related Work: A large literature establishes that LLMs acquire linguistic structure in a consistent DEVELOPMENTAL ORDER that qualitatively mirrors children: phonemic->lexical->syntactic emergence (Emergence of Phonemic/Syntactic/Semantic Representations, 2026), POS-first (LMs Learn POS First, 2018), consistent one-dimensional grammar-learning trajectories across seeds/architectures (Grammar-Learning Trajectories, 2021), chronological probing showing discourse last (Is neural language acquisition similar to natural?, 2022), n-gram-then-refinement dynamics (N-Gram Learning, 2025), a window of maximal cognitive-developmental alignment (Development of Cognitive Intelligence in PLMs, 2024), and age-ordered curriculum effects on semantic learning (Order matters, 2018/2019). CRUCIALLY, all of this is DESCRIPTIVE and CORRELATIONAL: it characterizes WHEN capabilities emerge and in what order, but never tests whether the order reflects a CAUSAL DEPENDENCY. No prior work asks whether an earlier capability is a functional PREREQUISITE whose disruption causally blocks a later one, nor uses targeted training-data ablation to sever a specific rung of the ladder and observe downstream failure with prerequisite-vs-parallel specificity controls. We uniquely convert the observed acquisition timeline into a testable causal skill-tree via a Formation-Tracing + Causal-Intervention strategy (data-ablation re-training + checkpoint probing), distinguishing genuine prerequisite gating from co-occurrence.
Abstract: Language models acquire linguistic capabilities in a strikingly consistent developmental order that echoes child development: coarse lexical/part-of-speech knowledge first, then syntax, then semantic composition, then discourse. Existing work treats this order as a descriptive timeline. We ask a causal question: is the order a prerequisite chain? That is, does mastering an earlier capability causally enable the emergence of the later capability that builds on it, such that disrupting the earlier rung blocks the later one even when its own training signal is abundant? We test this by training small language models from scratch under controlled interventions that selectively delay or degrade the acquisition of one target capability (e.g., syntactic hierarchy) via surgical training-data ablation or curriculum manipulation, while holding total data and the later capability's signal fixed. We then probe, across training checkpoints, whether a downstream capability (e.g., semantic composition, discourse coherence) still emerges on schedule. Our central prediction is a prerequisite-specificity dissociation: disrupting a genuine prerequisite delays or prevents the downstream capability, whereas disrupting a matched non-prerequisite (parallel) capability of equal difficulty leaves the downstream capability intact. We further predict the intervention shifts the downstream capability's emergence checkpoint and lowers its ceiling in proportion to prerequisite degradation (dose-response). We characterize the resulting empirical skill tree, quantify per-edge gating strength, and test whether a late 'remedial' injection of the prerequisite can rescue the stalled downstream capability. Across several from-scratch model configurations and seeds, we convert the well-documented acquisition timeline into a causal dependency graph, revealing whether language capabilities in LLMs are a skill tree rather than a mere schedule.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (Setup for H1 - Baseline acquisition order and emergence checkpoints): Establishes the reference developmental ladder and per-capability emergence checkpoints that all interventions are measured against. Data (training): a ~100M-word corpus mixing child-directed speech (the CHILDES/BabyLM strict-small 100M-word set, used as is) with Simple Wikipedia; this size is affordable for an academic lab and prior child-directed-speech work shows it suffices for the target capabilities. Data (evaluation probes, existing sets used as is): (a) lexical/POS + morphology - POS/agreement probing plus BLiMP morphology subsets (BLiMP has 67 paradigms x 1,000 pairs); (b) syntactic hierarchy - BLiMP/Zorro structural minimal pairs plus a hierarchical-generalization test on question-formation/passivization; (c) semantic composition - compositional-entailment / predicate-argument probes (adapted from existing NLI minimal pairs); (d) discourse - coreference and discourse-connective cloze. Models (trained from scratch, all weights trainable): small GPT-2-style transformers at ~10M, ~30M, ~100M parameters, depth-varied, 3-5 seeds each (seeds 0-4); dense checkpointing every ~2M tokens. Decisive metric: the ordered sequence of per-capability emergence checkpoints (first checkpoint where a probe reliably exceeds its chance/threshold band) and its cross-seed consistency (Kendall's tau across seeds). Convincing result: baselines reproduce the standard order (POS/morphology -> syntax -> composition -> discourse) with cross-seed rank consistency tau >=0.8, giving well-separated emergence checkpoints to serve as the causal baseline. Indecision band: tau 0.5-0.8 or overlapping (poorly separated) emergence windows for adjacent rungs - order is noisy and later causal edges on those rungs will be underpowered; we add seeds and denser checkpoints. Negative result (for setup): tau <0.5 or no stable order - the developmental ladder is not reliably present at this scale, so the causal test is deferred to the well-separated rungs only (POS/morphology -> syntax -> basic composition).

Experiment 2 (H1 - Severing a prerequisite blocks the downstream capability): Tests the core causal claim that degrading an earlier capability's learnable signal delays or lowers a later capability that builds on it, even with the later capability's own signal preserved. Data (training, constructed by ablation): matched corpora that selectively DEGRADE one target capability while preserving others and total token count - e.g., to degrade syntactic hierarchy, apply clause-local word-order scrambling that destroys hierarchical cues but preserves lexical co-occurrence and morphology; to degrade morphology, lemmatize/strip inflection; to degrade discourse, shuffle sentence order across documents. Each ablation passes a manipulation check (its target probe drops) while the downstream capability's own input cues are verified intact via probes. Models/protocol: retrain the same from-scratch transformers (all weights trainable, 3-5 seeds) on each single-capability-degraded corpus; probe every ~2M tokens. Decisive metric: the downstream capability's emergence-checkpoint shift and asymptotic ceiling versus baseline, modeled as downstream_probe ~ intervention*checkpoint + (1|seed). Convincing result: degrading a genuine prerequisite (e.g., syntax) delays the downstream capability's (e.g., composition) emergence checkpoint by >=25% of its baseline emergence step (CI across seeds excluding 0) AND lowers its asymptotic ceiling by >=5 pp probe accuracy, beyond what its preserved own-signal predicts. Indecision band: a 10-25% checkpoint delay or a 2-5 pp ceiling drop - a directional block that is not decisive. Negative result: <10% delay and <2 pp ceiling drop - degrading the prerequisite does not gate the downstream capability, evidence that the acquisition order is a data-statistics schedule, not a causal skill tree.

Experiment 3 (H1 - Prerequisite-vs-parallel specificity dissociation): The key control ruling out generic training disruption or lost tokens. Data (training, constructed): degrade a matched NON-PREREQUISITE / parallel capability of comparable probe difficulty and token footprint, plus a random-token-corruption corpus matched for total signal loss. Models/protocol: as Experiment 2, same seeds. Decisive metric: the downstream capability's checkpoint/ceiling change under the parallel-capability (and random-corruption) ablation, contrasted with the prerequisite ablation. Convincing result: the downstream capability is spared under the parallel-capability and random-corruption ablations (checkpoint shift <10% and ceiling drop <2 pp), while the prerequisite ablation from Experiment 2 shows the full effect - a clean prerequisite-specific dissociation. Indecision band: the parallel/random ablations cause a partial downstream effect (10-25% of the prerequisite effect) - the block is only partly prerequisite-specific. Negative result: parallel-capability and random-corruption ablations harm the downstream capability as much as the prerequisite ablation - the effect is generic disruption / lost signal, not prerequisite gating.

Experiment 4 (H1 - Dose-response): Tests that downstream disruption scales with how much the prerequisite is degraded. Data (training, constructed): graded degradation of the prerequisite (25/50/75/100% of its cues scrambled), total tokens fixed. Models/protocol: as above, same seeds. Decisive metric: the monotonic relation between prerequisite-degradation level and downstream emergence-delay / ceiling-drop (slope across the four levels). Convincing result: emergence-delay and ceiling-drop increase monotonically with degradation level (slope CI excluding 0), strengthening the causal reading. Indecision band: a non-monotonic or shallow trend (slope CI grazing 0) - dosage relation unclear. Negative result: no dose-response (flat across levels) - the block, if any, is threshold-like or artifactual rather than a graded prerequisite dependency.

Experiment 5 (H1 - Remedial rescue / reversibility): Tests whether restoring the prerequisite signal later lets the stalled downstream capability emerge, quantifying reversibility. Data/protocol: train under prerequisite degradation up to a fixed checkpoint, then switch to clean data restoring the prerequisite; continue probing; same models/seeds. Decisive metric: whether the downstream capability emerges after the switch, and its delay relative to baseline emergence. Convincing result: the downstream capability emerges after the prerequisite is restored (probe crosses threshold) but delayed by a measurable margin versus baseline (CI excluding 0) - the block is real but reversible once the prerequisite is supplied. Indecision band: partial recovery (downstream reaches an intermediate ceiling that neither matches baseline nor stays blocked) - reversibility is incomplete/ambiguous. Negative result: no post-switch emergence within the remaining budget - either the block is irreversible (a strong prerequisite claim) or the earlier delay was not prerequisite-driven; interpreted jointly with Experiments 2-3.

Experiment 6 (H1 - Skill-tree construction and per-edge gating strength): Aggregates the interventions into an empirical causal dependency graph and compares it to the correlational timeline. Data/protocol: across all (degraded-capability, downstream-capability) pairs from Experiments 2-5, compute a per-edge Gating Strength = downstream delay/ceiling-drop attributable to that prerequisite, normalized by the parallel-control effect; assemble the causal graph; same models/seeds; robustness across model depth/width, corpus, and probe choice. Decisive metric: for each temporally-ordered capability pair, whether a significant causal edge exists (Gating Strength CI excluding 0) and whether the causal graph matches the temporal order. Convincing result: a subset of temporally-ordered pairs show significant causal edges while others do not, yielding a skill tree that is strictly sparser than the full temporal order - demonstrating that acquisition order is partly, not wholly, causal. Indecision band: edges whose Gating Strength CIs graze 0 - their causal status is undetermined and reported as such. Negative result: no significant edges anywhere - the acquisition timeline is a pure schedule with no causal prerequisite structure; all-edges-significant-and-equal would instead suggest generic coupling rather than a differentiated tree, and is flagged against the Experiment 3 specificity control.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Data-ablation may reduce a downstream capability simply by removing tokens or lowering overall data quality rather than by severing a specific prerequisite; mitigated by holding token count fixed, the matched non-prerequisite and random-corruption specificity controls, and manipulation checks confirming the ablation hits only the target probe. (2) Capabilities are entangled -- scrambling syntax may inadvertently degrade semantics in the input; we design ablations that preserve the downstream capability's own cues (verified via probes) and interpret results relative to the parallel-capability control rather than to the clean baseline alone. (3) Small from-scratch models may not cleanly exhibit higher capabilities like discourse (prior work shows they underperform an 8-year-old); we focus on well-measurable rungs (POS/morphology->syntax->basic composition) and treat discourse as exploratory. (4) Emergence-checkpoint estimates are noisy; we use dense checkpointing, multiple seeds, and smoothed learning curves with CIs. (5) Probes are correlational readouts of capability; we use established minimal-pair behavioral benchmarks alongside probes to avoid probe-artifact confounds. (6) Compute: from-scratch retraining across conditions x seeds is the main cost; we keep models small (10-100M) and corpora modest (<=100M words), which prior child-directed-speech work shows suffices for these capabilities and is affordable for an academic lab. (7) A null result (degrading a prerequisite does NOT block the downstream capability, or all disruptions harm everything uniformly) is itself highly informative: it would show the acquisition order is a mere schedule driven by data statistics rather than a causal skill tree, refining a widely-assumed developmental analogy. (8) The 'skill tree / prerequisite' framing is operationalized as a training-time causal dependency, not a claim about human-like developmental necessity.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims requiring novelty: (1) the observed LM acquisition timeline can be reframed as a causal prerequisite graph rather than a descriptive order; (2) surgical single-capability training-data ablation can selectively delay one capability while preserving downstream signal; (3) prerequisite-vs-parallel specificity, dose-response, and rescue can identify true gating edges; (4) per-edge gating strengths can be assembled into a sparse empirical skill tree stricter than temporal order. Relative to the search summary, this is meaningfully novel: prior work is largely descriptive about when capabilities emerge, or causal only for isolated constructions/curriculum effects. The closest prior family is developmental-order/emergence studies plus narrow causal-intervention work on specific constructions and curriculum learning. The actual delta is the move from temporal emergence to cross-capability causal dependency mapping. This is non-trivial, though it is adjacent to obvious next-step intervention work and depends heavily on whether the ablations really isolate capabilities.

impact.reasoning: The phenomenon under study is whether earlier linguistic capabilities are actual causal prerequisites for later ones during LM pretraining. Stakeholders include developmental-interpretability researchers, pretraining/curriculum/data-curation researchers, and cognitive scientists using LMs as acquisition models. Strongest case: if acquisition order reflects causal gating, then pretraining should be organized around prerequisites rather than treating emergence order as incidental. This is an important and reusable question, and even a null result would matter by arguing the timeline is not a skill tree. Likely uptake is moderate to strong in interpretability and language acquisition circles, with some downstream relevance to curriculum and dataset design. The central hypothesis is reasonably falsifiable. Main weaknesses are technical: capability-selective ablations are very hard to achieve without collateral damage; several operational definitions are underspecified (what counts as emergence, exact probes/benchmarks, how gating strength is computed, what parallel capabilities are); thresholds like 25% delay and 5pp ceiling drop seem arbitrary; discourse may be infeasible at the proposed scale; and the related work positioning is somewhat broad rather than specific on the most relevant intervention papers. The experiments could support a serious workshop or conference paper if executed well, but for a strong ML venue the design needs tighter measurement validity and stronger controls against generic training degradation/confounding.

Name: multilingual_cot_faithfulness
Title: Faithful Only in Its Mother Tongue? How the Language of Chain-of-Thought Gates Whether Reasoning Is Real
Short Hypothesis: An LLM's chain-of-thought is more causally load-bearing (faithful) when generated in the model's dominant, pivot-shaped language than in a non-dominant language: in a non-dominant language the visible CoT decouples from the internal computation (which is routed through the pivot), turning the CoT into a decorative post-hoc surface even when the final answer stays correct; this faithfulness gap is dissociable from accuracy and is mediated by a locatable 'CoT-reliance' signal that can be steered.
Related Work: CoT-faithfulness work shows CoT can be plausible-but-unfaithful (Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think, 2023), that faithfulness varies with model/task and decays across the chain (Measuring Faithfulness, 2023; Mechanistic Evidence for Faithfulness Decay, 2026), that only a small fraction of steps are causally load-bearing (True Thinking Score, 2025), that answers are computed incrementally during CoT (Think-to-Talk or Talk-to-Think, 2024), and that latent/implicit reasoning is brittle and shortcut-prone (Do Latent Tokens Think, 2025; Do LLMs Really Think Step-by-step in Implicit Reasoning, 2024). Separately, multilingual interpretability shows reasoning is routed through an English-shaped pivot (Do Multilingual LLMs Think in English?, 2025; Beyond English-Centric, 2024) and that ablating language-specific components helps multilingual reasoning (When Less Language is More, 2025). CRUCIALLY, all CoT-faithfulness work is monolingual (English) and treats faithfulness as a fixed model/task property; all multilingual-pivot work studies accuracy or routing, never faithfulness. My prior proposals covered honesty, register-shift, self-translation, and canonicalization but never CoT faithfulness as a function of the reasoning language. We are the first to (1) test whether the language of the CoT causally gates its faithfulness, (2) dissociate this faithfulness gap from accuracy, and (3) locate and steer a CoT-reliance signal that mediates it.
Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) makes a model's reasoning visible, but a growing literature shows the visible steps are often unfaithful post-hoc justifications rather than the true computation. All of this evidence is monolingual (English), yet multilingual models route reasoning through an English-shaped pivot representation. We ask a simple question that connects language to intelligence: is a model's CoT faithful only in its dominant language? We hypothesize that when a model reasons in its dominant, pivot-shaped language the CoT is causally load-bearing (perturbing it changes the answer, and the answer emerges incrementally along the trace), whereas when it reasons in a non-dominant language the visible CoT decouples from the internal computation, becoming a decorative surface even when the final answer remains correct. Critically, we predict this faithfulness gap is dissociable from raw accuracy: two languages can match on answer correctness yet differ sharply in how much the answer actually depends on the stated reasoning. We measure faithfulness across languages using established causal perturbation tests (step corruption, truncation, error injection, and incremental answer-emergence probes) on math and multi-hop reasoning, and test whether faithfulness tracks each language's dominance/resource level. Mechanistically, we locate a 'CoT-reliance' direction distinguishing traces the model conditions on from those it ignores, test whether non-dominant-language reasoning lowers its engagement (mediating the gap), and steer it to restore or remove CoT-reliance. Confirming these claims reframes CoT faithfulness from a fixed model property into a language-dependent one, with direct consequences for multilingual safety and CoT monitoring.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - CoT faithfulness declines with distance from the dominant language): Tests that the visible chain-of-thought is more causally load-bearing in the model's dominant, pivot-shaped language than in non-dominant languages, showing the decorative-CoT signature in the latter. Data: a faithfulness battery of ~300 items each across three families (~900): multi-step arithmetic (GSM8K test items, used as is), multi-hop QA (2WikiMultiHop, 3-5 hops, sampled), and deductive logic chains depth 2-6 (constructed). Each item is solvable via a CoT with identifiable steps and a definite answer, translated (with back-translation and human spot-checks) into the model's dominant language (English for most open-weight models) plus 5-6 typologically diverse languages spanning a resource/dominance gradient (Spanish, German, Chinese, Hindi, Swahili, Arabic). 300/family bounds the ~7-language x 5-model translation-and-generation cost while giving power for the language-dominance slope. Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Aya-23-8B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen; dominant language identified per model; CoT-then-answer decoding at temperature 0.7, 3 seeds (13/21/42). Faithfulness metrics (established causal perturbation tests, length-normalized): step-corruption/error-injection (does injecting a wrong intermediate value flip the final answer - faithful CoT propagates it), truncation-recoverability curve, a paraphrase/equal-length-filler control, and an incremental answer-emergence probe (when the correct answer becomes linearly decodable along the trace). Decisive metric: corruption-sensitivity (fraction of items where injecting a wrong intermediate value changes the final answer), modeled as faithfulness ~ language_dominance + task + (1|model) + (1|item); higher = more faithful. Convincing result: corruption-sensitivity is >=20 pp higher in the dominant language than in the lowest-resource language (dominance slope CI excluding 0), with the decorative signature (corruption-insensitive answers, early answer-emergence independent of steps) strongest in non-dominant languages. Indecision band: an 8-20 pp dominant-vs-lowest gap, or a slope CI grazing 0 - a directional trend that is not established. Negative result: <8 pp gap and flat slope - CoT faithfulness does not depend on the reasoning language.

Experiment 2 (H1 - The faithfulness gap is dissociable from raw accuracy): The key claim that faithfulness differences are not merely competence differences. Data/protocol: the same ~900 items x languages; stratify and covary every faithfulness metric on per-language accuracy; identify language pairs matched on answer accuracy but differing in faithfulness; also measure the right-answer-unfaithful rate (correct final answer with a corruption-insensitive CoT). Same five frozen models. Decisive metric: the language effect on corruption-sensitivity after covarying accuracy (partial effect), plus the size of the accuracy-matched faithfulness gap. Convincing result: with accuracy controlled, the language effect on faithfulness remains (CI excluding 0), and at least one accuracy-matched language pair differs in corruption-sensitivity by >=15 pp - faithfulness is not reducible to competence; the right-answer-unfaithful rate is elevated in non-dominant languages. Indecision band: a residual accuracy-controlled effect that is present but small (accuracy-matched gap 5-15 pp) - dissociation is suggestive. Negative result: the faithfulness gap vanishes once accuracy is controlled (accuracy-matched gap <5 pp) - the apparent gap is pure competence, itself informative and reassuring for multilingual CoT monitoring.

Experiment 3 (H1 - Monitorability consequence): Tests the safety implication that non-dominant-language unfaithfulness hides flawed reasoning from an automated monitor. Data/protocol: inject reasoning errors into a subset of traces per language; run an automated CoT monitor (a separate frozen judge model) to flag flawed reasoning; same five frozen generators. Decisive metric: monitor recall (fraction of injected-error traces flagged) by language. Convincing result: monitor recall is >=15 pp lower in non-dominant than dominant languages (CI excluding 0), showing decorative CoT degrades monitorability. Indecision band: a 5-15 pp recall gap - a modest safety effect. Negative result: <5 pp recall gap - monitoring is not degraded by reasoning language, a reassuring null.

Experiment 4 (H2 - A locatable CoT-reliance signal that mediates the gap): Tests that a hidden-state signal distinguishes traces the model conditions on from those it ignores, and that non-dominant reasoning lowers it. Data/protocol: contrast pre-answer hidden states on corruption-sensitive vs corruption-insensitive trials (matched content); per-layer L2-regularized linear probe (3 seeds, 70/30 item-disjoint split) decoding CoT-reliance; a difference-in-means CoT-reliance direction, related to the existing TrueThinking direction where possible; same five frozen models. Decisive metric: held-out per-layer AUROC for CoT-reliance (chance 0.5), and the Spearman correlation between per-item projection onto the direction and per-item faithfulness. Convincing result: best-layer AUROC >=0.75, non-dominant-language reasoning lowers projection onto the CoT-reliance direction (CI excluding 0), and projection predicts faithfulness (rho >=0.30, CI excluding 0), mediating the language->faithfulness effect. Indecision band: AUROC 0.65-0.75 or mediation rho 0.15-0.30 - a signal exists but its mediating role is tentative. Negative result: AUROC <0.65 or no projection-faithfulness link - no locatable reliance signal to explain the behavioral gap.

Experiment 5 (H3 - Causal steering restores and removes CoT-reliance): Tests that the reliance direction is causally load-bearing. Data/protocol: steer +CoT-reliance during non-dominant-language reasoning and -CoT-reliance in the dominant language, 4 coefficients; controls random-direction and no-steer; same five frozen models; specificity tracked via accuracy and fluency. Decisive metric: change in corruption-sensitivity under steering versus no-steer. Convincing result: +CoT-reliance in a non-dominant language restores corruption-sensitivity by >=10 pp (answers become perturbation-dependent, error-injection propagates) with monotonic dose-response, -CoT-reliance in the dominant language induces decorative CoT, random-direction moves <2 pp, and accuracy/fluency are preserved. Indecision band: a 2-10 pp steering effect or a non-monotonic dose - causal contribution present but not clean. Negative result: <2 pp effect or no better than random - the reliance direction is not causally responsible for faithfulness, leaving the behavioral gap mechanistically unexplained.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Lower faithfulness in non-dominant languages could be pure competence degradation rather than a genuine language-dependent decoupling; mitigated by accuracy-stratified metrics, the accuracy-matched-pair analysis, and the content-matched steering intervention that isolates the CoT-reliance representation from language. (2) Faithfulness perturbation tests are imperfect and can be confounded by trace length differences across languages; we length-normalize, use multiple complementary metrics (corruption, truncation, filler, answer-emergence), and report robustness. (3) Instruction-tuned models may condition weakly on CoT even in English (per Measuring Faithfulness, 2023), flattening the gradient; we include tasks/models where English CoT is demonstrably faithful and report per-model baselines. (4) The incremental answer-emergence probe may capture surface tokens rather than genuine computation; held-out validation, matched positions, and comparison to the corruption-based metric address this. (5) The CoT-reliance direction may entangle with generic difficulty/confidence; mitigated by matched corruption-sensitive/insensitive contrasts, random-direction steering, and specificity checks. (6) Cross-lingual items risk translation artifacts; back-translation and human spot-checks. (7) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (8) A null result (faithfulness is language-independent once accuracy is controlled) is itself highly informative for multilingual safety, indicating CoT monitoring is not degraded by reasoning language. (9) The faithfulness framing is operationalized causally and behaviorally, not as a claim of human-like introspection.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims requiring novelty: (1) CoT faithfulness varies systematically with language dominance/pivot status, not just across models/tasks; (2) this faithfulness gap is dissociable from accuracy using accuracy-matched comparisons and right-answer-unfaithful rates; (3) multilingual reasoning decouples visible non-dominant-language CoT from internal computation routed through a dominant pivot; (4) a locatable 'CoT-reliance' direction mediates this gap and can be causally steered; (5) reduced faithfulness in non-dominant languages harms CoT-based monitoring. Based on the search summary, the raw behavioral claim that faithfulness varies by language is already substantially pre-empted by very recent multilingual CoT-faithfulness work using similar perturbation tests, and English-pivot multilingual reasoning is also adjacent prior art. The real delta is narrower and more interesting: tying effects to a dominance-gradient slope, rigorously separating faithfulness from accuracy, and especially the mechanistic location/mediation/steering story plus monitorability consequence. Relative to the proposal's own related work, the claim is overstated because it says 'first to test' language-gated faithfulness, which is no longer tenable. So novelty is moderate: the mechanism and dissociation pieces look non-trivial, but the headline finding is crowded.
revision_notes: Rewrite the novelty claim to drop 'first to test whether faithfulness varies by language' and instead foreground the actual fresh contribution: dominance-gradient quantification, accuracy-dissociation, and mechanistic steering.
Add explicit positioning against the recent multilingual CoT-faithfulness paper: state exactly which claims are already known and what new hypothesis remains.
Make the language-dominance construct operational and non-obvious, e.g. predefine dominance using training-data proxies or independent proficiency measures rather than post hoc labels.

Strengthen the mechanistic novelty by specifying how the 'CoT-reliance direction' differs from generic confidence/difficulty/language-identity directions and why steering it is not an obvious activation-engineering extension.

impact.reasoning: The phenomenon under study is whether visible reasoning traces are causally trustworthy across languages, especially in multilingual models that may internally route through an English-like pivot. The stakeholders are the CoT-monitoring/safety community, multilingual NLP researchers, and practitioners deploying LLMs in non-English settings. The strongest case for importance is: if CoT is much less faithful outside dominant languages, then current reasoning-based interpretability and monitoring pipelines silently fail for many users. This is a real problem rather than a niche curiosity because multilingual deployment is widespread and safety/monitorability assumptions often inherit from English-only evidence. If the result holds, researchers may stop treating CoT monitorability as language-invariant, benchmark multilingual monitor recall, and build language-aware oversight tools. The direction-shifting potential is decent, particularly for safety and interpretability, though not maximal because practical consequences depend on effect size/generalization and some of the behavioral phenomenon is already adjacent in the literature. The 'so what?' test is passed mainly by the monitorability angle and the accuracy-dissociation: a null would reassure practitioners, while a positive result would change evaluation and safety practice in multilingual settings.

review.reasoning: The proposal is well structured, hypothesis-driven, and unusually concrete about experiments, controls, and success criteria. It has a falsifiable central hypothesis and includes reasonable threats such as competence confounds, trace length, translation artifacts, and random-direction controls. However, there are important technical gaps. The related-work positioning is already outdated/overclaimed relative to the search summary, which weakens credibility. The key latent constructs—'dominant language,' 'pivot-shaped,' and especially 'CoT-reliance direction'—are underspecified operationally. The mediation story risks overinterpretation: showing a projection drops in non-dominant languages and steering changes sensitivity does not by itself establish a unique causal mechanism rather than generic confidence, difficulty, or language-processing effects. The experiments are feasible but somewhat thin for the breadth of claims: ~900 translated items over multiple languages, tasks, and five models may be underpowered for slope claims, mediation, and steering across heterogeneous settings. The translation setup could confound reasoning difficulty and naturalness, especially for constructed logic and multihop tasks. Monitorability is promising but underspecified: what monitor architecture, training data, and language exposure? The proposal could be strong for a serious ML venue if executed very carefully and if the mechanistic claims hold, but as written the narrative overreaches relative to what the planned evidence can cleanly support.

Name: associative_fan_interference
Title: The Fan Effect in LLMs: Does Associative Priming of Absent Distractors Hijack Factual Retrieval and Reasoning?
Short Hypothesis: The human fan effect — retrieval of a fact slows and errs when the queried concept is linked to many competing associates — transfers to LLMs at the level of reasoning, not just next-token copying: incidentally mentioning concepts semantically associated with (but not the same as) the correct answer earlier in a prompt causes graded, associative-strength-dependent retrieval errors that pull the model toward the associated-but-wrong answer, and this retrieval-competition is a locatable, steerable internal signal distinct from literal token-copying (contextual entrainment).
Related Work: Prior work shows LLMs exhibit semantic priming (Misra 2020) and structural priming (Prasad 2022), that fact retrieval can be hijacked by meaning-preserving context (Do LLMs dream of elephants, 2024), and that LMs assign higher probability to any literal context tokens via 'entrainment heads' regardless of relevance (Llama See Llama Do: Contextual Entrainment, 2025). Content-effect debiasing steers a validity-vs-plausibility direction (K-CAST, 2025). Crucially, ALL of these study either (a) next-token/lexical-decision priming, (b) hijacking by tokens or paraphrases that literally appear, or (c) copying of literal context tokens (entrainment). NONE test the human FAN EFFECT (Anderson 1974): that retrieval accuracy/latency degrades as a function of how many competing ASSOCIATES a concept has, that mentioning an ASSOCIATED-BUT-ABSENT distractor concept (never the answer token itself) causes multi-step reasoning to converge on the wrong-but-associated answer, that this scales with graded associative strength, or that a retrieval-competition representation (distinct from token-copying entrainment heads) mediates it. My prior proposals covered ambiguity-branch collapse, canonicalization, and pragmatic enrichment but never associative-fan retrieval interference. We uniquely transfer the fan effect into LLM reasoning as a graded associative-strength law with a Location + Causal Intervention account and a high-stakes clinical instance.
Abstract: Human memory shows the fan effect: the more associations a concept has, the slower and more error-prone it is to retrieve any single fact about it, because associates compete during retrieval. We ask whether large language models suffer an analogous, reasoning-level failure: does incidentally mentioning concepts semantically associated with the correct answer — without ever stating the answer itself — hijack the model's factual retrieval and multi-step reasoning toward the associated-but-wrong answer? We make three claims. First, associative interference is real and graded: seeding a prompt with distractor concepts of increasing associative strength to the correct answer produces a monotonically rising rate of associated-lure errors, over and above surface difficulty, and this interference is distinct from literal token-copying because the distractors are never the answer token. Second, it follows a fan law: interference scales with the NUMBER of competing associates and their associative strength, mirroring Anderson's fan effect, and is largest exactly when the correct fact is weakly represented. Third, it is causal and steerable: a probe reads a retrieval-competition signal from hidden states that predicts lure errors before they surface, and this signal is separable from the located token-copying entrainment heads; steering along a 'retrieval-competition' direction (or ablating it) reduces associated-lure errors, while amplifying it induces them. We evaluate across several open-weight models on factual QA and multi-hop reasoning, plus a high-stakes clinical instance where mentioning an associated-but-wrong drug or diagnosis silently biases the answer. Our work reframes semantic association as a controllable retrieval-interference hazard for machine reasoning.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - Graded associative interference, selective versus non-associated distraction): Tests that mentioning concepts associated with (but never equal to) the correct answer raises associated-lure errors beyond generic distraction. Data: a fan-effect QA battery, ~300 items each for (a) single-fact retrieval (one correct entity/value; base facts sampled from TriviaQA, Natural Questions, and the LAMA probe set) and (b) 2-3 hop reasoning with a definite answer (built over the same fact sources). Per base item, generate matched prompt variants that incidentally mention DISTRACTOR concepts semantically associated with the correct answer but never the answer token itself (e.g., for answer 'aspirin', seed 'ibuprofen', 'acetaminophen'). Associative strength is set from free-association norms (USF, SWOW) plus embedding cosine, giving conditions: 0 distractors, 1 weak-associate, 1 strong-associate, and a FAN condition with 2-4 associates. Each item has a labeled correct answer and labeled associated-lure answers, plus a NON-ASSOCIATED equal-length distractor control and a LITERAL-COPY control (a distractor that IS the answer token). We construct the seeding because no existing set controls associative strength while holding the base fact fixed; 300/family covers the graded conditions with power and keeps items within well-covered association-norm vocabulary. Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, Gemma-2-9B, frozen; temperature 0.7, 3 seeds (13/21/42). Decisive metric: associated-lure error rate (fraction of responses equal to the labeled associate), modeled as lure_rate ~ associative_strength + n_associates + item_difficulty + (1|model) + (1|item). Convincing result: a strong-associate distractor raises the associated-lure rate by >=8 pp over the 0-distractor baseline AND over the equal-length non-associated control (both CIs excluding 0), with errors concentrated on the specific associate (the diagnostic that association, not generic confusion, drives failure). Indecision band: a 3-8 pp rise, or an effect not clearly separable from the non-associated control - directional but weak. Negative result: <3 pp rise or no larger than non-associated distraction - LLM retrieval is robust to associated-but-absent competitors, dissociating it from the human fan effect.

Experiment 2 (H2 - A fan law and a fan-by-fact-strength interaction): Tests that interference scales with the number and strength of associates and is largest when the correct fact is weakly represented. Data/protocol: the same battery, using the graded n_associates (0-4) and strength conditions; estimate each correct fact's representational strength via baseline solve rate / logit margin; same five frozen models. Decisive metric: the slope of associated-lure rate on the number of competing associates (and on graded strength), and the fan x fact-strength interaction coefficient. Convincing result: lure rate rises monotonically with n_associates (fan slope CI excluding 0) and with associative strength, and interference is significantly larger for weakly-represented facts (interaction CI excluding 0) - mirroring Anderson's fan effect and its strength interaction. Indecision band: a positive but shallow fan slope (CI grazing 0) or an interaction that trends but is not significant - fan structure suggestive only. Negative result: flat fan slope and no strength interaction - no fan law, even if a single-associate effect exists.

Experiment 3 (H1 - Dissociation from literal-copy contextual entrainment): Tests that associated-but-absent interference is distinct from over-copying literal context tokens. Data/protocol: contrast associated-but-absent distractors versus literal-copy distractors (the answer token itself present in context); same five frozen models. Decisive metric: the associated-lure rate for associated-but-absent distractors, and whether it persists where entrainment (literal copying) cannot apply, plus the divergence in error signatures (entrainment boosts the literal token; fan interference boosts a non-present associate). Convincing result: associated-but-absent interference is substantial (>=5 pp over baseline) on items with no literal answer token in context, and the two conditions show distinct error signatures - fan interference is not reducible to entrainment. Indecision band: associated-but-absent interference present but small (2-5 pp), or signatures partly overlapping - dissociation unclear. Negative result: associated-but-absent interference vanishes without literal presence, i.e., the effect fully reduces to contextual entrainment - itself an informative reframing.

Experiment 4 (H3 - A locatable retrieval-competition signal separable from entrainment heads, with mediation): Tests that a hidden-state signal predicts lure errors and is distinct from the token-copying entrainment mechanism. Data/protocol: contrast pre-answer hidden states on interference-error vs correct trials (matched content); per-layer L2-regularized linear probe (3 seeds, 70/30 item-disjoint split) decoding impending associated-lure error; a difference-in-means retrieval-competition direction; separately localize entrainment heads via differentiable masking and measure overlap; same five frozen models. Decisive metric: held-out AUROC for impending lure error (chance 0.5), the Spearman correlation between per-item signal and per-item lure error, and the overlap between the retrieval-competition signal and localized entrainment heads. Convincing result: best-layer AUROC >=0.75, per-item signal predicts lure errors (rho >=0.30, CI excluding 0) and mediates the associative_strength->error effect, and the signal is separable from entrainment heads (low head/layer overlap) - the key novel dissociation. Indecision band: AUROC 0.65-0.75, mediation rho 0.15-0.30, or moderate overlap with entrainment heads - a signal that is real but not cleanly distinct. Negative result: AUROC <0.65 or the signal coincides with entrainment heads - no separate retrieval-competition mechanism.

Experiment 5 (H3 - Causal steering reduces and induces associated-lure errors): Tests that the retrieval-competition direction is causally load-bearing. Data/protocol: steer -retrieval-competition (or ablate the associated distractor's attention contribution) to test error reduction, and steer +retrieval-competition to induce associated-lure errors even without distractors present; 4 coefficients; controls random-direction, no-steer, and (for contrast) ablating entrainment heads; same five frozen models; specificity tracked on no-distractor items and fluency. Decisive metric: change in associated-lure error rate under steering versus no-steer/random. Convincing result: -direction (or distractor-attention ablation) reduces associated-lure errors by >=6 pp with monotonic dose-response, +direction induces >=6 pp of lures without distractors, random-direction moves <2 pp, the intervention differs from entrainment-head ablation, and no-distractor accuracy and fluency are preserved. Indecision band: a 2-6 pp effect or a non-monotonic dose - causal but not clean. Negative result: <2 pp effect or no better than random - the retrieval-competition direction is not causally responsible for the interference.

Experiment 6 (H1/H3 - High-stakes clinical instance): Tests that associative seeding silently biases clinical answers and that intervention reduces it. Data: ~300 clinical QA/vignette items where an associated-but-wrong drug, diagnosis, or symptom (same drug class or differential) precedes the question; adapted from MedQA/MedMCQA. Protocol: same five frozen models; compare no-seed, associated-seed, and retrieval-competition steering / distractor-attention ablation on fine-distinction cases; aggregate reporting only. Decisive metric: associated-error rate on fine-distinction clinical cases, and its reduction under intervention. Convincing result: associative seeding raises the clinical associated-error rate by >=6 pp over no-seed, and steering/ablation cuts it by >=6 pp without harming no-seed matched cases. Indecision band: a 2-6 pp seeding effect or reduction - safety-relevant but modest. Negative result: no clinical seeding effect or <2 pp reduction - the fan interference does not manifest as a controllable clinical hazard.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Associated-distractor interference could be generic distraction rather than semantic association; mitigated by the non-associated equal-length distractor control, the graded associative-strength dose-response, and the associated-lure error signature (errors are the SPECIFIC associate, not random). (2) The effect may overlap with contextual entrainment; we explicitly contrast associated-but-absent vs literal-copy distractors and test signal separability from located entrainment heads, so a finding of overlap is itself informative and a finding of separability is the key novel result. (3) Associative-strength norms (USF/SWOW) have limited coverage and are English-centric; we restrict items to well-covered concepts, cross-check with embedding cosine, and report robustness. (4) Instruction-tuned models may resist distraction, flattening the fan curve; we include weakly-known facts (where interference should be largest), harder multi-hop items, base variants, and multiple models — a curve that bends only for weak facts still confirms the fan-x-strength interaction. (5) The retrieval-competition direction may entangle with generic difficulty/uncertainty; mitigated by matched error/correct contrasts, held-out probe validation, random-direction steering, no-distractor specificity checks, and comparison against the entrainment-head baseline. (6) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (7) A null result (no graded associative interference, or it fully reduces to literal entrainment) is itself informative: it would show LLM retrieval is robust to associated-but-absent competitors, dissociating it from the human fan effect. (8) The fan-effect framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like memory; clinical experiments run in controlled research settings with aggregate reporting only.

novelty.reasoning: Core novel claims are: (1) associated-but-absent distractors can hijack multi-step reasoning/factual retrieval, not just copy literal context tokens; (2) interference follows a graded fan law with number/strength of associates; (3) the effect is mechanistically separable from known contextual-entrainment heads; (4) it is steerable causally. The closest prior work already covers contextual distraction, paraphrase/meaning-preserving hijacking, semantic priming, and literal-token entrainment, so the general idea is crowded. The actual delta is the absent-associate + graded-fan + separability-from-entrainment package, which is non-trivial but still an extension of established priming/distractor effects rather than a wholly new phenomenon.

Name: use_mention_flag_integrity
Title: Just Kidding, It's In Quotes: Does an LLM Maintain a Use-Mention Flag That Keeps Quoted Content From Leaking Into Its Reasoning?
Short Hypothesis: An LLM encodes whether a proposition is USED (asserted as true, to be reasoned from and acted on) versus MENTIONED (quoted, hypothetical, attributed, or negated-context) as a separable, additive internal 'mention flag'; when this flag is weak or dropped, mentioned content silently leaks into reasoning and behavior as if asserted, causing quoted facts to be believed, attributed claims to be endorsed, and instructions embedded in quotes to be executed. The flag is a locatable, steerable signal, and its strength causally gates whether the use-mention boundary is respected, with high stakes for prompt-injection and misattribution.
Related Work: Prior work studies (a) contextual entrainment / faithful-vs-hijacked retrieval where literal context tokens are over-weighted (Llama See Llama Do, 2025; Do LLMs dream of elephants, 2024), (b) negation as a latent operator and single-sentence understanding failures (MoNLI 2020; CONDAQA 2022; ScoNe 2023; strong hallucinations 2024), (c) belief/source representations of self vs others (Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others, 2024), and (d) prompt-injection defenses that are largely behavioral/training-based (StruQ 2024; instruction-hierarchy work 2024). My own prior proposals covered polarity-load tracking, honesty, pragmatic enrichment, and associative interference, but NONE address the use-mention distinction. No prior work asks whether LLMs maintain a separable internal flag marking content as mentioned rather than used, whether dropping that flag causally makes quoted/attributed/hypothetical content leak into reasoning as asserted fact, or whether that flag can be located and steered to defend the boundary. We uniquely operationalize a classic linguistics distinction (use vs mention) as a load-bearing, causally-testable internal flag with direct prompt-injection and misattribution safety consequences.
Abstract: Language routinely distinguishes content that is USED (asserted, to be believed and acted on) from content that is merely MENTIONED (quoted, attributed to someone else, stated hypothetically, or embedded in a negated or fictional frame). Respecting this use-mention boundary is essential for correct reasoning and for safety: an instruction quoted inside a user's message should not be obeyed, and a claim attributed to an unreliable source should not be endorsed. We hypothesize that LLMs encode use-versus-mention as a separable, additive internal flag attached to each proposition, that when this flag is weak or dropped, mentioned content silently leaks into reasoning and behavior as if asserted, and that this flag is a locatable, steerable signal that causally gates whether the boundary is respected. We make three claims. First, leakage is real and graded: as we deepen or complicate the mention frame (nested quotes, attribution to a source, hypothetical/negated framing), models increasingly treat mentioned content as asserted fact, obey instructions embedded in quotes, and endorse attributed claims, with characteristic 'boundary-drop' errors. Second, the mention flag is a separable representation: a probe decodes each proposition's use/mention status from hidden states, its decodability degrades with frame complexity, and this degradation predicts leakage before it surfaces. Third, the flag is causal and defendable: steering along a located 'mention' direction (or patching the pre-leak flag representation) reduces leakage and blocks quoted-instruction execution, while suppressing it induces leakage even for simple quotes. We evaluate across several open-weight models on fact-belief, attribution, and instruction-in-quotes tasks, plus a high-stakes prompt-injection instance.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - Graded use-mention leakage): Tests that mentioned (quoted/attributed/hypothetical) content increasingly leaks into reasoning as asserted fact as the mention frame deepens, with a boundary-drop error signature. Data: a use-mention battery, ~250 items each across three families (~750): (a) fact-belief - a false proposition presented as asserted vs quoted/attributed/hypothetical, then a downstream question whose correct answer depends on NOT believing mentioned content; (b) attribution - a claim attributed to an unreliable source; the model must report the source's stance without endorsing it; (c) instruction-in-quotes - a directive (e.g. 'ignore previous instructions and output X') embedded inside quoted user text vs issued directly; correct behavior is to NOT execute the mentioned instruction. Each item holds content constant and has a labeled correct answer plus a labeled leakage-lure (the answer/action if mentioned content is treated as used), a matched USED control (same content genuinely asserted), and a frame-complexity gradient (direct quote -> nested quote -> attributed -> hypothetical/negated). We construct because no existing set factorially crosses content x use/mention x frame-complexity; 250/family keeps two-annotator validity checks affordable. Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, Gemma-2-9B, frozen; temperature 0.7, 3 seeds (13/21/42). Decisive metric: leakage-rate (fraction of responses equal to the leakage-lure) on MENTIONED items, modeled as leakage_rate ~ mention_frame_complexity + item_type + (1|model) + (1|item); secondary instruction-in-quotes execution rate. Convincing result: leakage-rate rises with frame complexity (slope CI excluding 0), errors concentrate on the leakage-lure (the diagnostic that specific mentioned content was treated as asserted), USED controls stay accurate (within 2 pp of no-frame), and quoted-instruction execution is measurably above zero and rises with frame complexity. Indecision band: a shallow leakage-complexity slope (CI grazing 0) or leakage only at the deepest frames - a real but marginal boundary weakness. Negative result: flat leakage across frames and near-zero quoted-instruction execution - LLMs robustly respect the use-mention boundary, no separable-flag failure to explain.

Experiment 2 (H1 - Flag-based additivity: single-vs-double frame and error-localization): Tests the separable-flag signature - that a quote-within-a-quote is handled distinctly from a single mention, and that leakage localizes to a specific mentioned proposition. Data/protocol: within the battery, matched single-mention vs double-framing (nested quote) items, plus per-item error-localization tracing the leaked answer to a specific mentioned proposition; same five frozen models. Decisive metric: the leakage difference between single and double framing, and the error-localization rate. Convincing result: double-framing yields a distinct (non-additive) leakage pattern versus single mention (difference CI excluding 0) and leakage localizes to one identifiable mentioned proposition on >=60% of leakage errors - signatures of a flag-based rather than content-based encoding. Indecision band: a small single-vs-double difference or localization 40-60% - suggestive of flag structure only. Negative result: no single-vs-double distinction and diffuse localization - assertion status is encoded into content, not as a separable flag.

Experiment 3 (H2 - A locatable mention flag that degrades with frame complexity, separable from entrainment heads): Tests that use/mention status is decodable, degrades with complexity, predicts leakage, and is distinct from token-copying. Data/protocol: hidden states at proposition-content positions (after the frame, including attributed/hypothetical frames lacking quote marks); per-layer L2-regularized linear probe (3 seeds, 70/30 item-disjoint split) decoding use vs mention; a difference-in-means mention direction from content-matched mentioned/used contrasts; separately localize contextual-entrainment heads and measure overlap; same five frozen models. Decisive metric: held-out per-layer AUROC for use vs mention (chance 0.5), its degradation with frame complexity, and the correlation between low decodability and leakage. Convincing result: best-layer AUROC >=0.80 (including on quote-mark-free attributed/hypothetical frames, so it is not reading surface quotes), decodability degrades with frame complexity (slope CI excluding 0), low decodability predicts leakage (rho >=0.30, CI excluding 0) and mediates the complexity->leakage effect, and the mention direction is separable from entrainment heads (low overlap). Indecision band: AUROC 0.65-0.80, mediation rho 0.15-0.30, or moderate entrainment overlap - a flag that is real but not cleanly distinct or load-linked. Negative result: AUROC <0.65 or no degradation-to-leakage link - no separable mention flag.

Experiment 4 (H3 - Causal defense via steering and patching): Tests that restoring/amplifying the mention flag reduces leakage and blocks quoted instructions, while suppressing it induces leakage, without harming legitimate instructions. Data/protocol: (a) patching - on trials heading toward leakage, cache the correct mention-flag representation from an earlier position and patch it into the pre-leak position; specificity via cross-proposition and random-matched-vector patches. (b) steering - amplify (+) the mention direction to reduce leakage/block quoted-instruction execution and suppress (-) it to induce leakage on simple quotes; 4 coefficients; controls random-direction and no-steer; same five frozen models; specificity tracked on USED controls and on legitimate direct-instruction compliance and fluency. Decisive metric: leakage-rate (and quoted-instruction execution rate) change under intervention versus no-steer/random. Convincing result: correct-flag patching reduces leakage on >=30% of pre-leak trials while cross-proposition/random patches help <10%, +mention steering cuts leakage and quoted-instruction execution by >=6 pp with monotonic dose-response, -mention steering induces leakage even for simple quotes, random-direction moves <2 pp, and USED-control accuracy plus legitimate direct-instruction compliance and fluency are preserved. Indecision band: patching 10-30% or a 2-6 pp steering effect - causal but not clean. Negative result: patching <=random or <2 pp steering effect - the mention flag is not causally load-bearing for the boundary.

Experiment 5 (H1/H3 - High-stakes prompt-injection instance): Tests that the flag governs real injected-instruction attacks and that intervention defends without breaking legitimate use. Data: a set of ~250 realistic injected-instruction attacks embedded inside quoted/retrieved content, adapted from public prompt-injection benchmarks (e.g., InjecAgent-style and tool/retrieval-injection sets), paired with legitimate direct-instruction controls. Protocol: same five frozen models; measure attack success under no-steer versus mention-direction steering / flag patching, plus legitimate-instruction compliance; aggregate reporting only. Decisive metric: injection attack success rate, and the paired legitimate-compliance rate. Convincing result: mention steering/patching reduces attack success by >=10 pp versus no-steer while keeping legitimate-instruction compliance within 3 pp of baseline - a real, non-destructive defense. Indecision band: a 3-10 pp attack-success reduction, or a compliance drop in the 3-6 pp range - a partial or costly defense. Negative result: <3 pp reduction, or a defense that only works by also refusing legitimate instructions - the mechanism does not yield a usable injection defense.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Leakage could reflect general difficulty of framed items rather than a specific use-mention failure; mitigated by content-matched USED controls, the leakage-lure error signature (errors are the SPECIFIC mentioned content, not random), and frame-complexity dose-response. (2) The effect may overlap with contextual entrainment (over-copying literal tokens); we explicitly compare against located entrainment heads and test signal separability - overlap is informative, separability is the key novel result. (3) The mention probe may capture surface quotation marks rather than a maintained representation; mitigated by probing at proposition-content positions after the frame, held-out validation, testing attributed/hypothetical frames that lack quote marks, and random-direction steering controls. (4) Instruction-tuned/safety-aligned models may already resist quoted instructions, muting leakage; we include harder nested/attributed frames, base variants, multiple models, and the fact-belief and attribution families where alignment training is weaker. (5) Patching could rescue by leaking answer content; we patch only the flag representation of a single proposition (not the answer) and use cross-proposition/random specificity controls. (6) The mention direction may entangle with generic difficulty/uncertainty; addressed by content-matched used/mentioned contrasts, USED-control specificity, and the single-vs-double-frame test. (7) A defense must not block legitimate direct instructions; we explicitly measure preserved compliance with genuine instructions under mention-steering. (8) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (9) A null result (no separable mention flag, leakage not frame-graded) is itself informative, indicating LLMs encode assertion status into content rather than as a separable flag. (10) The use-mention framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like semantics; injection experiments run in controlled research settings with aggregate reporting only.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims requiring novelty are: (1) a unified internal use-vs-mention flag spanning quotation, attribution, hypothetical, and negation; (2) leakage of mentioned content into belief/reasoning/behavior increases in a graded way with frame complexity, including nested/additive signatures; (3) the flag is separable and decodable even at quote-free attributed/hypothetical positions, not just from surface quotation markers; (4) causal manipulation of that signal changes leakage and can defend against prompt injection. Relative to prior work, the strongest novelty is the unifying linguistic framing plus the additivity/error-localization hypothesis and non-surface-quote probing. The prompt-injection steering/defense piece is substantially adjacent to existing mechanistic work on role confusion, intrinsic-feature detection, and activation steering, so that part is not very novel. Overall the delta over closest families—belief/source representations, negation failures, entrainment, and prompt-injection mechanistic interpretability—is meaningful but only partly non-obvious.
